text:
### Gestational diabetes (GDM): screening, risk factors, management, glycaemic goals, complications and preconception plan

**Screening**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Screening | Universal screening (every pregnant woman) is recommended. If the woman has more than one risk factor, do an RBS/FBS at first contact. Screening should be done at 24-28 weeks (or at first contact if the patient presents late). Perform a 75 g OGTT: administer 75 g of glucose orally after an 8-hr overnight fast and measure blood glucose after 1 hour and 2 hours (1 standard level teaspoon = 5 g). | (same as left) |

**Risk factors for GDM**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Risk factors | Previous GDM; maternal age > 35 years; family history of diabetes (first-degree relative); obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m2); previous macrosomia (birthweight > 4000 g); polycystic ovary syndrome; iatrogenic: glucocorticoids and antipsychotic medication; hypertension. | Intermediate hyperglycaemia or impaired glucose tolerance: HbA1c ≥ 5.7%, impaired glucose tolerance or impaired fasting glucose. HbA1c >6.5%: diagnosis of pre-existing diabetes. Note: symptoms may be non-specific. |

**Management of GDM**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifestyle modification | Exercise 30-60 min moderate intensity. Diet: regular meal plan; 3 moderate-sized meals, 4 snacks; low sugar. Pharmacotherapy: see the GDM pharmacotherapy dosing schedule. | (same as left) |
| Glycaemic goal | Fasting and pre-prandial blood glucose <95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L). One-hour postprandial <140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L). Two-hour postprandial <120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L). Check HbA1c every 4-6 weeks; goal below 6.5%. | (same as left) |

**Complications**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Short term | Maternal-neonatal: preeclampsia; gestational hypertension; hydramnios; urinary tract/vaginal infections; caesarean delivery; traumatic labour/perineal tears; postpartum haemorrhage; difficulty initiating and/or maintaining breastfeeding. | Fetal: stillbirth or neonatal death; preterm birth; congenital malformations; macrosomia; cardiomyopathy; birth trauma (shoulder dystocia, bone fracture or brachial plexus injury); hypoglycaemia; hyperbilirubinaemia; respiratory distress syndrome. |
| Long term | Maternal-neonatal: recurrence of GDM; type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension; ischaemic heart disease; non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; dyslipidaemia; chronic kidney disease; metabolic syndrome; hyperinsulinaemia. | Fetal: childhood obesity; excess abdominal adiposity; higher blood pressure; possible earlier-onset cardiovascular disease; possible attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder; autism spectrum disorder. |

**Preconception plan**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prior to pregnancy | Optimize modifiable risk factors (e.g. BMI, diet, physical activity). Screen glycaemia in high-risk women. For pre-existing DM: maintain HbA1c below 6% with appropriate drugs (insulin and metformin). Screen for complications. | (same as left) |
| During pregnancy | Healthy diet and regular exercise unless there are obstetric contraindications. Possible personalized gestational weight gain. High-risk women: detect early DM in pregnancy (if preconception screening positive). Follow the protocol for all at 24-28 weeks according to recommended screening and diagnostic criteria. Delivery at 38 weeks is advised if sugars are well controlled; if poorly controlled, consult a specialist on timing of delivery. Consider steroids for lung maturation if early delivery is indicated. If steroids are given at any point in pregnancy, anticipate difficult glycaemic control; insulin therapy is advised. Aim for blood glucose 4-7 mmol/L during active labour and delivery. Anticipate maternal and fetal/neonatal complications at delivery and plan for necessary interventions. | (same as left) |
| Postpartum | Early postpartum OGTT to assess glucose status. Regular long-term follow-up focused on diabetes and cardiovascular risk factor modification. Family lifestyle support: optimizing diet, physical activity, and weight in the offspring. | (same as left) |

**Complications**

| Topic | Details | Further details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Short term | Maternal-neonatal: preeclampsia; gestational hypertension; hydramnios; urinary tract/vaginal infections; caesarean delivery; traumatic labour/perineal tears; postpartum haemorrhage; difficulty initiating and/or maintaining breastfeeding. | Fetal: stillbirth or neonatal death; preterm birth; congenital malformations; macrosomia; cardiomyopathy; birth trauma (shoulder dystocia, bone fracture or brachial plexus injury); hypoglycaemia; hyperbilirubinaemia; respiratory distress syndrome. |

| Topic | Details | Further details |

html:
Gestational diabetes (GDM): screening, risk factors, management, glycaemic goals, complications and preconception plan
TopicDetailsFurther details
Screening
ScreeningUniversal screening (every pregnant woman) is recommended. If the woman has more than one risk factor, do an RBS/FBS at first contact. Screening should be done at 24-28 weeks (or at first contact if the patient presents late). Perform a 75 g OGTT: administer 75 g of glucose orally after an 8-hr overnight fast and measure blood glucose after 1 hour and 2 hours (1 standard level teaspoon = 5 g).
Risk factors for GDM
Risk factorsPrevious GDM; maternal age > 35 years; family history of diabetes (first-degree relative); obesity (BMI > 30 kg/m2); previous macrosomia (birthweight > 4000 g); polycystic ovary syndrome; iatrogenic: glucocorticoids and antipsychotic medication; hypertension.Intermediate hyperglycaemia or impaired glucose tolerance: HbA1c ≥ 5.7%, impaired glucose tolerance or impaired fasting glucose. HbA1c >6.5%: diagnosis of pre-existing diabetes. Note: symptoms may be non-specific.
Management of GDM
Lifestyle modificationExercise 30-60 min moderate intensity. Diet: regular meal plan; 3 moderate-sized meals, 4 snacks; low sugar. Pharmacotherapy: see the GDM pharmacotherapy dosing schedule.
Glycaemic goalFasting and pre-prandial blood glucose <95 mg/dL (5.3 mmol/L). One-hour postprandial <140 mg/dL (7.8 mmol/L). Two-hour postprandial <120 mg/dL (6.7 mmol/L). Check HbA1c every 4-6 weeks; goal below 6.5%.
Complications
Short termMaternal-neonatal: preeclampsia; gestational hypertension; hydramnios; urinary tract/vaginal infections; caesarean delivery; traumatic labour/perineal tears; postpartum haemorrhage; difficulty initiating and/or maintaining breastfeeding.Fetal: stillbirth or neonatal death; preterm birth; congenital malformations; macrosomia; cardiomyopathy; birth trauma (shoulder dystocia, bone fracture or brachial plexus injury); hypoglycaemia; hyperbilirubinaemia; respiratory distress syndrome.
Long termMaternal-neonatal: recurrence of GDM; type 2 diabetes mellitus; hypertension; ischaemic heart disease; non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; dyslipidaemia; chronic kidney disease; metabolic syndrome; hyperinsulinaemia.Fetal: childhood obesity; excess abdominal adiposity; higher blood pressure; possible earlier-onset cardiovascular disease; possible attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder; autism spectrum disorder.
Preconception plan
Prior to pregnancyOptimize modifiable risk factors (e.g. BMI, diet, physical activity). Screen glycaemia in high-risk women. For pre-existing DM: maintain HbA1c below 6% with appropriate drugs (insulin and metformin). Screen for complications.
During pregnancyHealthy diet and regular exercise unless there are obstetric contraindications. Possible personalized gestational weight gain. High-risk women: detect early DM in pregnancy (if preconception screening positive). Follow the protocol for all at 24-28 weeks according to recommended screening and diagnostic criteria. Delivery at 38 weeks is advised if sugars are well controlled; if poorly controlled, consult a specialist on timing of delivery. Consider steroids for lung maturation if early delivery is indicated. If steroids are given at any point in pregnancy, anticipate difficult glycaemic control; insulin therapy is advised. Aim for blood glucose 4-7 mmol/L during active labour and delivery. Anticipate maternal and fetal/neonatal complications at delivery and plan for necessary interventions.
PostpartumEarly postpartum OGTT to assess glucose status. Regular long-term follow-up focused on diabetes and cardiovascular risk factor modification. Family lifestyle support: optimizing diet, physical activity, and weight in the offspring.

text:
### Gestational DM pharmacotherapy dosing schedule: metformin and insulin (starting dose, titration, timing, maximum), glucose targets and postpartum

**Metformin (oral, first line)**

| Agent | Indication | Starting dose | Titration | Timing | Max dose / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metformin 500 mg | Lifestyle measures failed after 1-2 weeks; FBG ≥5.3 or 2-hr PPG ≥6.7 mmol/L | 500 mg once daily | Add 500 mg every 1-2 weeks as tolerated | With evening meal | 2000-2500 mg/day in 2-3 divided doses |
| Metformin (week 2) | Targets not met on 500 mg daily | 500 mg twice daily | Increase to 3x daily if still not at target by week 3 | Morning + evening meal | ~46% will still require insulin: reassess every 1-2 weeks |

**Insulin (injectable, gold standard)**

| Agent | Indication | Starting dose | Titration | Timing | Max dose / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NPH insulin (Humulin N / Insulatard) | Fasting hyperglycaemia: FBG ≥5.3 mmol/L despite metformin | 0.1-0.2 units/kg at bedtime | Increase by 2 units every 3 days until FBG <5.3 mmol/L | Bedtime (22:00-23:00) | Formulary standard in SA & Eswatini public sector |
| Regular insulin (Actrapid / Humulin R) | Postprandial hyperglycaemia: 2-hr PPG ≥6.7 mmol/L | 4 units before highest-carb meal | Increase by 2 units every 3 days until 2-hr PPG <6.7 mmol/L | 30 min before meal | Extend to all 3 meals if multiple postprandial readings elevated |
| Basal-bolus (NPH + regular) | Both fasting & postprandial elevated | NPH 0.1-0.2 u/kg bedtime + 4 u regular before meals | Titrate each component separately; 2 units every 3 days | NPH at bedtime; regular 30 min pre-meal | Most physiological regimen; preferred for poorly controlled GDM |
| Insulin (specialist) | Severe: FBG ≥7.0 mmol/L at diagnosis | 0.2-0.3 u/kg/day total; split 2/3 AM + 1/3 PM (NPH) | Adjust based on full daily glucose profile | Split dose AM + bedtime | Refer to specialist (Mbabane GH or RFM Hospital in Eswatini) |

**Glucose targets & monitoring**

| Agent | Indication | Starting dose | Titration | Timing | Max dose / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Targets | Fasting BG < 5.3 mmol/L; 1-hr postprandial < 7.8 mmol/L; 2-hr postprandial < 6.7 mmol/L | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) |

**Postpartum**

| Agent | Indication | Starting dose | Titration | Timing | Max dose / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| All agents | Discontinue ALL pharmacotherapy at delivery | — | 75 g OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum to screen for persistent T2DM | — | Annual fasting glucose screening recommended long-term |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetes in Special Populations > Diabetes in HIV > Drug interactions between antidiabetic agents and ARVs
text:
### Drug interactions between antidiabetic agents and antiretrovirals (ARVs) (source: University of Liverpool hiv-druginteractions.org)

Diabetes in HIV: a dose adjustment of metformin should be considered when co-administering DTG with metformin to maintain glycaemic control. Monitor renal function and blood glucose when metformin and DTG are co-administered; patients with moderate renal impairment may be at increased risk of lactic acidosis due to increased metformin concentrations.

| Antidiabetic agent | TDF/TAF | AZT | 3TC | FTC | EFV | NVP | DTG | LPV/r | ATV/r | DRV/r |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metformin | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ CAUTION: metformin levels increased (limit metformin to 1,000 mg/day; monitor renal function) | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction |
| Glibenclamide | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Glipizide | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Gliquidone | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Gliclazide | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |
| Glimepiride | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | No interaction | ↑ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | No interaction | No interaction | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment | ↓ potential interaction: may need sulfonylurea dose adjustment |

Key: no interaction. Potential interaction with increased (↑) or decreased (↓) levels of the sulfonylurea, which may require dose adjustment: monitor blood glucose and adjust the sulfonylurea dosage as needed. CAUTION when co-administering metformin with DTG: metformin levels are increased and dose reduction of metformin should be considered. The US prescribing information recommends limiting the total daily dose of metformin to 1,000 mg when co-administered with DTG. Renal monitoring is recommended, as PLHIV with renal impairment are at increased risk of lactic acidosis due to increased metformin levels in the presence of DTG.
*Essential medicines list included atenolol, metoprolol, carvedilol as alternatives (as printed under the table). Refer to National HIV Management Guidelines.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetes in Special Populations > Diabetic emergencies in special populations
text:
### Diabetic emergencies (DKA/HHS) in special populations: HIV/TB co-infection, resource-limited settings, pregnancy, elderly

Diabetes and TB: anti-TB drugs can influence the metabolism of anti-diabetic medications. Rifampicin induces cytochrome P450 and increases the metabolism of most oral hypoglycaemic agents, which may worsen hyperglycaemia. Isoniazid inhibits cytochrome P450 and prolongs the effect of oral anti-diabetic drugs. Bedaquiline is also an enzyme inducer and reduces the effect of antidiabetic drugs.

| Population | Considerations |
| --- | --- |
| HIV/TB co-infection | Screen for HIV if status unknown (rapid test on admission). Immune reconstitution can unmask T1DM. ARVs (especially older PI-based) can cause insulin resistance. Opportunistic infections (PCP, cryptococcal, TB) are common DKA precipitants. Maintain ARTs during crisis; liaise with HIV team. |
| Resource-limited settings | No blood ketones: use urine ketones (≥2+ = significant). No VBG: treat on clinical picture + glucose + ketones. No syringe pump: 50 units in 500 ml NS (0.1 unit/ml) + drip control. No 0.45% NaCl: use 0.9% NaCl throughout with closer monitoring. Validate POC glucose meters for high glucose ranges >30 mmol/L. |
| Pregnancy | DKA can occur at lower glucose (euglycaemic DKA in pregnancy). Involve obstetric team immediately. Fetal monitoring from 24 weeks onwards. Higher insulin requirements: do not underdose. Avoid bicarbonate unless pH <7.0. |
| Elderly patients (HHS) | Reduced physiological reserve: higher risk of fluid overload. More gradual fluid replacement over 48-72 hours. Increased thromboembolic risk: early LMWH prophylaxis. Exclude silent MI, stroke, UTI, pneumonia as precipitant. Assess cognition, falls risk, social support before discharge. |

text:
### Risk factors for osteoporosis and fragility fractures (lifestyle, genetic, diseases, miscellaneous)

| Category | Risk factors |
| --- | --- |
| Lifestyle factors | Alcohol (two or more drinks per day)\*\*; smoking\*\*; low calcium intake; inadequate physical activity; immobilisation; vitamin D insufficiency; malnutrition; low body mass (BMI < 20)\*\*; falling; high salt/protein intake; high caffeine intake; excessive exercise; excess vitamin A; vitamin C, K, B6 and B12 deficiencies; trace element deficiencies |
| Genetic and ethnic factors | Elderly females\*\*; white, Asian and mixed race; family history of hip fracture\*\*; osteogenesis imperfecta; Marfan syndrome; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome; haemochromatosis; porphyria; homocystinuria; idiopathic hypercalciuria; Gaucher's disease; Riley-Day syndrome; Menkes disease |

**Diseases**

| Category | Risk factors |
| --- | --- |
| Hypogonadism | Premature menopause; anorexia nervosa/bulimia; athlete's amenorrhoea; delayed puberty; Turner's syndrome; Klinefelter's syndrome; Kallmann's syndrome |
| Gastrointestinal disorders | Gastric bypass; coeliac disease; gastrectomy; inflammatory bowel disease; chronic liver disease; pancreatic disease |
| Endocrinopathies | Cushing's syndrome; diabetes mellitus; hyperthyroidism; acromegaly; Addison's disease; prolactinoma |
| Haematological disorders | Multiple myeloma; systemic mastocytosis; thalassaemia; leukaemia and lymphomas; sickle cell disease; haemophilia |
| Rheumatology and immunology | Rheumatoid arthritis\*\*; psoriasis; systemic lupus erythematosus; ankylosing spondylitis |
| Miscellaneous | Alcoholism; malignancy; fracture after age 40 years\*\*; parenteral nutrition; amyloidosis; sarcoidosis; post-transplant bone disease; organ failure (lung, liver, kidney, heart); pregnancy-associated osteoporosis; bone-toxic drugs (see drugs table) |

### Drugs associated with increased risk of osteoporosis and of falling (fracture risk)

| Risk | Drugs |
| --- | --- |
| Increase risk of osteoporosis | Glucocorticoids; excessive thyroid replacement therapy; anticonvulsants\*; thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone); aromatase inhibitors; gonadotrophin-releasing hormone analogues; chemotherapy; immunosuppressives (cyclosporine, methotrexate); heparin/warfarin; chronic lithium therapy; prolonged parenteral nutrition; aluminium |

*May also cause osteomalacia.

x = do at this visit; blank = not routinely (some items, e.g. 25OHD, nystagmus, eGFR and ECG, have no marks in the PDF).
*Vertigo assessment: clinician may use any of: (1) the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre: the patient sits at the edge of the bed and the examiner turns the patient's head 30-45 degrees to the side being tested; the patient keeps eyes open on a stable point and then quickly lies supine with the neck hyperextended; horizontal nystagmus denotes a positive test (warn the patient it can induce vertigo). (2) Orthostatic blood pressure testing: a drop in systolic BP of more than 20 mmHg from lying to standing is significant for a postural drop (dehydration or autonomic dysfunction, which can cause vertigo). (3) Head impulse test: the patient looks at the examiner's nose and the examiner quickly turns the head 10-20 degrees; it is abnormal if the eyes move rapidly and repetitively, failing to re-fixate on the examiner's nose (disrupted vestibulo-ocular reflex).

(2) Orthostatic blood pressure testing: a drop in systolic BP of more than 20 mmHg from lying to standing is significant for a postural drop (dehydration or autonomic dysfunction, which can cause vertigo). text:
### Classification of osteoporosis by bone mineral density (BMD) T-score

| Definition | Criteria |
| --- | --- |
| Normal | BMD or BMC value (measured with DXA at either the spine, total hip or femur neck) within 1 SD of the young adult reference mean (T-score\* at or above -1.0) |
| Low bone mass | BMD or BMC value more than 1 SD but less than 2.5 SD below the young adult mean (osteopenia; T-score between -1.0 and -2.5) |
| Osteoporosis | BMD or BMC value 2.5 SD or more below the young adult mean |
| Severe osteoporosis | BMD or BMC value more than 2.5 SD below the young adult mean, plus one or more fragility fractures |

**Note:** These criteria were updated in 2008 and differ from those proposed by the WHO in 1994 by specifying a single reference site (the femoral neck) to measure BMD, providing a young normal reference range for women and men (the NHANES III reference data for femoral neck measurements in women aged 20-29 years), and by accommodating diagnostic criteria for men. *When standard deviation (SD) units are used in relation to the young healthy adult population, this is referred to as the T-score.

text:
### Algorithm for the management of osteoporosis in post-menopausal women and men aged 50 years and older

Clinical risk factors (CRFs): advanced age; prior fracture; family history; excessive leanness (printed 'excessive learners'); diet/alcohol/smoking; fall propensity; secondary osteoporoses.

Start: women and men with CRFs. Prior osteoporotic fracture?
- Yes: consider specific treatment/prophylaxis.
- No: measure BMD. By T-score:
  - T-score ≤ -2.5: consider specific treatment/prophylaxis.
  - T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 (printed '< -10 to > -2.5'; consider FRAX):
      - > 75 years: consider specific treatment/prophylaxis.
      - 65-75 years + ≥ 2 CRFs: yes: consider specific treatment/prophylaxis; no: individualised assessment of CRFs + BMD.
      - > 60 years: individualised assessment of CRFs + BMD.
    Individualised assessment outcome: yes: consider specific treatment/prophylaxis; uncertain (?): bone turnover markers (BTMs) or reassess in 24 months; no: lifestyle changes only.
  - T-score ≥ -1.0: lifestyle changes only.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Osteoporosis and Fragility Fractures > Pharmacological management of osteoporosis
text:
### Pharmacological management of osteoporosis: drug classes, typical dosage and common side effects

Non-pharmacological management: postmenopausal women and men aged ≥50 years with osteoporosis or at risk of fragility fracture are recommended: a healthy, nutrient-rich balanced diet; adequate calcium intake (minimum 700 mg daily), preferably from diet or otherwise by supplementation; vitamin D supplements of at least 800 IU/day if vitamin D insufficiency or risk factors for it are identified; regular weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercise tailored to the individual; advice on smoking and alcohol cessation; a falls assessment for all patients with osteoporosis and fragility fractures, with exercise programmes to improve balance for those at risk.

**Bisphosphonates**

| Drug class and name | Typical dosage | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alendronate (Fosamax) | 70 mg once weekly or 10 mg daily | Oesophageal irritation, musculoskeletal pain, nausea, abdominal pain |
| Risedronate (Actonel) | 35 mg once weekly or 150 mg once monthly | Abdominal pain, musculoskeletal pain, nausea |
| Ibandronate (Boniva) | 150 mg once monthly | Gastrointestinal irritation, musculoskeletal pain |
| Zoledronic acid (Reclast) | 5 mg once annually as an intravenous infusion | Flu-like symptoms, renal impairment, hypocalcaemia |

**Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs)**

| Drug class and name | Typical dosage | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raloxifene (Evista) | 60 mg daily | Hot flashes, leg cramps, increased risk of blood clots |

**Hormone replacement therapy (HRT)**

| Drug class and name | Typical dosage | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conjugated estrogens (Premarin) | Dosage varies | Increased risk of breast cancer, blood clots, stroke, and other side effects |
| Calcitonin (Miacalcin) | Typically 200 IU daily as nasal spray | Nasal irritation, epistaxis (nosebleeds), flushing |

**Parathyroid hormone analogs**

| Drug class and name | Typical dosage | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Teriparatide (Forteo) | 20 mcg once daily (subcutaneous) | Dizziness, leg cramps, injection site reactions |
| Abaloparatide (Tymlos) | 80 mcg once daily (subcutaneous) | Hypercalcaemia, dizziness, nausea, headache |

**Monoclonal antibodies**

| Drug class and name | Typical dosage | Common side effects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Denosumab (Prolia) | 60 mg once every six months (subcutaneous) | Infections, back pain, dermatitis, hypocalcaemia |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hypothyroidism > Diagnostic criteria
text:
### Hypothyroidism symptoms by system affected (diagnostic criteria)

The symptoms of hypothyroidism depend on the deficiency of thyroid hormone, but can include the following. Investigations: thyroid hormone profile. Diagnosis: may be primary or secondary hypothyroidism.

| System affected | Common symptoms |
| --- | --- |
| General & metabolic | Fatigue; weight gain; trouble tolerating cold; slowed heart rate; increased cholesterol levels |
| Skin, hair & nails | Dry, rough skin; dry or thinning hair; hair loss |
| Musculoskeletal | Joint pain; muscle pain or weakness |
| Reproductive (female) | Heavy or irregular menstrual periods; fertility problems |
| Neurological & psychological | Depression; memory loss |
| Gastrointestinal & voice | Constipation; hoarse voice |

### Congenital hypothyroidism: clinical features by category

| Category | Features |
| --- | --- |
| General | Lethargy, somnolence, delayed physical and mental development, subnormal temperature |
| Skin/hair | Dry skin, coarse and scanty hair |
| Facial/head | Wide open fontanelles, enlarged tongue (macroglossia), periorbital oedema, coarse cry, hoarse voice, goitre |
| Growth/development | Delayed dentition, short and thick neck, broad hands, hypotonia |
| Cardiovascular | Bradycardia |
| Abdomen | Abdominal distension, umbilical hernia, constipation |
| Extremities | Oedema of extremities and genitals |
| Haematologic | Anaemia |
| Respiratory | Apnoeic episodes |
| Feeding | Feeding difficulties |
| Other | Prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hypothyroidism in Older Children and Adolescents > Pharmacological treatment
text:
### Levothyroxine dose by age for hypothyroidism in children and adolescents (oral, once daily on an empty stomach)

Hypothyroidism in older children and adolescents: low growth velocity or short stature with short limbs and a normal or elevated BMI; subtle features include cold intolerance, dry skin, brittle hair, pallor and myxoedema. Investigations: elevated TSH and low thyroxine. Levothyroxine, oral, once daily on an empty stomach. Refer all cases for investigation and initiation of therapy. (Neonates with congenital hypothyroidism: levothyroxine 10-15 mcg/kg once daily, started ideally within the first three weeks of life.)

| Age group | Levothyroxine dose |
| --- | --- |
| 1-6 months | 8-10 mcg/kg |
| 6-12 months | 6-8 mcg/kg |
| 1-5 years | 5-6 mcg/kg |
| 6-12 years | 4-5 mcg/kg |
| >12 years | 2-3 mcg/kg |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism > Diagnostic algorithm for primary hyperthyroidism
text:
### Diagnostic algorithm for primary hyperthyroidism (by radioactive iodine uptake)

Primary hyperthyroidism: ↓ TSH, ↑ free T4, ↑ total T3. Next: radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU).
- Diffuse uptake: homogeneous: Graves' disease; heterogeneous: toxic multinodular goitre.
- Focal uptake: functioning adenoma.
- No uptake: measure serum thyroglobulin: low (↓): thyrotoxicosis factitia; high (↑): thyroiditis, iodine load, or struma ovarii.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism > Management of hyperthyroidism > Antithyroid drug therapy
text:
### Antithyroid drug therapy for hyperthyroidism and thyroid storm: medicines, dosing and comments

| Medicine | Dosing | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Propylthiouracil\* (D) | 500-1000 mg load, then 250 mg 4-hourly | Blocks new hormone synthesis; blocks T4-to-T3 conversion. Breastfeeding clients: propylthiouracil (up to a maximum dose of 450 mg/day). |
| Carbimazole (C) | 40-60 mg/day | Blocks new hormone synthesis. Breastfeeding clients: carbimazole (up to maximum 15 mg/day). |
| Propranolol (A) | 60-80 mg every 4 hours | Consider invasive monitoring in congestive heart failure patients. Blocks T4-to-T3 conversion in high doses. Alternative medicine: esmolol infusion. |
| Iodine (saturated solution of potassium iodide) (B) | 5 drops (0.25 mL or 250 mg) (PO) 6-hourly | Do not start until 1 hour after antithyroid medicines. Blocks new hormone synthesis; blocks thyroid hormone release. |

text:
### Interpreting TSH and FT4/FT3 results (thyroid function test flowchart)

Start with TSH.

TSH low:
- FT4 and/or FT3 high (printed 'Nor FT4 and/or FT3 high'): primary hyperthyroidism. Perform test for TRAb/TSI; consider ordering thyroid scintigraphy. Repeat TFT in four weeks to determine course or impact of treatment. Specialist referral*.
- FT4 and FT3 normal*: subclinical/mild hyperthyroidism. Repeat TSH, FT4 and FT3 in 1-3 months; may require further investigation.
- FT4 and/or FT3 low: discordant: non-thyroidal illness; central hypothyroidism. Repeat TSH, FT4 and FT3 and follow to assess trend; if persistently abnormal, refer for further investigation.

TSH normal: thyroid dysfunction excluded.

TSH high:
- FT4 low: primary hypothyroidism. Repeat TSH and FT4; check anti-TPO; treat with levothyroxine.
- FT4 normal: subclinical/mild hypothyroidism. Repeat in 1-3 months; check anti-TPO antibody; monitor TFT annually if stable; consider treatment with levothyroxine*.
- FT4 high: discordant: TSHoma; thyroid hormone resistance; assay interference. Repeat TSH and FT4 to assess trend; refer for further investigation.

text:
### Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS) for diagnosis of thyroid storm: criteria, points and interpretation

Thyroid storm/thyrotoxic crisis is a rare but potentially life-threatening syndrome of exaggerated hyperthyroidism: hyperthermia, severe tachycardia with or without cardiac failure, severe agitation, possible jaundice, and mental disorientation, culminating in stupor and coma.

| Category | Feature | Criteria (points) | Score range |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Thermoregulatory dysfunction | Temperature (°C) | 37.2-37.7: 5; 37.8-38.3: 10; 38.4-38.8: 15; 38.9-39.4: 20; 39.5-39.9: 25; ≥40.0: 30 | 5-30 |
| Central nervous system effects | Manifestations | Mild (agitation): 10; moderate (delirium, psychosis, extreme lethargy): 20; severe (seizure, coma): 30 | 0-30 |
| Gastrointestinal-hepatic dysfunction | Symptoms | Moderate (diarrhoea, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain): 10; severe (jaundice): 20 | 0-20 |
| Cardiovascular dysfunction | Tachycardia (bpm) | 90-109: 5; 110-119: 10; 120-129: 15; 130-139: 20; ≥140: 25 | 5-25 |
| Cardiovascular dysfunction | Atrial fibrillation | Present: 10 | 0-10 |
| Cardiovascular dysfunction | Congestive heart failure | Mild (pedal oedema): 5; moderate (bibasilar rales): 10; severe (pulmonary oedema): 15 | 0-15 |
| Precipitating event | Trigger (e.g., infection, surgery, trauma, withdrawal of antithyroid drugs) | Present: 10 | 0-10 |

**Note:** Interpretation of total score: ≥45: thyroid storm highly likely; 25-44: impending storm; <25: thyroid storm unlikely.

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism > Management of thyroid storm > Recognition and management (flowchart)
text:
### Thyroid storm: recognition and management (flowchart)

1. Suspect thyroid storm (BWPS ≥45).
2. Identify precipitant(s).
3. Initial stabilization (ABC). Propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole.
4. Block thyroid hormone synthesis (≥ 1 h after ATD): Lugol's iodine 8 drops PO q6-8h, or NaI IV 0.25-0.5 g q6h.
5. Block peripheral effects: propranolol 60-80 mg OG 6-hourly, or 1 mg IV q10min (max 3); hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q8h.
6. Continuous monitoring & support: ECG, vitals, fluid balance, electrolytes. Adjust therapy as needed.

In addition to general supportive measures, therapy should be directed at the thyroid gland and the hypermetabolism and tachycardia. Patients should be monitored in an intensive or high care setting. The underlying precipitant should be actively treated and managed. Prevention is key: correct thyroid function before elective surgery.

text:
### Thyroid storm treatment steps: therapeutic targets, drugs and doses

| Step | Therapeutic target | Drug / intervention | Dose / notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Block thyroid hormone synthesis | Antithyroid drugs (ATDs) | Propylthiouracil (PTU): 500-1000 mg loading, then 250 mg q4h; preferred early as it inhibits T4-to-T3 conversion. Methimazole: 60-80 mg/day if PTU unavailable. | Start immediately on diagnosis |
| Block hormone release (give ≥1 hr after ATD) | Iodine therapy | Lugol's iodine: 8 drops q6-8h. Sodium iodide IV: 0.25-0.5 g q6h. Administer ≥1 hr after ATD to avoid iodine-fuelled synthesis. | Reduces preformed hormone release |
| Block peripheral effects | Beta-blockade; corticosteroid therapy | Propranolol: 60-80 mg PO q6h or 1 mg IV q10min (max 3 doses); esmolol IV infusion is an alternative in heart failure. Hydrocortisone: 100 mg IV q8h (reduces T4-to-T3 conversion and prevents adrenal crisis). | Controls adrenergic effects; protects against adrenal failure |

heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Thyroid Disorders > Hyperthyroidism in Pregnancy > Management of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy
text:
### Management of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy (flowchart)

Two entry points:
- Known hyperthyroidism on ATD and wishing to conceive/pregnant: switch to a 'dose titration' regimen if on 'block and replace'. Use PTU pre-conception and in the 1st trimester; use CBZ (carbimazole) thereafter.
- New diagnosis of hyperthyroidism during pregnancy: commence anti-thyroid medication: PTU in the first trimester, CBZ thereafter.

Both: refer to endocrine physician. Then two parallel tracks:

Track 1 - check TFTs every 4 weeks (and LFTs every 4 weeks if on PTU):
- Free T4 above normal reference range: increase dose of ATD.
- Free T4 at or just above upper end of normal reference range: continue on current dose of ATD.
- Free T4 below upper end of normal reference range: decrease dose of ATD.
Repeat the 4-weekly checks throughout pregnancy. TFTs to be checked 6-8 weeks post-partum (printed 'at first ante-natal check').

Track 2 - check TRAb at 22 weeks and 36 weeks. If TRAb > 2-3 times the upper limit of normal: obstetric ultrasound for monitoring for fetal thyrotoxicosis.

Reference: Girling JC. Thyroid disease in pregnancy. The Obstetrician and Gynaecologist 2008; 10:237-243.

text:
### Hypertension definitions by office/clinic vs home blood pressure (normotensive, sustained, masked, white coat)

Hypertension is defined as a systolic blood pressure [SBP] of 140 mmHg or more, or a diastolic blood pressure [DBP] of 90 mmHg or more.

| Definition | Office/Clinic BP/healthcare setting | Home/non-healthcare setting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normotensive | No Hypertension | No Hypertension |
| Sustained Hypertension | Hypertension | Hypertension |
| Masked Hypertension | No Hypertension | Hypertension |
| White Coat Hypertension | Hypertension | No Hypertension |

text:
### Classification of office BP and definitions of hypertension grades

| Category | Systolic (mmHg) |  | Diastolic (mmHg) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Optimal | <120 | and | <80 |
| Normal | 120-129 | and | 80-84 |
| High-normal | 130-139 | and/or | 85-89 |
| Grade 1 Hypertension | 140-159 | and/or | 90-99 |
| Grade 2 Hypertension | 160-179 | and/or | 100-109 |
| Grade 3 Hypertension | ≥180 | and/or | ≥110 |
| Isolated Systolic Hypertension\* | ≥140 | and | <90 |
| Isolated Diastolic Hypertension\* | <140 | and | ≥90 |

The BP category is defined by the highest level of BP, whether systolic or diastolic.
*Isolated systolic or diastolic hypertension is graded 1, 2 or 3 according to SBP and DBP values in the ranges indicated. The same classification is used for adolescents ≥16 years old.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > How to measure blood pressure correctly
text:
> **How to measure blood pressure correctly: checklist and position**
>
> Checklist:
> - No exercise, smoking, caffeine or food 30 min before
> - Quiet environment
> - Comfortable temperature
> - 3-5 min rest before measurement
> - No talking before or during measurements
> - Take 3 measurements at 1 min intervals and use the average of the last two
> 
> Position (illustrated in the PDF): back supported; suitable cuff size; bare arm resting at heart level; feet flat on floor.
html:
How to measure blood pressure correctly: checklist and position

Checklist:

- No exercise, smoking, caffeine or food 30 min before

- Quiet environment

- Comfortable temperature

- 3-5 min rest before measurement

- No talking before or during measurements

- Take 3 measurements at 1 min intervals and use the average of the last two

Position (illustrated in the PDF): back supported; suitable cuff size; bare arm resting at heart level; feet flat on floor.

### Patient assessment in hypertension: history, examination, tests and tasks at the initial visit, 3-6 monthly and annually

At every visit, patients with hypertension should have a medical history taken, undergo a clinical examination and have blood and urine evaluation done as needed. Follow up management should be individualised.

**Patient History**

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

text:
### Pharmacological management of hypertension: stepwise treatment by age and ethnicity (flowchart, NICE CG34)

Abbreviations: A = ACE inhibitor (consider angiotensin-II receptor antagonist if ACE-intolerant); C = calcium channel blocker; D = thiazide-type diuretic.

- Step 1:
  - Younger than 55 years: A.
  - 55 years or older, or black patients of any age: C or D.
- Step 2 (both groups): A + C or A + D.
- Step 3: A + C + D.
- Step 4: Add further diuretic therapy, or an alpha-blocker, or a beta-blocker. Consider seeking specialist advice.

Black patients are those of African or Caribbean descent, and not mixed-race, Asian or Chinese patients.
Key: ACE = angiotensin-converting enzyme; BHS = British Hypertension Society; NICE = National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. Reproduced with permission from: NICE. CG 34 Hypertension: management of hypertension in adults in primary care. London: NICE, 2006.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > Non-Pharmacological Management of Hypertension
text:
### Non-pharmacological management of hypertension: lifestyle recommendations by risk factor (alcohol, smoking, physical activity, DASH diet) Lifestyle modifications are recommended as they have demonstrated benefit in lowering blood pressure. | Risk Factor | Recommendations | | --- | --- | | Alcohol | If you do not drink alcohol DO NOT START. AVOID or STOP drinking. Alcohol: there is no safe level of alcohol. | | Smoking | Smoking cessation is highly recommended irrespective of conventional or electronic cigarettes. The 5 As of smoking cessation: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange. | | Physical Activity | Advise patients to attain an ideal BMI of 18.5-24.9 kg/m². Recommended: regular aerobic exercise ≥30-60 min/day OR moderate intensity exercise ≥150 min/week.
\*High intensity exercise not recommended for uncontrolled HTN (SBP >160 mmHg). | | Diet | A Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet is recommended and entails:
- Reduce salt intake. Consume ≤5 g (1 teaspoon of table salt per day!)
- Strategies for reduced salt intake: choose unsalted nuts or seeds, dried beans, peas, and lentils; avoid canned vegetables with added salt; keep the saltshaker off the table; avoid salt when cooking or before you taste your food; use spices and herbs to enhance the natural flavours of food; check nutrition labels; avoid processed, prepared, and pre-packaged foods. |

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > Antihypertensive Drug Classes
text:
### Antihypertensive drug classes compared (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazide diuretics): mechanism, benefits, side effects, dosing and notes First line: any of these unless there are compelling contra-indications: CCB (nifedipine, amlodipine); ACE inhibitor (captopril, enalapril, lisinopril); ARB if not on an ACE inhibitor [DO NOT COMBINE THE TWO] (irbesartan, telmisartan, losartan); diuretic (thiazide or thiazide-like: hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide). Second line: beta-blockers (carvedilol, propranolol, nebivolol, metoprolol, labetalol), alpha blockers (prazosin, doxazosin). Third line: aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone). | Drug Class | Example | Mechanism of Action | Key Benefits | Common Side Effects | Dosing and Prescription | Important Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | ACE Inhibitors (ACE-I) | Enalapril, Captopril, Lisinopril | Decreases mortality in HF, effective for hypertension, post-MI LV dysfunction, slows diabetic nephropathy/retinopathy. | Decreases mortality in HF, effective for hypertension, post-MI LV dysfunction, slows diabetic nephropathy/retinopathy. | Hypotension, hyperkalemia, cough (bradykinin-induced), angioedema, fetal anomalies, reversible kidney decline. | Enalapril: 5-40mg once a day
Lisinopril: 5-40mg once a day
Captopril: 12.5-150mg in 2-3 divided doses | Universal in HF treatment; cough is a common reason for discontinuation. Interacts with potassium supplements/sparing diuretics, diuretics, and NSAIDs. | | Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs) | Irbesartan, Valsartan, Telmisartan, Losartan | Bind to and inhibit the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, leading to vasodilation and renal sodium excretion | Effective for hypertension, CKD, slows diabetic nephropathy/retinopathy; alternative to ACE-I for cough. | Generally well tolerated, lower incidence of cough/angioedema than ACE-I, hypotension, renal failure | Valsartan: 80-320mg once a day
Telmisartan: 40-80mg once a day
Irbesartan: 150-300mg once a day
Losartan: 50-100mg once a day | ACE Inhibitors (ACE-I) | | Thiazide Diuretics | Hydrochlorothiazide, Indapamide, Chlorthalidone | Inhibit NaCl reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule; enhance Ca2+ reabsorption. | As effective as other regimens in lowering BP and reducing CV mortality, can regress LV hypertrophy | Increased uric acid, hypokalemia, possible lipid/glucose tolerance changes, impotence (rare at low doses). | Hydrochlorothiazide: 12.5-50mg once a day
Indapamide: 1.5-2.5mg once a day
Chlorthalidone: 25-50mg once a day | Benefits in hypertension are well-established; dose-dependent side effects. Interacts with potassium supplements/sparing |

text:
### Beta-blockers and other antihypertensives (amiloride, spironolactone, clonidine, hydralazine, methyldopa, prazosin): usual dosage and remarks

**Beta-blockers**

| Antihypertensive | Usual dosage |
| --- | --- |
| Atenolol | 25-100mg daily |
| Carvedilol | 12.5-50mg daily in one or two doses |
| Labetalol | 100-200mg twice daily |
| Metoprolol | 50-100mg once or twice daily; CR 23.75-190mg once daily |
| Propranolol | 40-320mg daily in two or three doses |

**Remarks (applies to every row in this section):** Atenolol: Not recommended as monotherapy. Side effects: bradycardia, postural hypotension, worsening of heart failure, bronchospasm, cold extremities

**Other Antihypertensives**

| Antihypertensive | Usual dosage | Remarks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amiloride | 2.5-5mg daily | Action: Aldosterone antagonist or potassium sparing diuretics. Use: resistant hypertension or hyperaldosteronism. Adverse effects: hyperkalemia |
| Spironolactone | 12.5-50mg daily | Action: Aldosterone antagonist or potassium sparing diuretics. Use: resistant hypertension or hyperaldosteronism. Adverse effects: hyperkalemia |
| Clonidine | 50-300mcg daily | Adverse effects: postural hypotension, bradycardia, dry mouth |
| Hydralazine | 50-100mg daily in two doses | Adverse effects: Palpitation, flushing, headache, edema |
| Methyldopa | 250-2000mg daily in two to four doses | Adverse effects: sedation, hepatitis, hemolytic anemia |
| Prazosin | 0.5-20mg daily in two or three doses | Action: selective alpha blocker or peripheral vasodilator. Adverse effects: hypotension |

Other antihypertensives: first prescription should be done by a physician or by a medical officer WITH the physician's discussion.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > Secondary Hypertension
text:
### Secondary hypertension: clinical clues, basic biochemistry and further diagnostic tests by cause (renal, aldosteronism, renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's, coarctation, sleep apnoea, thyroid) Consider screening for secondary hypertension in (1) patients with early onset hypertension (<30 years of age) especially in the absence of hypertension risk factors (obesity, metabolic syndrome, familial history etc.), (2) those with resistant hypertension, (3) individuals with sudden deterioration in BP control, (4) hypertensive urgency and emergency, (5) those presenting with high probability of secondary hypertension based on strong clinical clues. | Secondary Hypertension | Clinical History and Physical Examination | Basic Biochemistry and Urine Analysis | Further Diagnostic Tests | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Renal Parenchymal Disease | - Personal/familial history of CKD | - Proteinuria, hematuria, leukocyturia on dipstick urine analysis
- Decreased estimated GFR | - Kidney ultrasound | | Primary Aldosteronism | - Symptoms of hypokalemia (muscle weakness, muscle cramps, tetany) | - Spontaneous hypokalemia or diuretic-induced hypokalemia on blood biochemistry (50% - 60% of patients are normokalemic)
- Elevated plasma aldosterone-renin activity ratio | - Confirmatory testing (eg, intravenous saline suppression test)
- Imaging of adrenals (adrenal CT)
- Adrenal vein sampling | | Renal Artery Stenosis | - Abdominal bruit
- Bruits over other arteries (ie, carotid and femoral arteries)
- Drop in estimated GFR >30% after exposure to ACE-inhibitors/ARBs
- For suspected atherosclerotic RAS, history of flash pulmonary edema or history of atherosclerotic disease or presence of cardiovascular risk factors
- For suspected fibromuscular dysplasia, young women with onset of hypertension <30 years | - Decrease in estimated GFR | - Imaging of renal arteries (duplex ultrasound, abdominal CT or MR angiograms depending on availability and patient's level of renal function) | | Pheochromocytoma | - Headaches
- Palpitations
- Perspiration
- Pallor
- History of labile hypertension | - Increased plasma levels of metanephrines
- Increased 24-hour urinary fractional excretion of metanephrines and catecholamines | - Abdominal/pelvic CT or MRI | | Cushing's Syndrome and Disease | - Central obesity
- Purple striae
- Facial rubor
- Signs of skin atrophy
- Easy bruising
- Dorsal and supraclavicular fat pad
- Proximal muscle weakness | - Hypokalemia
- Increased late-night salivary cortisol | - Dexamethasone suppression tests
- 24-hour urinary free cortisol
- Abdominal/pituitary imaging | | Coarctation of the Aorta | - Higher blood pressure in upper than lower extremities
- Delayed or absent femoral pulses | | - Echocardiogram
- CT angiogram
- Magnetic resonance angiogram | | Obstructive Sleep Apnea | - Increased BMI
- Snoring
- Daytime sleepiness
- Gasping or choking at night
- Witnessed apneas during sleep
- Nocturia | | - Home sleep apnea testing (e.g., level 3 sleep study)
- Overnight polysomnography testing | | Thyroid Disease | - Symptoms of hyperthyroidism: heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, palpitations
- Symptoms of hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, weight gain, dry brittle hair | - TSH, Free T4 | | **Note:** REFER for further investigation and management of suspected secondary hypertension to a specialist centre with access to appropriate expertise and resources.

text:
### Hypertensive emergency: clinical assessment (symptoms, history, examination, laboratory, bedside and targeted investigations, secondary causes) A hypertensive emergency is the association of substantially elevated BP with acute HMOD (hypertension-mediated organ damage). | Category | Details | | --- | --- | | Symptoms | - Headaches
- Visual disturbances
- Chest pain
- Dyspnoea
- Neurologic symptoms (confusion, focal deficits, seizures)
- Dizziness
- Non-specific complaints (fatigue, malaise, nausea, etc.) | | Medical History | - Pre-existing hypertension
- Onset & duration of current symptoms
- Contributing factors: nonadherence to antihypertensives; lifestyle changes (diet, alcohol, stress); concomitant use of BP-elevating drugs (NSAIDs, corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, sympathomimetics, cocaine, antiangiogenic therapy) | | Physical Examination | - Comprehensive cardiovascular assessment
- Detailed neurologic examination | | Laboratory Analysis | - FBC: haemoglobin, platelets
- Renal function: creatinine, Na+, K+
- Haemolysis markers: LDH, haptoglobin
- Urinalysis: proteinuria, urine sediment | | Bedside/Basic Examinations | - Fundoscopy (haemorrhages, exudates, papilloedema)
- ECG | | Additional/Targeted Investigations | - Troponins → if chest pain
- Chest X-ray → if pulmonary congestion/fluid overload
- Transthoracic echocardiogram → cardiac structure & function
- CT/MRI brain → suspected cerebral haemorrhage, stroke, encephalopathy
- CT-angiography thorax/abdomen → suspected acute aortic disease | | Secondary Causes (20-40% of cases) | - Renal artery stenosis
- Primary aldosteronism
- Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma
- Cushing's syndrome
- Thyroid disease
- Chronic kidney disease |

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > Hypertensive Emergencies > Hypertensive emergencies requiring immediate BP-lowering with IV drug therapy
text:
### Hypertensive emergencies requiring immediate BP lowering with IV drugs: timing, BP target, first-line and alternative treatment by clinical presentation

Management principles: the overall therapeutic goal is a controlled BP reduction to safer levels to prevent or limit further hypertensive damage while avoiding hypotension. The type of acute HMOD is the main determinant of the preferred treatment. Labetalol and nicardipine are generally safe in all hypertensive emergencies. Nitroglycerin and nitroprusside are specifically useful in hypertensive emergencies involving the heart and the aorta.

| Clinical Presentation | Timing and BP Target | First-line Treatment | Alternative |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Malignant hypertension with or without acute renal failure | Several hours. Reduce MAP by 20-25% | Labetalol or Nicardipine | Nitroprusside or Urapidil |
| Hypertensive encephalopathy | Immediately reduce MAP by 20-25% | Labetalol or Nicardipine | Nitroprusside |
| Acute coronary event | Immediately reduce SBP to <140 mmHg | Labetalol or Nicardipine | Nitroprusside |
| Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema | Immediately reduce SBP to <140 mmHg | Nitroprusside or nitroglycerin (with loop diuretic) | Urapidil (with loop diuretic) |
| Acute aortic dissection | Immediately reduce SBP to <120 mmHg and heart rate to <60 bpm | Esmolol plus nitroprusside or nitroglycerin or nicardipine | Labetalol or Metoprolol |
| Eclampsia and severe preeclampsia/HELLP | Immediately reduce SBP to <160 mmHg and DBP to <105 mmHg | Labetalol or nicardipine and magnesium sulphate | Consider delivery |

text:
### IV drugs for hypertensive emergencies: onset, duration, dose, contraindications and adverse effects (esmolol, metoprolol, labetalol, nicardipine, nitroglycerine, nitroprusside, enalaprilat, urapidil, clonidine, phentolamine)

| Drug | Onset of Action | Duration of Action | Dose | Contraindications | Adverse effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Esmolol | 1 min | 10-30 min | 0.5-1 mg/Kg IV bolus, 50-300 mcg/Kg/min IV infusion | Second-degree or third-degree AV block, systolic heart failure, asthma, bradycardia | Bradycardia |
| Metoprolol | 1-2 min | 5-8 h | 2.5-5 mg IV bolus over 2 min; may repeat every 5 min to a maximum dose of 15 mg | Second-degree or third-degree AV block, systolic heart failure, asthma, bradycardia | Bradycardia |
| Labetalol | 5-10 min | 3-6 h | 0-20 mg IV bolus in 1 min; incremental doses ≥20mg may be administered IV at 10 min intervals (max 80 mg) or 1-3 mg/min IV infusion until goal BP is reached | Second-degree or third-degree AV block, systolic heart failure, asthma, bradycardia | Bronchoconstriction, fetal bradycardia |
| Nicardipine | 5-15 min | 4-6 h | 5-15 mg/h IV infusion, starting dose 5 mg/h, increase every 15-30 min with 2.5 mg until goal BP, maximum 15 mg/h | Liver failure | Headache, reflex tachycardia |
| Nitroglycerine | 1-5 min | 5-10 min | 5-200 mcg/min IV infusion, 5 mcg/min increase every min |  | Headache, reflex tachycardia |
| Nitroprusside | Immediate | 1-3 min | 0.3-0.5 mcg/Kg/min IV infusion, increase by 0.5 mcg/Kg/min every 5 min until goal BP (maximum dose 10 mcg/Kg/min) | Liver/kidney failure (relative) | Cyanide intoxication |
| Enalaprilat | 5-15 min | 4-6 h | 0.62-1.25 mg IV bolus given over 5 min every 6h | History of angioedema |  |
| Urapidil | 3-5 min | 4-6 h | 12.5-25 mg IV bolus; 5-40 mg/h as continuous infusion |  |  |
| Clonidine | 30 min | 4-6 h | 0.2-0.5 mcg/Kg/min IV |  | Sedation, rebound hypertension |
| Phentolamine | 1-2 min | 10-30 min | 1-5 mg IV bolus or continuous IV infusion at a rate of 0.5-20 mcg/Kg/min |  | Tachyarrhythmia, chest pain |

### Management by CVD risk level (>20%, 10-20%, 5-10%, <5%): counselling, when to treat hypertension, statin

| Action | >20% | 10 - 20% | 5 - 10% | <5% |

| Counsel | Consultation on diet (which includes lipid-lowering diet), physical activity, smoking cessation and avoiding harmful use of alcohol | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) |
| Treat HTN | Consider drug treatment if persistent BP ≥ 130/80 mmHg | Consider drug treatment if persistent BP ≥ 130/80 mmHg | Consider if persistent BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg | Consider if BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg |
| Lipid lowering | Give a statin | Give a statin | Give a statin | Give a statin |

**Note:** 1. Use a formal estimation of cardiovascular risk to discuss prognosis and healthcare options with people with hypertension, both for raised blood pressure and other modifiable risk factors. 2. Estimate cardiovascular risk in line with the WHO recommendations (see desk guides). 3. Use the clinic blood pressure measurements to calculate cardiovascular risk.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Hypertension > How to use Aspirin for CV Disease Primary Prevention
text:
### How to use aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease (decision flowchart)

Aspirin for primary prevention, by age:
- 60 years or above: don't start aspirin for primary prevention.
- 40-59 years: calculate the 10-year CV risk.
  - Risk <10%: don't start aspirin for primary prevention.
  - Risk >10%: share the decision with the individual, weighing:

text:
### Appendix 2: drugs and substances that raise blood pressure or induce hypertension (NSAIDs, combined oral contraceptives, antidepressants, acetaminophen, others, herbal)

| Drug/Substance | Comments on Specific Drugs and Substances\* |
| --- | --- |
| Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) | No difference or an increase of up to 3/1 mm Hg with celecoxib; 3/1 mm Hg increase with nonselective NSAIDs. No increase in blood pressure with aspirin. NSAIDs can antagonize the effects of RAAS-inhibitors and beta blockers |
| Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill | 6/3 mm Hg increase with high doses of estrogen (>50 mcg of estrogen and 1–4 mcg progestin) |
| Antidepressants | 2/1 mm Hg increase with SNRI (selective norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake inhibitors). Increased odds ratio of 3.19 of hypertension with tricyclic antidepressant use. No increases in blood pressure with SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) |
| Acetaminophen | Increased relative risk of 1.34 of hypertension with almost daily acetaminophen use |
| Other Medications | Steroids. Antiretroviral therapy: inconsistent study findings for increased blood pressure. Sympathomimetics: pseudoephedrine, cocaine, amphetamines. Antimigraine serotonergic drugs. Recombinant human erythropoietin. Calcineurin inhibitors. Anti-angiogenesis and kinase inhibitors. 11ß-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 inhibitors |
| Herbal and Other Substances | Alcohol, ma-huang, ginseng at high doses, liquorice, St. John's wort, yohimbine |

*Average increase in blood pressure or risk of hypertension. However, the effect of these medications/substances on blood pressure may vary highly between individuals.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Heart Failure > Algorithm for Diagnosis and Management of Heart Failure
text:
### Algorithm for diagnosis and management of heart failure (by facility level, echo availability, congestion; guideline-directed therapy and CRT)

1. Suspected heart failure? Take a history and examine.
   - Clinic history: symptoms (acute: raised JVD, PND, lower limb swelling); function limitation (NYHA class); prior cardiac disease, pregnancies; prior comorbidities (HTN, disease, others); drugs, toxins.
   - Physical exam: vital signs; signs of congestion (raised JVD, hepatomegaly); lower limb swelling; murmur; crackles.
2. Investigations by facility level:
   - Health Center: LABS: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, CXR, ECG. If congested with SatO2 <90%: give IV Lasix (furosemide) 40 mg and transfer to the regional hospital.
   - Regional Hospital: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, HbA1c, chest X-ray, ECG, +/- cardiac ultrasound. Refer on to the referral hospital as needed.
   - Referral Hospital: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, HbA1c, ferritin, chest X-ray, cardiac ultrasound, ECG, coronary CTA, cardiac MRI.
3. Still suspect heart failure? (at DH/PH/referral hospital) Yes → Is heart ultrasound (echo) available?
   - No: treat as HFrEF (EF ≤40%) and refer to cardiology.
   - Yes: HFrEF & HFmrEF on echo → look for cardiomyopathy or valvular heart disease.
     - Not congested: work up causes (genetics, inflammatory, toxins, pregnancy, metabolic).
4. If congested (from either path): IV Lasix (8-hourly), morphine (if no low BP), nitrates (if available), oxygen (if low SpO2).
   - Cardiogenic shock: IV inotropes/pressors, until euvolemic.
5. When euvolemic, start guideline-directed medical therapy: 1. RAASi; 2. beta-blocker; 3. MRA (EF ≤35%); 4. SGLT2i → RAASi + BB + MRA ± SGLT2i.
6. After 3 months of GDMT, if EF ≤35% plus LBBB: CRT (cardiac resynchronisation therapy).

   - Regional Hospital: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, HbA1c, chest X-ray, ECG, +/- cardiac ultrasound. Refer on to the referral hospital as needed.
   - Referral Hospital: U&Es, CBC, glycemia, HbA1c, ferritin, chest X-ray, cardiac ultrasound, ECG, coronary CTA, cardiac MRI.
3. Still suspect heart failure? (at DH/PH/referral hospital) Yes → Is heart ultrasound (echo) available?
   - No: treat as HFrEF (EF ≤40%) and refer to cardiology.
   - Yes: HFrEF & HFmrEF on echo → look for cardiomyopathy or valvular heart disease.
     - Not congested: work up causes (genetics, inflammatory, toxins, pregnancy, metabolic).
4. If congested (from either path): IV Lasix (8-hourly), morphine (if no low BP), nitrates (if available), oxygen (if low SpO2).
   - Cardiogenic shock: IV inotropes/pressors, until euvolemic.
5. When euvolemic, start guideline-directed medical therapy: 1. RAASi; 2. beta-blocker; 3. MRA (EF ≤35%); 4. SGLT2i → RAASi + BB + MRA ± SGLT2i.
6. After 3 months of GDMT, if EF ≤35% plus LBBB: CRT (cardiac resynchronisation therapy).

text:
### Heart failure with LVEF >50%: hypertensive heart disease (HFpEF) and mitral stenosis (algorithm, continued)

Still suspect heart failure? (at HC/PH/referral hospital) → Heart ultrasound available? Yes → LVEF >50%:
- With BP >180/110 mmHg: hypertensive heart disease (HFpEF); calculate the H2FPEF score.
  - If congested: IV Lasix (8-hourly), oxygen (if low SpO2), position semi-sitting.
  - Screen for comorbidities: diabetes, dyslipidemia, AF, CAD, HTN.
  - BP control: 1. SGLT2i; 2. beta-blocker (if AF); 3. RAASi; 4. CCB.
- With mitral restricted opening, hockey-stick deformity, dilated LA on echo, and an apical diastolic murmur: mitral stenosis.
  - Causes: 1. rheumatic; 2. calcific; 3. congenital; 4. valvulitis.
  - Treat: Lasix (if congested); penicillin V (rheumatic); beta-blocker (atenolol).

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Heart Failure > Algorithm for Diagnosis and Management of Heart Failure > Valvular, right heart and pericardial disease
text:
### Heart failure algorithm (continued): valvular heart disease, right heart failure, pericardial disease, other diagnoses and precipitants of acute heart failure; inotrope dosing

Still suspect heart failure? (at HC/PH/referral hospital) → Heart ultrasound available? Yes → LVEF >50%:
- BP normal or high, valvular heart disease & CHD: 1. Lasix (if overloaded); 2. RAASi (high BP or LV remodelling); 3. +/- penicillin V; 4. cardiology consult.
  - If congested: IV Lasix (8-hourly), oxygen (if low SpO2), position semi-sitting.
- Dilated RV + D-shape sign, TAPSE <1.7 cm, loud P2: right heart failure. 1. Lasix (if congested); 2. screen for the cause of pulmonary HTN (acute/chronic lung disease, PE, other).
- Pericardial effusion: pericardial disease. 1. Pericardiocentesis (if tamponade): refer to cardiologist; 2. screen for and treat the cause: infections (TB, HIV, CMV, EBV), metabolic (thyroid disorders, uremia), malignancy, connective tissue disease; 3. others.
- Heart failure unlikely and normal heart ultrasound: consider other plausible diagnoses.

Precipitants of acute heart failure: 1. dietary indiscretion (alcohol, high salt); 2. medical non-adherence; 3. renal failure (acute/CKD progression); 4. new drugs (BB, CCB, NSAIDs, others); 5. arrhythmias, valve dysfunction; 6. new infection (pneumonia, others); 7. myocardial ischemia/infarction, PE; 8. metabolic (thyroid, DKA, pancreatitis); 9. hypertensive crisis.

Inotropes: IV dobutamine or dopamine 200 mg. Dose: 10-20 mcg/kg/min. Example for a 70 kg adult: 2 ampoules in 50 cc NS by syringe pump at 5.25-10.5 cc/h; or, if no syringe pump, 5 ampoules in 500 cc NS over 24 hours = 21 cc/h ≈ 7 drops/min. Keep MAP ≥ 65.

text:
### ACE inhibitors and ARBs in heart failure: starting and target doses (enalapril, ramipril, losartan), contraindications and when to reduce or stop | Drug | Starting Dose | Target Dose | | --- | --- | --- | | Enalapril | Adult: 2.5 mg twice daily
Pediatric: 0.1 mg/kg/d PO divided OD/BID, not to exceed 0.5 mg/kg/d | 10mg twice daily | | Ramipril | 1.25mg once daily
Pediatric doses not established | 10mg once daily | | Losartan | Adult: 25mg daily
Pediatric doses not established | 150mg daily | **Note:** Contraindications to ACEI and ARB: bilateral renal (artery) stenosis, history of angioedema, pregnancy, and known allergy to the drugs. Seek specialist advice when serum potassium >5 mmol/l, serum creatinine >2.25 mg/dl, or symptomatic hypotension. Halve the ACEI/ARB dose if creatinine increases more than 50% compared to baseline. Stop ACEI/ARB if the increase is more than 100% and serum potassium is more than 5.5 mmol/l.

text:
### Strategies for treatment of atrial fibrillation: rate control, rhythm control, anticoagulation

| Strategies | Drugs and Considerations |
| --- | --- |
| Rate control – for hemodynamically stable patients with chronic AF and fast AV conduction | Digoxin, calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers |
| Rhythm control – for hemodynamically unstable patients with AF of recent onset | Electrical cardioversion. Pharmacological cardioversion – amiodarone |
| Anticoagulation – for all patients | Warfarin to achieve INR of 2-3 |

text:
### Ischaemic heart disease (stable angina): non-pharmacological and pharmacological management, and risk-factor targets

| Non-Pharmacological Management | Pharmacological Management |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Smoking cessation – Complete cessation is essential. | 1. Short-acting nitrates – For immediate relief of angina (e.g., sublingual GTN). |
| 2. Exercise therapy – ≥30 min moderate-intensity aerobic exercise ≥3 times/week. | 2. Beta-blockers – First-line for long-term symptom control and heart rate reduction. |
| 3. Weight management – Aim for BMI <22.9 kg/m²; waist circumference <90 cm (men), <80 cm (women). | 3. Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs) – Alternative or addition to beta-blockers. Avoid combining non-DHP CCBs with beta-blockers if risk of AV block. |
| 4. Lipid control – Use statins (atorvastatin 20–80 mg/day or rosuvastatin 10–40 mg/day) to achieve LDL-C <70 mg/dL | 4. Add-on agents – If symptoms persist or beta-blockers/CCBs are contraindicated: |

**Note:** Also (highlighted box): Blood pressure control – target <130/80 mmHg. Ivabradine – for patients with HR >70 bpm who can't tolerate beta-blockers or in whom BBs are ineffective (refer to cardiologist). Glycaemic control – HbA1c target <7.0% in diabetic patients. Dietary counselling – promote heart-healthy nutrition.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Ischemic Heart Disease > Approach to Patient with Chest Pain
text:
### Approach to the patient with chest pain (flowchart: ACS, STEMI/NSTEMI/unstable angina, pericarditis, pneumothorax, pneumonia, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism)

1. Initial assessment with vitals (BP, all peripheral pulses, RR, temperature, JVP, SpO2) and physical examination (CVS, respiratory system, GIS).
   - Hemodynamically unstable: stabilize and immediately assess for STEMI, aortic dissection, massive pulmonary embolism, pericardial tamponade.
   - Hemodynamically stable: evaluate the causes of chest pain.
2. Obtain a 12-lead ECG, echo and CXR (all patients).
3. ECG diagnostic or suggestive of ACS? YES → Does the patient have typical or atypical angina pattern, radiation, diaphoresis, cardiac risk factors?
   - ST elevation → STEMI.
   - ST depression and/or T wave inversion → check cardiac markers (troponin, CK-MB) at baseline and repeat at 6 hrs:
     - Suggestive history, positive cardiac enzymes and ECG changes = NSTEMI.
     - Cardiac markers negative, new onset, crescendo or rest angina = unstable angina.
   - Pericarditis.
4. History and ECG suggestive of ACS? NO → X-ray chest or echo:
   - X-ray chest: area of lucency in lung parenchyma and chest wall → pneumothorax; infiltrate (with history and labs consistent with infection) → pneumonia.
   - Widened mediastinum (and history consistent with aortic dissection) and flap on echo → refer for dedicated imaging (CT aortogram): aortic dissection.
5. Assess risk for pulmonary embolism:
   - Low risk: send D-dimer, X-ray evaluation. Elevated D-dimer, or echo showing dilated RA/RV or McConnell sign → high risk.
   - High risk for pulmonary embolism (D-dimer elevated): refer for CT pulmonary angiogram to rule out PE.
6. If ECG, X-ray, cardiac markers and echo are normal: rule out other causes of chest pain based on history and available investigations. Patients with nonspecific chest pain, no ECG changes at presentation and at discharge from emergency, and normal cardiac enzymes can be discharged and followed up in OPD.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Acute Coronary Syndromes > Visual Illustration for Acute Coronary Syndromes (ACS)
text:
### Visual illustration of acute coronary syndromes: clinical setting, ECG, troponin level and change, triage decision and diagnosis (from low to high probability of MI)

A chart running from LOW to HIGH probability of myocardial infarction:
I. Clinical setting, symptoms and vital signs: from localised chest discomfort (low) to widespread pain (higher) to cardiac arrest needing CPR/shock (high).
II. ECG: normal ECG → mild ST depression → ST depression → ST elevation.
III. Troponin level at 0 h: − (low); −/+; +; ++; +++ (high).
IV. Troponin change within 1, 2 or 3 h: −; −/+; +; ++; at the highest level, if any of the above, consider direct rule-in.
Triage decision:
- Troponin − at 0 h and no change: rule out MI.
- Troponin −/+ or +: observe.
- Troponin ++ or more, or ST elevation: rule in MI.
Diagnosis: rule-out → mostly noncardiac (some unstable angina or other cardiac); observe → unstable angina, other cardiac, or NSTEMI; rule-in → NSTEMI or STEMI (some other cardiac).

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Acute Coronary Syndromes > Algorithm for ACS Management > Steps 1-3: suspect ACS, immediate actions, ECG and troponins
text:
### ACS management algorithm, steps 1-3: presentations, immediate actions in the first 10 minutes (monitoring, oxygen, aspirin, nitrates, morphine, labs), 12-lead ECG and serial troponins **STEP 1: SUSPECT ACS — Presentations** | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | Classic presentations | - Chest pain, pressure, tightness, or heaviness
- Radiation to left arm, jaw, neck, or back
- Dyspnea, diaphoresis, palpitations
- Nausea/vomiting, epigastric discomfort
- Syncope or near-syncope | | Atypical (especially in women, elderly, diabetics) | - Fatigue, weakness, malaise
- Isolated dyspnea without chest pain
- Epigastric pain resembling indigestion
- Jaw or arm pain without chest discomfort | **STEP 2: IMMEDIATE ACTIONS (0–10 minutes)** | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | Monitoring | - Continuous 12-lead ECG, cardiac monitoring
- Blood pressure, SpO2, HR monitoring
- IV access × 2 — large bore | | Oxygen | - Administer ONLY if SpO2 < 90%; avoid routine O2 | | Aspirin | - 162–325 mg PO — chewed immediately
- Hold if true allergy (use Clopidogrel 300 mg instead) | | Nitrates | - SL NTG 0.4 mg q5 min × 3 doses
- HOLD if: SBP < 90 mmHg, HR < 50 or > 100, RV infarct, recent PDE5 inhibitor use | | Morphine | - 2–4 mg IV if pain uncontrolled after nitrates
- Use cautiously — associated with possible increased mortality in some studies | | Labs | - Troponin I or T (high-sensitivity preferred), CK-MB
- BMP, CBC, coagulation (PT/INR/aPTT), BNP/NT-proBNP
- Lipid panel, HbA1c if diabetic history
- Type & Screen | **STEP 3: 12-LEAD ECG + SERIAL TROPONINS (< 10 minutes)** | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | ECG and imaging | - Obtain and interpret 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival
- Repeat ECG every 15–30 min if initial non-diagnostic
- Right-sided leads (V3R–V4R) if inferior ST elevation — rule out RV infarct
- Serial troponins: 0h, 3h, 6h (standard) OR 0h and 1–2h (high-sensitivity)
- Chest X-ray (portable) to assess for pulmonary edema, aortic dissection
- Bedside echo if hemodynamically unstable |

text:
### NSTE-ACS risk stratification: very high and high-risk criteria, timing of invasive strategy, and initial treatment | Risk | Criteria | Invasive strategy | Treatment | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Very High Risk | - Hemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock
- Refractory or recurrent chest pain despite treatment
- Life-threatening arrhythmias
- Mechanical complications of MI
- Heart failure due to NSTE-ACS
- ST depression >1 mm in ≥6 leads plus ST elevation in aVR and/or V1 | Immediate invasive strategy (within 2 hours) | - Dual antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor)
- Anticoagulant (e.g. enoxaparin or UFH)
- Beta-blocker (if not contraindicated)
- Nitrates
- Statins
- Oxygen if SpO2 <90% | | High Risk | - Diagnosis of NSTEMI
- Dynamic or new contiguous ST/T changes
- Transient ST-segment elevation
- GRACE risk score >140 | Early invasive strategy (within 24 hours) | - Dual antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor)
- Anticoagulant (e.g. enoxaparin or UFH)
- Beta-blocker (if not contraindicated)
- Nitrates
- Statins
- Oxygen if SpO2 <90% | **Note:** Refer all patients with very high and high-risk criteria to a tertiary care center after initial stabilization.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Acute Coronary Syndromes > Algorithm for ACS Management > Step 4: interpret ECG and classify ACS type (STEMI vs NSTEMI/unstable angina)
text:
### ACS management, step 4: interpret the ECG and classify (STEMI/new LBBB vs NSTEMI/unstable angina) with reperfusion or risk stratification, antiplatelet, anticoagulant and adjunctive doses | | STEMI / New LBBB | NSTEMI / Unstable Angina | | --- | --- | --- | | Diagnosis | ECG criteria:
- ST elevation ≥1mm in ≥2 contiguous leads
- New or presumed new LBBB
- Posterior ST depression in V1–V3 | ECG + Troponin:
- ST depression or T-wave inversion ± ↑Troponin = NSTEMI
- Normal ECG + ↑Troponin = NSTEMI
- Normal ECG + normal Troponin + symptoms = UA | | Reperfusion / risk | ACTIVATE CATH LAB NOW.
Primary PCI (preferred):
- Door-to-balloon < 90 min (first medical contact < 120 min)
- Transfer to PCI-capable center if needed
Fibrinolysis (if PCI not available):
- Door-to-needle < 30 min
- No contraindications (recent surgery, stroke, bleeding)
- Transfer post-lysis within 3–24h for angiography | RISK STRATIFY — TIMI or GRACE score.
High-risk features (early invasive strategy):
- Ongoing/refractory chest pain
- Hemodynamic or electrical instability
- Elevated troponin or rising pattern
- New ST changes > 0.5 mm
- TIMI score ≥3 or GRACE score > 140
- → Angiography within 2–24 hours
Low-risk (conservative/ischemia-guided):
- No high-risk features
- TIMI score 0–2, GRACE score < 109
- → Stress testing before discharge or outpatient | | Antiplatelet | ASA 162–325 mg PLUS P2Y12 inhibitor:
- Ticagrelor 180 mg loading (preferred) OR
- Clopidogrel 600 mg loading | ASA + Ticagrelor 180 mg OR Clopidogrel 300–600 mg | | Anticoagulation | - UFH: 60 units/kg IV bolus (max 4000 units)
- Enoxaparin 0.5 mg/kg IV
- Bivalirudin (alternative for PCI) | - Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h
- Fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC daily (preferred if conservative)
- UFH infusion if invasive strategy planned | | Adjunctive / beta-blocker | Adjunctive:
- GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor if high thrombus burden
- DO NOT delay reperfusion for workup | Beta-blocker:
- Start within 24h if no contraindications (HF, bradycardia, heart block, severe reactive airway disease) |

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Acute Coronary Syndromes > Algorithm for ACS Management > Step 5: in-hospital management (all ACS)
text:
### ACS management, step 5: in-hospital management for all ACS (beta-blocker, ACEi/ARB, statin, monitoring, complications) | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | Beta-Blocker | - Metoprolol succinate/tartrate — initiate orally within 24h
- Target HR 50–60 bpm; avoid if decompensated HF, bradycardia, or high-degree AV block | | ACEi / ARB | - Start within 24h in all ACS, especially EF < 40%, HTN, or DM
- Ramipril, Lisinopril, or Enalapril preferred; use ARB if ACEi intolerant | | Statin | - High-intensity: Atorvastatin 40–80 mg OR Rosuvastatin 20–40 mg
- Initiate regardless of baseline LDL; target LDL < 70 mg/dL (< 55 preferred) | | Monitoring | - Continuous telemetry ≥ 24h; watch for arrhythmias, AV block
- Serial ECGs and troponins until peak identified
- Echocardiogram to assess EF and wall motion
- Daily weights; strict fluid balance | | Complications | - Arrhythmias: VF/VT → defibrillation; AV block → pacing
- Acute HF/Pulmonary edema: diuresis, afterload reduction, consider IABP
- Cardiogenic shock: vasopressors, mechanical support (IABP, Impella)
- Mechanical (papillary rupture, VSD, free wall rupture): urgent surgery
- Pericarditis / Dressler syndrome: NSAIDs, colchicine |

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Acute Coronary Syndromes > Algorithm for ACS Management > Step 6: discharge and secondary prevention
text:
### ACS management, step 6: discharge and secondary prevention (DAPT, medications, lifestyle, follow-up) | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | DAPT | - ASA 75–100 mg indefinitely
- P2Y12 (Ticagrelor or Clopidogrel) for 12 months post-ACS
- Consider extended DAPT (> 12 months) in high ischemic, low bleeding risk patients | | Medications | - High-intensity statin therapy — lifelong
- ACEi or ARB — especially if EF ≤40%
- Beta-blocker — continue for minimum 3 years, indefinitely if reduced EF
- Aldosterone antagonist (Eplerenone/Spironolactone) if EF ≤35% + HF or DM
- SGLT2 inhibitor if DM or HFrEF for added cardioprotection | | Lifestyle | - Smoking cessation — most effective single intervention
- Mediterranean or DASH diet
- Moderate aerobic exercise 150 min/week after cardiac rehab clearance
- Weight management: target BMI 18.5–24.9
- Blood pressure control: target < 130/80 mmHg
- Diabetes management: HbA1c < 7% target | | Follow-up | - Cardiac rehabilitation enrollment — strongly recommended for all ACS
- Cardiology follow-up within 1–2 weeks of discharge
- Repeat echo at 6–12 weeks if EF reduced or not assessed
- Assess for ICD if EF remains ≤35% after 3 months of optimal therapy
- Ongoing lipid and renal function monitoring |

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Acute Coronary Syndromes > Contraindications for Fibrinolytic Therapy
text:
### Contraindications for fibrinolytic therapy in STEMI: absolute and relative | Absolute Contraindications | Relative Contraindications | | --- | --- | | - Previous intra-cranial hemorrhage (ICH)
- Stroke of unknown origin at any time
- Ischemic stroke in the past 6 months
- Central nervous system damage
- Malignant intracranial neoplasm
- Other intracranial lesions (aneurysm or AV malformation)
- History of closed head or facial trauma within 3 months
- Major trauma/surgery within the preceding 3 weeks
- Suspected aortic dissection
- Active bleeding or known bleeding diathesis (excluding menses)
- Gastrointestinal bleeding within the past month
- Non-compressible punctures in [the past 24 hours] | - Previous ischemic stroke beyond 12 months
- Transient ischemic attack in the preceding 6 months
- Oral anticoagulation therapy
- Pregnancy or within 1 week postpartum
- Recent (2-4 weeks) internal bleeding
- Prolonged or traumatic CPR
- Active peptic ulcer (only if the ulcer is actively bleeding; if only stool occult blood positivity, may be considered for thrombolysis)
- Severe uncontrolled hypertension (SBP >180 mm Hg and/or DBP > 110 mm Hg). Patients presenting with hypertension should be given beta-blockers, nitroglycerin and analgesics promptly to lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of ICH following thrombolysis
- Patients on warfarin therapy have higher rates of hemorrhage: the higher the INR, the higher the risk
- Advanced liver disease
- Infective endocarditis |
