heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Diagnosis of Stroke > Steps 1-2: recognise stroke and pre-hospital actions
text:
### Stroke, steps 1-2: recognise stroke (BE-FAST and additional symptoms) and EMS/pre-hospital actions **STEP 1: RECOGNIZE STROKE — BE-FAST + Symptoms** | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | BE-FAST screening tool | - B — Balance: Sudden loss of balance or coordination
- E — Eyes: Sudden vision change (blurred, double, or loss of vision in one or both eyes)
- F — Face: Facial drooping or asymmetry — ask patient to smile
- A — Arms: Arm weakness or drift — ask patient to raise both arms
- S — Speech: Slurred, confused, or inability to speak or understand
- T — Time: Call emergency services IMMEDIATELY — note exact time of last known well (LKW) | | Additional symptoms to recognize | - Sudden severe headache with no known cause ('thunderclap') — consider SAH
- Sudden confusion or altered level of consciousness
- Unilateral numbness or weakness (face, arm, or leg)
- Difficulty walking, dizziness, or loss of coordination
- Transient symptoms resolving < 24h = TIA — treat as emergency | **STEP 2: EMS & PRE-HOSPITAL ACTIONS** | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | Priority | - Activate Stroke Management | | Assessment | - Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale (CPSS): Facial droop, arm drift, speech
- LAPSS or FAST-ED if available
- Blood glucose
- 12-lead ECG (rule out AF as cause, detect STEMI mimics) | | Management | - Airway: Protect airway; supplemental O2 only if SpO2 < 94%
- IV access × 2; NS (not dextrose unless hypoglycaemic)
- Position: HOB 0–15° unless airway concern
- Do NOT lower BP unless > 220/120 and clear hypertensive emergency
- NPO – aspiration risk | **Note:** An NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score sheet is shown as a small image below the table.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Ischemic vs hemorrhagic stroke treatment
text:
### Acute treatment of ischaemic stroke (IV tPA/alteplase, contraindications, thrombectomy, antiplatelets) vs haemorrhagic stroke (ICH reversal of anticoagulation, BP control, surgery, SAH) | ISCHEMIC STROKE (~87%) | HEMORRHAGIC STROKE (~13%) | | --- | --- | | CT: No hemorrhage visible | CT: Hyperdense lesion = blood | | IV tPA (Alteplase) — 0–4.5h window:
- 0.9 mg/kg IV (max 90 mg): 10% bolus over 1 min, remainder over 60 min
- Onset ≤ 4.5h from LKW (or wake-up stroke with DWI/FLAIR mismatch)
- BP must be < 185/110 before administration | Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH): reverse anticoagulation IMMEDIATELY
- Warfarin: Vitamin K 10 mg IV + 4-factor PCC (25–50 units/kg)
- DOAC: PCC or specific reversal agent (Idarucizumab for Dabigatran; Andexanet alfa for Xa inhibitors)
- Heparin: Protamine sulfate 1 mg per 100 units UFH
- Antiplatelet reversal: Desmopressin 0.4 mcg/kg IV if urgent surgery | | tPA absolute contraindications:
- Hemorrhage on CT or prior intracranial hemorrhage
- BP > 185/110 mmHg (uncontrolled after treatment)
- INR > 1.7, aPTT > 40s, platelets < 100,000
- Recent surgery/trauma < 14 days (serious), < 3 months (head/spine)
- Active internal bleeding
- Glucose < 50 or > 400 mg/dL
- NIHSS = 0 (resolved) or rapidly improving | BP control (ICH):
- Target SBP 130–150 mmHg within 1h of presentation
- IV Labetalol, Nicardipine, or Clevidipine infusion
- Avoid rapid drops > 90 mmHg in chronic hypertensives | | Mechanical thrombectomy (LVO) — 0–24h:
- Confirmed LVO on CTA: ICA, M1, M2, basilar artery
- 0–6h: All eligible LVO patients (mRS 0–1 premorbid)
- 6–24h: DAWN / DEFUSE-3 criteria (CTP or MRI mismatch)
- Target door-to-puncture < 60 min; reperfusion < 90 min
- Alteplase + thrombectomy — do NOT delay tPA for thrombectomy | Surgical considerations:
- Neurosurgery consultation for all ICH
- Evacuation if: cerebellar hemorrhage > 3 cm, posterior fossa compression, obstructive hydrocephalus
- Lobar ICH > 30 mL with neurological deterioration
- EVD for hydrocephalus with impaired consciousness | | Antiplatelet therapy (if tPA NOT given):
- Aspirin 325 mg PO within 24–48h of onset
- Dual antiplatelet (ASA + Clopidogrel 75 mg) for 21 days for minor stroke/high-risk TIA (NIHSS ≤3, ABCD² ≥4) | Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH):
- 'Thunderclap' headache — worst of life
- CT head (90% sensitive within 6h); LP if CT negative
- CTA or DSA to identify aneurysm
- Nimodipine 60 mg PO q4h for 21 days (vasospasm prevention)
- Neurosurgical/Neurointerventional: coiling or clipping
- ICP management, euvolemia, avoid hyponatremia |

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Ischemic vs hemorrhagic stroke treatment
text:
### Acute treatment of ischaemic stroke (IV tPA/alteplase, contraindications, thrombectomy, antiplatelets) vs haemorrhagic stroke (ICH reversal of anticoagulation, BP control, surgery, SAH) | ISCHEMIC STROKE (~87%) | HEMORRHAGIC STROKE (~13%) | | --- | --- | | CT: No hemorrhage visible | CT: Hyperdense lesion = blood | | IV tPA (Alteplase) — 0–4.5h window:
- 0.9 mg/kg IV (max 90 mg): 10% bolus over 1 min, remainder over 60 min
- Onset ≤ 4.5h from LKW (or wake-up stroke with DWI/FLAIR mismatch)
- BP must be < 185/110 before administration | Intracerebral Hemorrhage (ICH): reverse anticoagulation IMMEDIATELY
- Warfarin: Vitamin K 10 mg IV + 4-factor PCC (25–50 units/kg)
- DOAC: PCC or specific reversal agent (Idarucizumab for Dabigatran; Andexanet alfa for Xa inhibitors)
- Heparin: Protamine sulfate 1 mg per 100 units UFH
- Antiplatelet reversal: Desmopressin 0.4 mcg/kg IV if urgent surgery | | tPA absolute contraindications:
- Hemorrhage on CT or prior intracranial hemorrhage
- BP > 185/110 mmHg (uncontrolled after treatment)
- INR > 1.7, aPTT > 40s, platelets < 100,000
- Recent surgery/trauma < 14 days (serious), < 3 months (head/spine)
- Active internal bleeding
- Glucose < 50 or > 400 mg/dL
- NIHSS = 0 (resolved) or rapidly improving | BP control (ICH):
- Target SBP 130–150 mmHg within 1h of presentation
- IV Labetalol, Nicardipine, or Clevidipine infusion
- Avoid rapid drops > 90 mmHg in chronic hypertensives | | Mechanical thrombectomy (LVO) — 0–24h:
- Confirmed LVO on CTA: ICA, M1, M2, basilar artery
- 0–6h: All eligible LVO patients (mRS 0–1 premorbid)
- 6–24h: DAWN / DEFUSE-3 criteria (CTP or MRI mismatch)
- Target door-to-puncture < 60 min; reperfusion < 90 min
- Alteplase + thrombectomy — do NOT delay tPA for thrombectomy | Surgical considerations:
- Neurosurgery consultation for all ICH
- Evacuation if: cerebellar hemorrhage > 3 cm, posterior fossa compression, obstructive hydrocephalus
- Lobar ICH > 30 mL with neurological deterioration
- EVD for hydrocephalus with impaired consciousness | | Antiplatelet therapy (if tPA NOT given):
- Aspirin 325 mg PO within 24–48h of onset
- Dual antiplatelet (ASA + Clopidogrel 75 mg) for 21 days for minor stroke/high-risk TIA (NIHSS ≤3, ABCD² ≥4) | Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH):
- 'Thunderclap' headache — worst of life
- CT head (90% sensitive within 6h); LP if CT negative
- CTA or DSA to identify aneurysm
- Nimodipine 60 mg PO q4h for 21 days (vasospasm prevention)
- Neurosurgical/Neurointerventional: coiling or clipping
- ICP management, euvolemia, avoid hyponatremia |

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Step 3: ED arrival
text:
### Stroke, step 3: ED arrival, door-to-CT < 25 min (immediate actions, labs, imaging) Arrange brain CT < 1 hour of arrival. Use the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) to stratify the severity of stroke: score < 6 mild stroke; 6-24 moderate to severe stroke; >25 severe stroke. **STEP 3: ED ARRIVAL — DOOR-TO-CT < 25 MIN** | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | Immediate (0–10 min) | - Activate Stroke Team / Neurology alert
- Rapid triage — priority 1
- IV access × 2, blood draws (see Labs below)
- 12-lead ECG, continuous cardiac monitoring
- Vitals: BP both arms, SpO2, temperature, glucose
- NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) assessment by trained provider | | Labs (Immediate) | - Glucose (point-of-care STAT — must be done before tPA decision)
- CBC, BMP, coagulation (PT/INR/aPTT), type & screen
- Troponin, liver function tests
- Pregnancy test (women of childbearing age)
- Toxicology screen if altered consciousness | | Imaging (< 25 min) | - Non-contrast CT head STAT — rule out hemorrhage
- CT Angiography (CTA) head + neck if tPA candidate or large vessel occlusion (LVO) suspected
- CT Perfusion (CTP) if extended window (6–24h) or uncertain onset
- MRI/DWI preferred if available and does not delay tPA; better for posterior fossa |

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Step 4: acute stroke unit management
text:
### Stroke, step 4: acute stroke unit management for all stroke types (BP targets, glucose, temperature, airway, neuro monitoring, DVT prophylaxis, fluids) | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | BP Targets | - Ischemic + tPA given: Maintain < 180/105 mmHg for ≥24h post-tPA
- Ischemic + NO tPA: Permissive hypertension; treat only if BP > 220/120 or end-organ damage
- ICH: Target SBP 130–150 mmHg
- SAH: Avoid hypotension; SBP 140–160 mmHg until aneurysm secured | | Glucose | - Target blood glucose 7.8–10.0 mmol/L
- Avoid hypoglycaemia < 3.3 mmol/L (worsens ischemic penumbra)
- Insulin infusion if persistent hyperglycaemia > 10.0 mmol/L | | Temperature | - Treat fever aggressively: target normothermia (< 37.5°C)
- Acetaminophen 650 mg q4–6h; cooling blankets if refractory
- Investigate source: aspiration pneumonia, UTI, DVT | | Airway / O2 | - Supplemental O2 only if SpO2 < 94%
- Intubation if GCS ≤8, airway not protected, or respiratory failure
- Swallow evaluation before oral intake (bedside or formal SLP assessment)
- HOB 30–45° to reduce aspiration risk (except permissive hypotension phase) | | Neuro Monitoring | - Neuro checks q1h for first 24h, then q4h if stable
- Repeat CT head at 24h post-tPA or if neurological deterioration
- Continuous EEG if seizure suspected or altered consciousness without clear cause
- ICP monitoring if cerebral edema, large infarct, or haemorrhagic transformation | | DVT Prophylaxis | - Pneumatic compression devices from admission (all stroke patients)
- Ischemic stroke: Add LMWH (Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily) after 48h if no haemorrhagic transformation
- ICH: Mechanical prophylaxis only for first 48–72h; LMWH after imaging confirms stability | | Fluids | - Normal saline (isotonic); avoid hypotonic fluids (worsen cerebral edema)
- Euvolemia — target CVP 8–12, avoid dehydration
- NPO if dysphagia; NG tube for medications and nutrition |

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Step 5: secondary prevention and etiology workup
text:
### Stroke, step 5: secondary prevention and etiology workup (workup, antiplatelets, anticoagulation for AF, carotid disease, BP, lipids and lifestyle) | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | Etiology Workup | - Prolonged cardiac monitoring ≥24h (preferably 72h) for paroxysmal AF detection
- Echocardiogram: Transthoracic (TTE) ± Transoesophageal (TEE) for cardioembolic source
- MRI brain with DWI for infarct characterization
- Carotid duplex ultrasound for ipsilateral carotid stenosis
- Fasting lipid panel, HbA1c, homocysteine if cryptogenic
- Hypercoagulable workup (young patients, cryptogenic): Factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid Ab, Protein C/S
- TOAST classification: Large artery, Cardioembolic, Small vessel, Other, Cryptogenic | | Antiplatelet (Ischemic) | - Minor stroke/TIA: DAPT (ASA 81 mg + Clopidogrel 75 mg) × 21 days, then monotherapy
- Moderate-severe stroke: ASA 81 mg monotherapy (or Clopidogrel if ASA-intolerant)
- Do NOT use DAPT long-term (> 3 months) — increases bleeding risk without benefit | | Anticoagulation (AF/Embolic) | - AF-related stroke: Start DOAC 3–14 days after stroke (1–2 weeks for severe strokes)
- DOAC preferred over warfarin: Apixaban, Rivaroxaban, Dabigatran, or Edoxaban
- Cardioembolic (non-AF): Warfarin (INR 2–3) for mechanical valves; DOAC for others
- Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO) + cryptogenic stroke < 60 years: Consider closure device | | Carotid Disease | - Symptomatic stenosis 50–99%: Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) within 2 weeks of event
- Asymptomatic stenosis > 70%: CEA vs. CAS individualized decision
- Carotid artery stenting (CAS) alternative in high surgical-risk patients | | BP Control | - Long-term target: < 130/80 mmHg for most stroke patients
- Restart or initiate antihypertensive therapy 24–48h after acute phase
- Preferred agents: ACEi or ARB, Thiazide diuretics, or combination | | Lipids & Lifestyle | - High-intensity statin: Atorvastatin 40–80 mg or Rosuvastatin 20–40 mg; target LDL < 70 mg/dL
- Smoking cessation — most impactful modifiable risk factor
- Diabetes management: HbA1c < 7%
- Mediterranean diet; limit alcohol; weight management
- Regular aerobic exercise 150 min/week after rehabilitation clearance |

- Cardioembolic (non-AF): Warfarin (INR 2–3) for mechanical valves; DOAC for others
- Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO) + cryptogenic stroke < 60 years: Consider closure device. Carotid Disease: Action: - Symptomatic stenosis 50–99%: Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) within 2 weeks of event
- Asymptomatic stenosis > 70%: CEA vs. CAS individualized decision
- Carotid artery stenting (CAS) alternative in high surgical-risk patients.

- Echocardiogram: Transthoracic (TTE) ± Transoesophageal (TEE) for cardioembolic source

- Moderate-severe stroke: ASA 81 mg monotherapy (or Clopidogrel if ASA-intolerant)
- Do NOT use DAPT long-term (> 3 months) — increases bleeding risk without benefit | | Anticoagulation (AF/Embolic) | - AF-related stroke: Start DOAC 3–14 days after stroke (1–2 weeks for severe strokes)
- DOAC preferred over warfarin: Apixaban, Rivaroxaban, Dabigatran, or Edoxaban
- Cardioembolic (non-AF): Warfarin (INR 2–3) for mechanical valves; DOAC for others
- Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO) + cryptogenic stroke < 60 years: Consider closure device | | Carotid Disease | - Symptomatic stenosis 50–99%: Carotid endarterectomy (CEA) within 2 weeks of event
- Asymptomatic stenosis > 70%: CEA vs. CAS individualized decision
- Carotid artery stenting (CAS) alternative in high surgical-risk patients | | BP Control | - Long-term target: < 130/80 mmHg for most stroke patients

text:
### Stroke, step 6: rehabilitation and discharge planning (early rehab, rehab team, discharge planning, prognosis tools) | Item | Action | | --- | --- | | Early Rehab | - Mobilization within 24–48h of ischemic stroke if stable (avoid in severe stroke or ICH)
- Physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology — begin in acute phase
- Dysphagia screening before any oral intake; formal SLP evaluation if any concern
- Nutritional support: NG tube if oral intake unsafe; dietitian referral | | Rehab Team | - Physiatrist, PT, OT, SLP, neuropsychology, social work, case management
- Inpatient rehabilitation facility (IRF) if patient can tolerate 3 hours therapy/day
- Skilled nursing facility (SNF) if medical needs require nursing oversight
- Home therapy if good function and support system | | Discharge Planning | - Antiplatelet or anticoagulation medication reconciliation and education
- BP log; home BP monitoring device
- Fall risk assessment; assistive device provision
- Driving: Typically prohibited for 3–6 months; assess per local regulations
- Outpatient neurology follow-up within 2–4 weeks
- Stroke support groups and caregiver education | | Prognosis Tools | - mRS (Modified Rankin Scale) at discharge and 90-day follow-up
- Barthel Index for ADL independence
- NIHSS trajectory: improvement correlates with functional outcome |

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Stroke Management > Emergency Management of Stroke > Stroke management flowchart by facility level
text:
### Stroke management by facility level (primary clinic, health centre, regional/referral hospital) with key time targets and CT decision (flowchart)

Key time targets: door-to-CT < 25 minutes; door-to-needle (tPA) < 60 minutes; door-to-puncture (thrombectomy) < 60 min; tPA window ≤4.5 hours from last known well (LKW); thrombectomy window ≤24 hours (selected patients); CEA for TIA/minor stroke < 2 weeks.

1. Primary clinic: identify signs and symptoms of stroke (SPOT A STROKE: F face drooping on one side; A arm or leg weakness; S speech difficulty; T time to call for ambulance immediately). Take vital signs, check glucose level, support ABCs and give oxygen if available.
2. Health centre: take vital signs, support ABCs, and give oxygen if needed; establish time of symptom onset; check glucose level; transfer to hospital.
3. Regional and referral hospital: take vital signs, support ABCs, give oxygen if needed; obtain IV access, do FBC, U&E, PT & PTT, lipid profile, HbA1c and glycemia; treat hypo- and hyperglycemia (according to protocol); obtain a 12-lead ECG; emergent brain CT/MRI; assess stroke severity scales (NIH Stroke Scale or Canadian Neurological Scale); see neurologist.
4. Does CT/MRI show hemorrhage?
   - Hemorrhage: consult neurologist & neurosurgeon.
   - No hemorrhage: probable or confirmed acute ischemic stroke. Repeat brain CT/MRI if the first CT brain was negative:
     - Ischemic changes: confirmed ischemic stroke.
     - No ischemic changes: consider other plausible diagnoses.

text:
### rtPA (alteplase) eligibility criteria in acute ischaemic stroke: inclusion (all must be met) and exclusion (any = contraindicated) | INCLUSION — All must be met | EXCLUSION — Any = contraindicated | | --- | --- | | - Ischemic stroke diagnosed
- Onset < 4.5 hours
- Age 18–80 years old | - Acute/severe head trauma within 3 months
- Ischemic stroke within 3 months
- Previous ICH
- Suspected SAH
- Intracerebral tumor
- Intracranial/intraspinal surgery within 3 months
- Active internal bleeding
- GI malignancy or serious GI bleed within 3 months
- Extensive hypoattenuation or hemorrhage on CT
- Known bleeding diathesis
- Aortic dissection
- Infective endocarditis
- Recent myocardial infarction
- Heparin within 48h (APTT prolonged) or LMWH within 24h
- Direct thrombin or factor Xa inhibitor within 48h
- NIHSS < 6 or > 25
- BP > 185/110 mmHg
- Platelets < 100,000/mm³
- Glucose > 22.2 mmol/L or < 2.7 mmol/L |

text:
### Acute ischaemic stroke: acute management (alteplase, labetalol, thrombectomy, cerebral oedema), thrombolysis contraindications (absolute and relative), and secondary stroke prevention | Acute Stroke Management | Thrombolytic Contraindications Absolute | Thrombolytic Contraindications Relative | Secondary Stroke Prevention | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1. IV Alteplase (0.9 mg/kg: 10% bolus in 1 min, rest over 1 hour) given if 3-4.5 hours from stroke symptom onset. No anticoagulation or antiplatelets within 24h of lysis.
2. IV labetalol if SBP > 220 mmHg or DBP > 120 mmHg, or active ischemic coronary heart disease, heart failure, aortic dissection, hypertensive encephalopathy, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia: 15% lowering during the first 24 h; if lysis, keep BP < 180/105 mmHg.
3. Endovascular thrombectomy.
4. Cerebral edema: HOB > 30°, IV mannitol, or hemicraniectomy. | 1. Any prior ICH
2. Intracranial neoplasm, aneurysm, AVM
3. Ischemic stroke within 3 months, 2 months' head/spine surgery
4. Bleeding diathesis
5. Suspected aortic dissection
6. Severe uncontrolled HTN | 1. Severe HTN SBP > 180 or DBP > 110 mmHg
2. Ischemic stroke > 3 months
3. CPR > 10 min, trauma/major surgery within 3 weeks
4. Internal bleed within 2-4 weeks, active PUD
5. Pregnancy
6. Non-compressible vascular punctures
7. Platelets < 100k, INR [>] 1.7, PTT > 40, glycemia < 50 mg/dl | 1. Antiplatelets: ASA 100 mg OD
2. Anticoagulants: consider in AF (CHA2DS2-VASc score), cardiac and paradoxical emboli (except endocarditis), hypercoagulable state; e.g. NOACs (rivaroxaban 20 mg OD) or warfarin (INR 2-3)
3. Statin: atorvastatin 40-80 mg OD, or rosuvastatin 20 mg OD (for life)
4. Blood pressure reduction (24-48 h after stroke onset; goal blood pressure '< 130/< 180' as printed; see Hypertension protocol)
5. Carotid revascularization
6. DVT prophylaxis: SC Lovenox (enoxaparin) 40 mg OD
7. Lifestyle modification: smoking cessation, management of obesity, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome, alcohol moderation/cessation |

text:
### Diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever by the revised Jones criteria (2015): major and minor manifestations, evidence of preceding GAS infection, and diagnostic rules

Diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) by the revised Jones criteria (2015):
- Major manifestations: carditis (clinical/subclinical); polyarthritis/migratory arthritis; Sydenham's chorea; erythema marginatum.
- Minor manifestations: 1. fever (≥38°C); 2. monoarthralgia; 3. prolonged PR interval on ECG; 4. increased acute phase reactants (ESR ≥30 mm/hour or CRP ≥3.0 mg/dl).
- Evidence of preceding GAS infection: 1. GAS on throat swab (positive culture); 2. raised ASO titre; 3. raised anti-DNase B; 4. positive quick strep test.

The diagnosis of ARF is confirmed in any of these situations:
1. Two major manifestations and any evidence of preceding GAS infection, OR
2. One major and two minor manifestations and any evidence of preceding GAS infection, OR
3. Presence of rheumatic chorea.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Rheumatic Heart Disease > Algorithm with the Initial Evaluation and Management of RHD in Children
text:
### Initial evaluation and management of acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease in children (algorithm: Jones criteria, primary and secondary penicillin prophylaxis by weight, valve involvement)

Acute rheumatic fever (ARF):
- 2-4 weeks after Group A Streptococcus. Diagnosis based on the revised Jones criteria:
  - Major manifestations: pancarditis; subcutaneous nodules; Sydenham chorea; erythema marginatum; arthritis (usually migratory polyarthritis).
  - Minor manifestations: fever 38°C; prolonged PR interval (on ECG); ESR 60 mm in the first hour and/or CRP 3.0 mg/dL; arthralgia.
  - Diagnosis, initial ARF: 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor. Recurrent ARF: criteria for initial ARF OR 3 minor.
- Management:
  - Primary prevention: penicillin V. If <27 kg: 250 mg 2 to 3 times daily for 10 days. If >27 kg: 500 mg 2 to 3 times daily for 10 days.
  - Secondary prevention: Extencilline (benzathine penicillin G), as printed: 'If >27 kg: 600,000 IU IM single dose every 28 days'; 'If >27 kg: 1.2M IU IM single dose every 28 days'.
  - If allergic to penicillins: azithromycin 6 mg/kg/day, maximum dose 250 mg.
  - Supportive treatment: arthritis, >2 years old: ibuprofen PO 10 to 20 mg/kg/day every 12 hours (maximum daily dose 1000 mg).

Rheumatic heart disease (RHD): still prevalent in resource-limited settings; sequela of untreated ARF; definitive diagnosis by echocardiography. By valve:
- Mitral valve involvement (most common): mitral regurgitation/mitral stenosis. Presentation: dyspnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, systolic murmur at the apex, hepatomegaly, lower-limb oedema.
- Aortic valve involvement (commonly with mitral valve): aortic regurgitation, aortic stenosis. Presentation: wide pulse pressure, syncope, thrill, diastolic/systolic (AR/AS) murmur, hepatomegaly, lower-limb oedema.
- Tricuspid valve involvement (less common, very rarely isolated). Presentation: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, systolic murmur at the LLSB, hepatomegaly, lower-limb oedema.
- For every valve: secondary prevention with Extencilline: if <27 kg 600,000 IU IM single dose every 28 days; if >27 kg 1.2M IU IM single dose every 28 days (the mitral column prints 'If <27 kg: 1.2M IU'). Treat heart failure as in the HF algorithm. A paediatric cardiologist decides the indication and timing of cardiac surgery.

*To prevent pain from the Extencilline injection, mix the drug with low-dose lidocaine hydrochloride 1% (3.5-5 mls) solution.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Rheumatic Heart Disease > Algorithm with the Initial Evaluation and Management of RHD in Children
text:
### Initial evaluation and management of acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease in children (algorithm: Jones criteria, primary and secondary penicillin prophylaxis by weight, valve involvement)

Acute rheumatic fever (ARF):
- 2-4 weeks after Group A Streptococcus. Diagnosis based on the revised Jones criteria:
  - Major manifestations: pancarditis; subcutaneous nodules; Sydenham chorea; erythema marginatum; arthritis (usually migratory polyarthritis).
  - Minor manifestations: fever 38°C; prolonged PR interval (on ECG); ESR 60 mm in the first hour and/or CRP 3.0 mg/dL; arthralgia.
  - Diagnosis, initial ARF: 2 major OR 1 major plus 2 minor. Recurrent ARF: criteria for initial ARF OR 3 minor.
- Management:
  - Primary prevention: penicillin V. If <27 kg: 250 mg 2 to 3 times daily for 10 days. If >27 kg: 500 mg 2 to 3 times daily for 10 days.
  - Secondary prevention: Extencilline (benzathine penicillin G), as printed: 'If >27 kg: 600,000 IU IM single dose every 28 days'; 'If >27 kg: 1.2M IU IM single dose every 28 days'.
  - If allergic to penicillins: azithromycin 6 mg/kg/day, maximum dose 250 mg.
  - Supportive treatment: arthritis, >2 years old: ibuprofen PO 10 to 20 mg/kg/day every 12 hours (maximum daily dose 1000 mg).

Rheumatic heart disease (RHD): still prevalent in resource-limited settings; sequela of untreated ARF; definitive diagnosis by echocardiography. By valve:
- Mitral valve involvement (most common): mitral regurgitation/mitral stenosis. Presentation: dyspnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, systolic murmur at the apex, hepatomegaly, lower-limb oedema.
- Aortic valve involvement (commonly with mitral valve): aortic regurgitation, aortic stenosis. Presentation: wide pulse pressure, syncope, thrill, diastolic/systolic (AR/AS) murmur, hepatomegaly, lower-limb oedema.
- Tricuspid valve involvement (less common, very rarely isolated). Presentation: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, systolic murmur at the LLSB, hepatomegaly, lower-limb oedema.
- For every valve: secondary prevention with Extencilline: if <27 kg 600,000 IU IM single dose every 28 days; if >27 kg 1.2M IU IM single dose every 28 days (the mitral column prints 'If <27 kg: 1.2M IU'). Treat heart failure as in the HF algorithm. A paediatric cardiologist decides the indication and timing of cardiac surgery.

*To prevent pain from the Extencilline injection, mix the drug with low-dose lidocaine hydrochloride 1% (3.5-5 mls) solution.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Rheumatic Heart Disease > Algorithm for Management of Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) at Secondary Care Level
text:
### Management of rheumatic heart disease at secondary care level (algorithm by valve lesion: mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, aortic insufficiency, aortic stenosis)

1. Suspect RHD at the health centre if a patient presents with new onset dyspnoea, fatigue or palpitations, plus: fast and irregular pulse; hyperactive precordium; loud murmur; distended jugular veins; ankle/leg oedema.
2. Transfer to the district hospital: order CXR, FBC, RFTs, 12-lead ECG. Confirm the diagnosis with echocardiography.
3. By lesion:
   - Mitral stenosis (leaflet and sub-valvular thickening, commissural fusion, calcification and accelerated forward flow on colour Doppler; left atrium usually dilated): start PO atenolol 25 mg if HR >90 bpm and BP >90/60 mmHg; PO penicillin V 250 mg BID; check for AF to start warfarin 5 mg OD (therapeutic INR 2-3). If in pulmonary oedema, admit for IV furosemide. Early referral for balloon mitral valvotomy (BMV).
   - Mitral regurgitation (leaflet and sub-valvular thickening, restricted leaflet motion, accelerated backward flow on colour Doppler; LV dilation +/- dysfunction): EF <60%: treat per HFrEF protocol, add penicillin V 250 mg BID, urgent referral to a cardiologist. EF >60%: low-dose PO furosemide, penicillin V 250 mg BID, non-urgent referral to a cardiologist.
   - Aortic insufficiency (thickened cusps with rolled edges; accelerated backward flow on colour Doppler; usually with rheumatic mitral valve lesions; LV dilation +/- dysfunction): EF <60%: treat per HFrEF protocol, add penicillin V 250 mg BID, urgent referral to a cardiologist. EF >60%: low-dose PO furosemide, penicillin V 250 mg BID, non-urgent referral to a cardiologist.
   - Aortic stenosis (thickened cusps with rolled edges; accelerated forward flow on colour Doppler; usually with rheumatic mitral valve lesions): aortic stenosis is a surgical condition. Refer to a cardiologist to quantify severity and plan surgery. Avoid afterload reduction unless AI or MR is associated.

Please note: women should be educated and offered reproductive health services upon RHD diagnosis. Patients on warfarin should have their INR checked regularly and kept within the therapeutic range. Estimate RVSP by TR jet CW if it can inform management; check the tricuspid valve for rheumatic changes. Mixed mitral or aortic valve disease can be challenging for less experienced practitioners: consult for management. Secondary prophylaxis with penicillin is recommended until 40 years of age.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Congenital Heart Disease > Screening and Diagnosis > Congenital Heart Diseases Screening
text:
### Newborn pulse oximetry screening for congenital heart disease (flowchart: abnormal, indefinite, normal; repeat at 1 hour)

Measure O2 saturation in the right hand and any foot of all newborns between 24-36 hours of age.
- O2 sat <90% in the right hand or any foot = abnormal → screening failed: paediatric cardiologist consult.
- O2 sat 90-94% in the right hand and any foot, or >3% difference between right hand and any foot = indefinite → repeat measurements in 1 hour.
- O2 sat ≥95% in the right hand or any foot and ≤3% difference between right hand and any foot = normal → screening passed.
Second measurement (1 hour later): same three outcomes; indefinite → repeat measurements in 1 more hour.
Third measurement: O2 sat 90-94% or >3% difference = abnormal → screening failed (paediatric cardiologist consult); O2 sat ≥95% and ≤3% difference = normal → screening passed.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Congenital Heart Disease > Approach to suspected congenital heart disease
text:
### Approach to suspected congenital heart disease (decision tree: central cyanosis, hyperoxia test, acyanotic vs cyanotic CHD)

Suspect congenital heart disease with: blue since birth or soon after birth and persistently blue, worsened by crying; poor or intermittent feeding, excessive sweating during feeding, crying and sleeping; precordial bulge, exercise intolerance; recurrent lower respiratory tract infection; recurrent episodes of heart failure; squatting, cyanotic spells, loss of consciousness; chest pain, shortness of breath and palpitations at rest and on exertion.

Central cyanosis/hypoxia?
- No: acyanotic CHD → chest X-ray, ECG, echocardiography.
- Yes: cyanotic CHD or pulmonary disease; consider non-cardiac causes like sepsis. Do a hyperoxia test (formal or informal, 15 L of O2) and check O2 sat:
  - O2 sat rises (Yes): pulmonary disease / non-cardiac causes. N.B. the hyperoxia test is not definitive; it does not completely exclude CHD.
  - O2 sat does not rise (No): cyanotic CHD → chest X-ray, ECG, echocardiography.

heading_path: Chapter 3: Cardiology > Congenital Heart Disease > Acyanotic and cyanotic congenital heart disease
text:
### Acyanotic and cyanotic congenital heart disease: types, clinical features, imaging and management (pressure vs volume overload; decreased vs increased pulmonary blood flow)

ACYANOTIC CHD
A. Pressure overload (clinical manifestations depend on the severity of the obstruction):
- Pulmonary stenosis: If critical: ductal dependent; presents in the first days of life in shock. If non-critical: tachypnoea, poor weight gain, poor feeding, ejection murmur over the pulmonary area.
- Aortic stenosis: If critical: ductal dependent; presents in the first days of life in shock. If non-critical: tachypnoea, poor weight gain, poor feeding, ejection murmur over the pulmonary area.
- Coarctation of the aorta: If critical: ductal dependent; presents in the first days of life in shock. If non-critical: HTN in the upper limbs, radial-to-femoral pulse delay, systolic murmur radiating to the back.
B. Volume overload (clinical manifestations depend on the severity of the left-to-right shunt):
- ASD: asymptomatic; can present with recurrent chest infections and poor weight gain. Physical findings: no respiratory distress, ejection murmur (most of the time absent) at the pulmonary area, fixed split S2.
- VSD/AVSD: symptoms appear in the first weeks of life: diaphoresis, poor weight gain, poor feeding, tachypnoea, tachycardia. Physical findings: chest retraction, holosystolic murmur at the LLSB, hepatomegaly, Harrison sulcus.
- PDA/AOW: symptoms appear in the first weeks of life: diaphoresis, poor weight gain, poor feeding, tachypnoea, tachycardia. Physical findings: chest retraction, continuous murmur at the left infraclavicular area, hepatomegaly.
Management of acyanotic CHD: 1. General measures: nutritional support, prevention of URTI and infective endocarditis. 2. Medical treatment if in heart failure: Lasix (furosemide) 1-3 mg/kg/day; Aldactone (spironolactone) 1-3 mg/kg/day; captopril (with caution) 0.3-0.5 mg/kg/day. 3. Treat the underlying pathology surgically or by catheterization.

CYANOTIC CHD
A. Decreased pulmonary blood flow:
- Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF): clinical features depend on the severity of the RVOTO; tet spells, squatting, poor weight gain; cyanosis, SEM at the ULSB, no hepatomegaly. Imaging: chest X-ray normal heart size with a boot shape, oligaemic lungs; ECG: RAD, RAE, RVH. Management of tet spells: knee-chest position, oxygen, IV fluids 10-20 ml/kg NS, propranolol 0.1 mg/kg/dose. Definitive management: paediatric cardiologist decides the indication and timing of cardiac surgery.

text:
### Atopic dermatitis symptoms and sites by age group (infants, older children and adolescents, adults)

| Age Group | Typical Symptoms | Common Sites / Distribution | Additional Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Infants & Young Children (0–2 years) | Pruritic, red, scaly, crusted lesions | Extensor surfaces, cheeks, scalp; may be diffuse | Diaper area usually spared |
| Older Children & Adolescents | Lichenified plaques | Flexural areas: antecubital & popliteal fossae, volar wrist, ankles, neck | Chronic scratching can lead to thickened skin |
| Adults | Localized, lichenified lesions | Mainly skin flexures | Lesions more persistent; may be less widespread |

text:
### Atopic dermatitis (eczema) stages and key characteristics: acute, subacute, chronic Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, pruritic inflammatory skin condition that occurs most frequently in children but may also affect adults, with a relapsing course. Dry skin and severe pruritus are cardinal signs of AD. | Stage | Key Characteristics | | --- | --- | | Acute Eczema | - Intensely pruritic (itchy)
- Erythematous papules and vesicles
- Exudation and crusting | | Subacute Eczema | - Features overlap between acute and chronic stages
- Lesions are slightly elevated, red, brownish, or purplish
- Variable scaling | | Chronic Eczema | - Dry, scaly, or excoriated papules/plaques
- Skin thickening from chronic scratching
- May lead to fissuring and lichenification |

heading_path: Chapter 4: Dermatology > Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema) > Summary of Patient Management
text:
### Atopic dermatitis (eczema): summary of patient management by severity (flowchart: mild vs moderate/severe, flare treatment, follow-up, hospitalisation)

1. Assess disease history, extent and severity, and the impact on the patient's and family's quality of life.
2. Educate the patient and carer about eczema care, trigger avoidance, and recognising and responding to eczema flares and infections.
3. Mild eczema: follow the eczema management plan: 1. daily bathing; 2. moisturiser applied top to toe at least twice per day; 3. trigger avoidance advice. Follow up within two weeks.
   - Improved: support optimal care at home, e.g. consider referral to community-based services.
   - Not improved: manage as moderate or severe eczema (step 4).
4. Moderate or severe eczema: assess for skin infections and compliance with correct eczema treatments.
   - Unwell or febrile: consider hospitalisation and/or IV antimicrobials.
   - Well: commence eczema flare treatment: increase moisturiser use to at least four times daily; eczema baths; topical steroids; wet dressings and compresses; commence oral antimicrobials if appropriate. Follow up within one week.
     - Improved: support optimal care at home.
     - Not improved: consider hospitalisation and/or IV antimicrobials.

heading_path: Chapter 4: Dermatology > Psoriasis > Definition of Psoriasis > Types
text:
### Types of psoriasis: plaque, guttate, flexural (inverse), pustular, erythrodermic, palmoplantar Psoriasis is a common, chronic, and recurrent multisystem immune-mediated inflammatory disease of the skin characterised by circumscribed, erythematous, dry, scaling plaques of various sizes, covered by silvery white scales. | Type | Description | | --- | --- | | 1. Plaque Psoriasis | - Most common type (80–90% of cases)
- Thick, silvery or waxy scales on localized or generalized plaques | | 2. Guttate Psoriasis | - Small, 'teardrop'-shaped lesions with widespread distribution
- Often triggered by streptococcal throat infection
- Common in children | | 3. Flexural (Inverse) Psoriasis | - Affects skin folds: genitocrural area, navel, axillae, sub-mammary region
- Lesions are red, shiny, well-demarcated, and lack scaling | | 4. Pustular Psoriasis | - Sterile pustules, either generalized or localized (commonly on palms and soles) | | 5. Erythrodermic Psoriasis | - Generalized skin redness (erythroderma)
- Severe and potentially life-threatening
- May follow worsening of existing psoriasis or be the first sign | | 6. Palmoplantar Psoriasis | - Sterile, yellow pustules with erythema and scaling localized to palms and soles |

TypeDescription
1. Plaque Psoriasis- Most common type (80–90% of cases)<br/>- Thick, silvery or waxy scales on localized or generalized plaques
2. Guttate Psoriasis- Small, 'teardrop'-shaped lesions with widespread distribution<br/>- Often triggered by streptococcal throat infection<br/>- Common in children
3. Flexural (Inverse) Psoriasis- Affects skin folds: genitocrural area, navel, axillae, sub-mammary region<br/>- Lesions are red, shiny, well-demarcated, and lack scaling
4. Pustular Psoriasis- Sterile pustules, either generalized or localized (commonly on palms and soles)
5. Erythrodermic Psoriasis- Generalized skin redness (erythroderma)<br/>- Severe and potentially life-threatening<br/>- May follow worsening of existing psoriasis or be the first sign

heading_path: Chapter 4: Dermatology > Psoriasis > Diagnosis of Psoriasis > Clinical Manifestations of Psoriasis
text:
### Clinical manifestations of psoriasis and their findings (plaque by site: flexural, nail, scalp, palmoplantar; other variants: guttate, pustular, erythroderma, annular)

| Clinical Manifestation | Clinical Findings |
| --- | --- |
| Plaque psoriasis | Well circumscribed, erythematous, scaly plaques > 0.5 cm in diameter, either as single lesions or as generalized disease. Classified further according to anatomic sites: |
| Plaque: Flexural | Also known as intertriginous or inverse psoriasis. Well circumscribed, minimally scaly, thin plaques localized to the skin folds (inframammary, axillary, groin, genital, natal cleft regions) |
| Plaque: Nail | Can present without concomitant skin plaques. Pitting, distal onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, oil drop sign, splinter hemorrhages, leukonychia, crumbling, red lunula. Nail involvement is a predictor of psoriatic arthritis |
| Plaque: Scalp | One of the most common sites of psoriasis. Often difficult to treat |
| Plaque: Palmoplantar | Localized to the hands and soles of feet. Ranges from confluent redness and scaling without obvious plaques, to poorly defined scaly or fissured areas, to large plaques covering the palm or sole |

**Other Variants**

| Clinical Manifestation | Clinical Findings |
| --- | --- |
| Guttate | Acute eruption of 'dewdrop', salmon-pink, fine-scaled, small papules on the trunk or limbs. Can follow group A streptococcal pharyngitis or perianal group A streptococcal dermatitis |
| Pustular | Sheets of monomorphic pustules on painful, inflamed skin. Most commonly localized to the palms or soles |
| Erythroderma | Acute or subacute onset of generalized erythema covering 90% or more of the patient's entire body with little scaling. Might be associated with hypothermia, hypoalbuminemia, electrolyte imbalances, and high-output cardiac failure. Life-threatening emergency |
| Annular | Well demarcated erythematous scaly plaques with central clearing |

heading_path: Chapter 4: Dermatology > Psoriasis > Pharmacological Management > Measures of Disease Severity
text:
### Psoriasis severity: mild (<3% BSA), moderate (3-10% BSA), severe (>10% BSA) with impact on quality of life

Treatment is conventionally based on the morphological type and severity of psoriasis: topical agents first, then phototherapy, then systemic agents. First-line systemic therapy is indicated if topical therapy is impractical.

| Severity | Measures\* |
| --- | --- |
| Mild | < 3% BSA†. Disease with a minimal effect on the patient's QoL; patient can achieve an acceptable level of symptomatic control by routine skin care measures and topical therapy |
| Moderate | 3% to 10% BSA†. heading_path: Chapter 4: Dermatology > Psoriasis > Pharmacological Management > Systemic Agents in the Treatment of Psoriasis
text:
### Systemic agents for psoriasis (second-line therapy): methotrexate, cyclosporine A, acitretin, biologics: doses and key details Choice of treatment is largely based on disease severity, comorbid conditions such as psoriatic arthritis, and treatment history (responsiveness to topical therapy, tolerability). Topical therapy is the standard treatment for mild to moderate disease. Systemic therapy is reserved for moderate to severe disease. | Drug | Key Details | | --- | --- | | Methotrexate | - Effective for all severe forms
- Dose: 5-25 mg/week
- Requires folic acid (daily except MTX day)
- Monitor with routine labs | | Cyclosporine A | - Dose: 2.5-5 mg/kg/day, divided
- Rapid clearance
- Monitor for nephrotoxicity, hypertension, lipids, gingival hyperplasia | | Acitretin | - Dose: 0.5–1 mg/kg/day, titrated
- High risk of adverse effects
- Teratogenic: contraindicated in women of childbearing age
- Requires strict monitoring | | Biologics | - Reserved for refractory or severe disease
- Examples include TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, IL-23 inhibitors, depending on patient profile and comorbidities |

text:
### Algorithm of psoriasis diagnosis and treatment (stepwise: psoriasis vulgaris mild vs moderate-severe, joint symptoms, erythrodermic and pustular psoriasis, biologics)

Pharmacological management of psoriasis should follow a stepwise approach.
1. Psoriasis patient → assessment of disease activity index and complications, and implementation of patient education. Then by presentation:
   - Psoriasis vulgaris:
     - Mild: topical agents.
     - Moderate-severe: (no next step printed).
   - Joint symptoms: confirm the diagnosis, record severity and complications → NSAIDs and DMARDs → if ineffective ('Invalid' as printed): biological agents.
   - Erythrodermic and pustular psoriasis: topical therapy, systemic treatment, phototherapy → if ineffective ('Invalid'): biological agents.
NSAID: non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; DMARD: disease modifying antirheumatic drug.

heading_path: Chapter 5: Gastroenterology and Hepatology > Chronic Liver Disease > Clinical Presentation > Symptoms and physical findings of liver cirrhosis
text:
> **Symptoms and physical findings of liver cirrhosis (with illustration of signs)**
>
> Symptoms of liver cirrhosis: general malaise, fatigue; anorexia/weight loss; feeling of an enlarged abdomen; swollen abdomen/legs; nose bleeds/bleeding from lower limbs; jaundice/itch; hand tremors.
> 
> Physical findings: skin pigmentation; xanthoma; spider angioma; palmar erythema; finger clubbing (hepatopulmonary syndrome); caput medusae; gynecomastia; fever; hepatocellular carcinoma ('Hepatoceleoma' as printed); hepatic halitosis (dimethylsulphide, ketones in the expired breath); jaundice; ascites, lower limb oedema; hepatic encephalopathy; bleeding plaques/purpura.
> 
> An illustration shows: xanthoma, jaundice, spider angioma, paper-money skin, gynecomastia, hepatomegaly/hepatic atrophy, caput medusae, ascites, palmar erythema, oedema, finger clubbing, white nails, bloody spots.

### Child-Pugh staging of cirrhosis: points for bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time/INR, ascites and encephalopathy; class A/B/C and prognosis

| Parameter | 1 Point | 2 Points | 3 Points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Total bilirubin, μmol/L (mg/dL) | <34 (<2) | 34–50 (2–3) | >50 (>3) |
| Serum albumin (g/L) | >35 | 28–35 | <28 |
| Prothrombin time prolongation (sec) or INR | <4 sec or INR <1.7 | 4–6 sec or INR 1.7–2.3 | >6 sec or INR >2.3 |
| Ascites | None | Mild (controlled) | Moderate to severe (poorly controlled) |
| Hepatic encephalopathy | None | Grade I–II (mild/moderate) | Grade III–IV (severe) |

**Child-Pugh class (total points) and prognosis**

| Parameter | 1 Point | 2 Points | 3 Points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Class A | 5–6 points | Well-compensated disease | Well-compensated disease |
| Class B | 7–9 points | Significant functional compromise | Significant functional compromise |
| Class C | 10–15 points | Decompensated disease, poor prognosis | Decompensated disease, poor prognosis |

text:
### Investigations in chronic liver disease and their purpose (LFTs, INR, CBC, viral hepatitis screen, renal function, ultrasound, elastography, endoscopy, Child-Pugh)

| Investigation | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Liver function tests (AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, bilirubin, albumin) | Assess hepatocellular injury, cholestasis, and synthetic function |
| Coagulation Profile (INR) | Evaluate liver synthetic function and risk of bleeding |
| Complete blood count | Detect anaemia, leukopenia, or thrombocytopenia |
| Viral hepatitis screen (HBsAg, HCV Ab) | Identify viral causes of chronic liver disease |
| Renal function (Creatinine, BUN) | Assess kidney function, important in advanced liver disease |
| Abdominal Ultrasound | Evaluate liver size, texture, ascites, and portal hypertension |
| Elastography (FibroScan) | Assess degree of liver fibrosis / non-invasively stage disease |
| Upper GI endoscopy | Detect and manage oesophageal or gastric varices |
| Child-Pugh Score (A, B, C) | Assess severity of cirrhosis and prognosis |

heading_path: Chapter 5: Gastroenterology and Hepatology > Diagnosis and Management of Chronic Liver Disease > Management of Complications
text:
### Management of complications of chronic liver disease: ascites, variceal bleeding, infections (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis) General management: avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs; vaccinations (hepatitis A, B, influenza, pneumococcal); nutrition with adequate protein, low sodium if ascites. Monitor liver function, coagulation and renal function; screen for HCC with ultrasound ± AFP every 6 months in cirrhosis; variceal surveillance. | Complication | Management | | --- | --- | | Ascites | - Sodium restriction: <2 g/day
- Diuretics: Spironolactone ± Furosemide
- Large-volume paracentesis for tense ascites
- Monitor electrolytes and renal function | | Variceal Bleeding | - Resuscitation: IV fluids, blood products
- IV antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g., Ceftriaxone)
- Endoscopic variceal ligation
- Non-selective beta-blockers for prophylaxis | | Infections | - Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP): Ceftriaxone IV
- Early recognition vital
- Monitor for other infections (UTI, pneumonia, skin infections) |

heading_path: Chapter 5: Gastroenterology and Hepatology > Diagnosis and Management of Chronic Liver Disease > Hepatic Encephalopathy Grading (West Haven)
text:
### Hepatic encephalopathy: West Haven grading (unimpaired, grade 0-1 minimal/covert, grades 2-4) and management

West Haven grading, as summarised in the text:
- Grade 0: minimal, normal exam. Grade 1: mild confusion, sleep disturbance. Grade 2: lethargy, disorientation. Grade 3: somnolent but arousable. Grade 4: coma.

West Haven grading chart (beside the text):
- Unimpaired: 1. no signs or symptoms; 2. normal psychometric or neuropsychological tests.
- Grade 0-1: 1. also known as minimal or covert hepatic encephalopathy; 2. no overt clinical symptoms to mild decrease in attention span, awareness, altered sleep rhythm; 3. abnormal psychometric or neuropsychological tests.
- Grade 2: 1. obvious personality change, inappropriate behaviour, asterixis, dyspraxia, disoriented, lethargy; 2. objectively disoriented to time.
- Grade 3: 1. somnolence, gross disorientation, bizarre behaviour; 2. objectively disoriented to time and space.
- Grade 4: 1. coma.

text:

heading_path: Chapter 5: Gastroenterology and Hepatology > Peptic Ulcer Disease > Helicobacter Pylori Related Peptic Ulcer Disease > Pharmacological Treatment
text:
### H. pylori eradication regimens: triple, alternative triple, concomitant and bismuth-based therapy: drug, dose, frequency and duration

Triple therapy is indicated for complete eradication of the organism. Diagnosis: positive stool antigen test (stop PPI 2 weeks before testing), positive urease breath test, positive urease test on endoscopic biopsy, or identification by histopathology.

| Therapy Type & Indication | Drug & Dose | Frequency | Duration | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Triple Therapy (complete eradication) | Omeprazole 20 mg PO | 12 hourly | 10–14 days | — |
| Triple Therapy (complete eradication) | Amoxicillin 1000 mg PO | 12 hourly | 10–14 days | — |
| Triple Therapy (complete eradication) | Metronidazole 400 mg PO | 12 hourly | 10–14 days | — |
| Alternative Triple Therapy | Lansoprazole 30 mg PO | 12 hourly | 10–14 days | — |
| Alternative Triple Therapy | Clarithromycin 500 mg PO | 12 hourly | 10–14 days | — |
| Alternative Triple Therapy | Tinidazole 500 mg PO | 12 hourly | 14 days | — |
| Concomitant Therapy | Omeprazole 20 mg PO | 12 hourly | 7 days | — |
| Concomitant Therapy | Amoxicillin 1000 mg PO | 12 hourly | 7 days | — |
| Concomitant Therapy | Metronidazole 400 mg PO | 12 hourly | 7 days | — |
| Concomitant Therapy | Clarithromycin 500 mg PO | 12 hourly | 7 days | — |
| Bismuth-Based Therapy (treatment failure) | Pantoprazole 40 mg PO OR Esomeprazole 40 mg PO | 12 hourly | 10–14 days | — |
| Bismuth-Based Therapy (treatment failure) | Bismuth subsalicylate 525 mg PO | 6 hourly | 10–14 days | — |
| Bismuth-Based Therapy (treatment failure) | Metronidazole 250 mg PO (6 hourly) OR 500 mg PO (8 hourly) | — | 10–14 days | — |
| Bismuth-Based Therapy (treatment failure) | Tetracycline 500 mg PO | 6 hourly | 10–14 days | — |

Note: H. pylori diagnostic tests should be repeated 5 weeks after the last dose of eradication therapy, and the PPI should be stopped 2 weeks before the H. pylori stool antigen test to confirm eradication.

heading_path: Chapter 5: Gastroenterology and Hepatology > Gastrointestinal Bleeding > Upper GI Bleeding > Differential diagnosis of UGIB
text:
### Differential diagnosis of upper GI bleeding by presentation (peptic ulcer, varices, Mallory-Weiss tear, oesophagitis, cancer, erosions)

Upper GI bleeding: PUD caused by H. pylori or NSAID use is the most common cause of nonvariceal UGI bleeding. Characteristic findings are hematemesis, melena, or (infrequently) bright-red blood per rectum, or a high serum BUN/creatinine ratio.

| Presentation | Diagnosis |
| --- | --- |
| Dyspepsia, H. pylori infection, NSAID use, anticoagulation, severe medical illness | Peptic ulcer disease |
| Stigmata of chronic liver disease, evidence of portal hypertension or risk factors for cirrhosis (alcohol use, viral hepatitis) | Variceal bleeding |
| History of heavy alcohol use and retching before hematemesis, hematemesis following weightlifting, or young adult with bulimia | Mallory-Weiss tear |
| Heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia; usually small-volume or occult bleeding | Esophagitis |
| Progressive dysphagia, weight loss, early satiety, or abdominal pain; usually small-volume or occult bleeding | Oesophageal or gastric cancer |
| NSAID use, heavy alcohol intake, severe medical illness; usually small-volume or occult bleeding | Gastroduodenal erosions |

heading_path: Chapter 5: Gastroenterology and Hepatology > Gastrointestinal Bleeding > Lower GI Bleeding > Differential Diagnosis of LGIB
text:
### Differential diagnosis of lower GI bleeding by presentation (diverticular, angiodysplasia, polyp/cancer, ischaemic colitis, IBD, Meckel and others); transfusion threshold and colonoscopy

| Presentation | Diagnosis |
| --- | --- |
| Painless, self-limited, massive haematochezia | Diverticular bleeding (most common overall cause) |
| Chronic blood loss or acute painless haematochezia in an older adult patient | Angiodysplasia |
| Stool positive for occult blood in an asymptomatic patient | Colonic polyp or cancer |
| Risk factors for atherosclerosis and evidence of vascular disease in an older adult patient; typically with LLQ abdominal pain | Ischemic colitis |
| Aortic stenosis | Angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome) |
| History of bloody diarrhoea, tenesmus, abdominal pain, fever | IBD |
| Rapid UGI bleeding | Dieulafoy lesion (large, tortuous, submucosal arteriole) |
| Large hiatal hernia | Cameron lesion (mucosal erosions) |
| Recent liver or biliary procedure | Hemobilia |
| Necrotizing pancreatitis | Hemosuccus pancreaticus (bleeding from pancreas) |
| Aortic aneurysm repair | Aortoenteric fistula |
| Painless haematochezia in a young patient and normal upper endoscopy and colonoscopy | Meckel diverticulum |
| Mucocutaneous telangiectasias | Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia |

According to expert opinion, the blood transfusion threshold for patients with colonic bleeding is a haemoglobin value <9 g/dL (different from the evidence-based threshold for UGI bleeding).
If the patient is hemodynamically unstable, resuscitate before diagnostic studies. Most episodes of LGI bleeding resolve spontaneously.
Colonoscopy is recommended early, usually within the first 48 hours of admission; endoscopic therapy is used to control continued bleeding.
If colonoscopy does not identify a discrete lesion or endoscopic therapy does not control the bleeding, interventional angiography or surgery may be indicated.

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Burns > Classification of Burns
text:
### Classification of burns by skin depth (first to fourth degree): cause, surface and colour, pain

| Skin depth | Cause | Surface and colour | Pain |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Superficial (epidermal) (FIRST DEGREE) | Sunburn, flash burn or minor scald | Dry, erythema, and brisk capillary return. No blisters | Painful |
| Partial thickness (superficial dermal) (SECOND DEGREE) | Scald | Moist, pale pink, broken blisters, and brisk capillary return. Blanches with pressure. Weeping blisters | Painful to temperature and air |
| Partial thickness (mid dermal) (SECOND DEGREE) | Scald, flame and contact | Moist, dark pink, and sluggish capillary return | May or may not be painful. Perceptive of pressure only |
| Partial thickness (deep dermal) (SECOND DEGREE) | Scald, flame and contact | Moist, blotchy red, white, mottled, sluggish or absent capillary return. No blanching with pressure. Easily unroofed blisters | Painless OR on deep pressure only |
| Full thickness (THIRD DEGREE) | Flame, severe scald and electrical | Dry, charred, whitish, leathery, and an absence of capillary return | Painless or on deep pressure only |

Fourth degree burns have the same characteristics as third degree burns but extend into fascia and/or muscle.

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Burns > Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) Burns Estimation
text:
> **Total body surface area (TBSA) burn estimation: Lund and Browder chart with age-specific percentages for head, thigh and leg; palm rule**
>
> Lund and Browder chart (body diagrams of adult, child and infant, front and back), with a form to record the % burnt for: head, neck, trunk (front), trunk (back), arm (right/left), hand (right/left), buttock (right/left), genitals, leg (right/left), feet (right/left), total burn area.
> 
> Areas that change with age (% of body surface for each region):
> | Age (years) | Under 1 | 2–4 | 5–9 | 10–14 | 15 | Adult |
> |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
> | A — ½ of head | 9½ | 8½ | 6½ | 5½ | 4½ | 3½ |
> | B — ½ of one thigh | 2¾ | 3¼ | 4 | 4½ | 4½ | 4¾ |
> | C — ½ of one leg | 2½ | 2½ | 2¾ | 3 | 3¼ | 3 |
> 
> Do not include first degree burns in the calculation of % TBSA. The surface area of a patient's palm (including fingers) is roughly 1% of TBSA. The palmar surface can be used to estimate relatively small burns (< 15% of total surface area) or very large burns (> 85%, when unburnt skin is counted). For medium-sized burns it is inaccurate.

text:
### Burn degrees 1 to 5: depth, common causes, appearance, healing and scarring | Degree | Features | | --- | --- | | 1st Degree Burns | - Epidermis only
- Commonly caused by UV light or very short flash or flame exposure
- Skin is red, dry & hypersensitive
- No treatment except analgesia
- Leaves no scarring on healing | | 2nd Degree Burns: superficial | - Epidermis + upper third of dermis
- Commonly caused by scald (spill or splash)
- Red, moist, weeping blisters that blanch with pressure
- Painful - due to nerve exposure; heals in 7-14 days
- Leaves no scarring on healing but there are potential pigmentary changes | | 2nd Degree Burns: deep | - Epidermis + upper part of dermis (deeper)
- Commonly caused by scald, flame, chemicals, oil & grease
- Cheesy white, wet or waxy dry; do not blanch with pressure
- Healing takes > 21 days
- Severe scarring & risk of contractures | | 3rd Degree Burns (Full Thickness Burns) | - Full epidermis + dermis are destroyed, leaving no cells to heal
- Commonly caused by scald, steam, flame, chemicals, oil, grease & high voltage electricity
- Grey to charred & black, insensate, contracted, pale, leathery tissue
- Severe scarring & high risk of contractures | | 4th Degree Burns | - Muscle involvement | | 5th Degree Burns | - Bone involvement - especially in epileptics who convulse during burning |

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Burns > Burn care: first aid and wound care
text:
### Burn care by stage: first aid, initial wound care, daily wound care (topical agents), special care of hands, surgical care | Stage | Key Actions | | --- | --- | | First Aid (Immediate Care) | - Drench burn with cool water to prevent further damage
- Remove burned clothing if easily removable
- If burn area is limited → immerse in cold water for 30 min (reduces pain, oedema, tissue damage)
- If burn area is large → cover with clean wraps to prevent hypothermia
- Beware of hypothermia risk: especially in young children
- Critical window: first 6 hours → transport severe burn cases to hospital urgently | | Initial Wound Care | - Administer tetanus prophylaxis in all cases if possible
- Debride bullae (except very small burns) & excise necrotic tissue (continue over first few days)
- Gentle scrubbing to remove loose tissue
- Cleansing: use 0.25% chlorhexidine, 0.1% cetrimide, or other mild antiseptic (avoid alcohol-based solutions)
- Apply thin layer of antibiotic cream (silver sulfadiazine)
- Dress with petroleum gauze + dry gauze thick enough to prevent seepage | | Daily Wound Care | - Change dressing daily (twice daily if seepage)
- Remove loose tissue during each change
- Inspect wounds for discoloration or haemorrhage (infection signs)
- Systemic antibiotics: for haemolytic streptococcal infection or septicaemia
- Pseudomonas infection → treat with systemic aminoglycosides
- Topical agents: silver nitrate 0.5% (cheap, occlusive dressings, no eschar penetration, causes electrolyte loss & stains); silver sulfadiazine 1% (with single-layer dressing, limited eschar penetration, may cause neutropenia); mafenide acetate 11% (no dressings, penetrates eschar, may cause acidosis). Strategy: alternate agents if needed | | Special Care – Hands | - Cover with silver sulfadiazine & place in loose polythene gloves/bags, secured with crepe bandage
- Elevate hands for first 48 hrs → then start hand exercises
- Once daily: remove gloves, bathe, inspect burns, reapply cream & gloves | | Surgical Care | - If skin grafting is required → refer to a specialist after healthy granulation tissue appears |

### Spinal injury assessment after trauma (flowchart: when spine injury is possible vs can be excluded clinically)

1. Blunt trauma with a mechanism suspicious for spine trauma? Yes →
2. Is the patient awake, alert and reliable?
   - No → possible spine injury.
   - Yes → 3. Severely injured patient? Evidence of intoxication? Neurological deficit? Thoracic or other significant distracting injury?
     - Yes → possible spine injury.
     - No → 4. Significant spine pain or tenderness (7/10)?
       - Yes → possible spine injury.
       - No → 5. Is the patient voluntarily able to flex, extend and rotate the spine in each plane regardless of pain (45° cervical spine, 30° thoracolumbar)?
         - Yes → no spine injury.
         - No → possible spine injury.
Isolated penetrating trauma: Yes → no spine injury.

text:
### Spinal injury management by level of care: facilities without vs with an orthopaedic surgeon Investigations: plain spinal radiographs; CT scan or MRI where available. It is critical to maintain cervical stability during transfer and examination, hence apply a cervical collar. | Level of Care | Management | | --- | --- | | Health facilities without orthopaedic surgeon | - Give anti-inflammatory analgesics.
- If open wound: administer tetanus toxoid (per EPI schedule) and appropriate antibiotics.
- Maintain spinal precautions: apply cervical collar or secure on a hard board; practice log rolling always; provide spinal immobilization during transport; continue resuscitation during transportation.
- Perform surgical toilet for associated injuries if facilities are available before referral.
- Refer to orthopaedic and neurosurgery department for acute treatment.
- Transfer even if clinical manifestations appear minor. | | Health facilities with orthopaedic surgeon | - Manage bone injuries with appropriate orthopaedic surgeries.
- Perform spinal decompression and stabilization as indicated.
- Maintain skin, bladder, and bowel care.
- Initiate rehabilitation: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, prosthetic and orthotic fittings. |

text:
### Snakebite envenomation syndromes in Eswatini: venom type, snake species, clinical features and antivenom (cytotoxic, neurotoxic, mixed, haemotoxic)

| Venom type | Snake species | Clinical features of envenomation | Antivenom (when indicated) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cytotoxic | Puff adder, Gaboon adder, spitting cobras (Mozambique, black-necked, zebra), stiletto snake, night adders, horned adders | Pain, swelling, bruising, blisters, necrosis, regional lymphadenopathy, hypotension, coagulopathy, compartment syndrome | Polyvalent antivenom for puff adder, Gaboon adder and spitting cobras only |
| Neurotoxic | Black and green mamba, non-spitting cobras (Cape, forest, snouted) | Pins and needles, metallic taste, visual disturbances, ptosis, drowsiness, sweating, drooling, dysphagia, progressive weakness, respiratory paralysis | Polyvalent antivenom for all species |
| Mixed (cytotoxic and neurotoxic) | Rinkhals, Berg adder, Peringuey's adder, desert mountain adder, garter snakes, shield nose snake, coral snake | Combined cytotoxic and neurotoxic features | Polyvalent antivenom for rinkhals only |
| Haemotoxic | Boomslang, vine snakes | Spontaneous bleeding (can present late, >24 hours after bite), headaches, dizziness, fainting | Boomslang monovalent antivenom for boomslang bites only |

text:
### Snakebite management by venom type: supportive treatment, signs of severe envenomation, antivenom type, administration, starting and additional doses (mixed, cytotoxic, neurotoxic, haemotoxic)

| Step | PPS/PW syndrome: mixed cytotoxic & neurotoxic venom | PPS syndrome: cytotoxic venom | Neurotoxic venom (mambas, non-spitting cobras) | B. syndrome: haemotoxic venom |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Snakes | Rinkhals, berg adder, desert mountain adder, garter snakes, shield-nose snake | Puff adders, Gaboon vipers, spitting cobras (Mozambique, black-necked, black, zebra), stiletto snakes, night adders, horned adders | Black and green mamba, non-spitting cobras (snouted, Cape forest) | Boomslang, vine snake |
| Supportive treatment | IV fluids; analgesia; protect airway | IV fluids; elevate limb; analgesia | IV fluids; protect airway by mask or ventilation | IV fluids; blood or blood component therapy. Heparin and anti-fibrinolytics are of no value and may be dangerous |
| Analgesia (all) | Paracetamol. NOT aspirin or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) |
| Severe envenomation anticipated if | Drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, mild pyrexia, dyspnoea, general weakness | Severe pain; swelling > 5 cm/hour; swelling to elbow or knee by 6 hours; swelling of whole limb in 12 hours; bleeding abnormalities | Metallic taste; profuse sweating; paraesthesia; excessive salivation; shortness of breath; difficult swallowing; ptosis; fasciculation | Fang punctures do not stop bleeding; severe headaches; dizziness; fainting; convulsions. NB: 20 min clot test |
| Antivenom administration (all) | Insert IV line (not in the bitten limb). Pretreatment: predose of adrenaline 0.25 mg (quarter ampoule) subcutaneously on either thigh, abdominal wall or forearm. A doctor administers the antivenom. No test dose required. | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) |
| Antivenom needed to treat (life over limb) | Rinkhals | Puff adder, spitting cobras, Gaboon adder | All species | Boomslang |
| Antivenom type and how to give | Polyvalent: add antivenom vials to 200 ml saline, infuse over 30 minutes. Example: if 8 vials are used, remove 80 ml (10 ml per vial) from the saline bag and add the 8 vials of antivenom | (same as left) | Polyvalent. Atropine + neostigmine: cobras only | Monovalent: IV push 1 ampoule/min OR diluted 50/50 in isotonic fluid infused over 15-30 minutes |
| Starting dose of antivenom IV | Rinkhals: 50 ml | Puff adder: 50-100 ml. Mozambique spitting cobra: 100 ml+. Gaboon adder: 200 ml | Black mamba, snouted cobra: 80-200 ml | Boomslang, vine snake: 20 ml |
| Additional antivenom | Monitor progression of swelling hourly. If swelling continues, give 2 additional ampoules of antivenom until swelling stops | (same as left) | Monitor neurological symptoms closely. If no improvement after 30 minutes, give an additional 4 vials. Repeat as necessary | If the blood remains incoagulable 6 hours after the first antivenom dose, repeat the dose until blood coagulability is restored |
| Monitoring (all) | Monitor for signs of reactions and anaphylaxis: urticaria, itchiness, bronchospasm, and BP every 3 minutes for hypotension, with continuous O2 saturation monitoring | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) |

Sources printed: adapted from the South African Snakebite Symposium 2022; Snake Management South African Consensus Guideline (SAA 2022); Swaziland Antivenom Foundation 2018; Netcare ISO ED 00107 V1 Nov 2019; Blaylock 2005 and Muller et al SAMJ 2012 (use of atropine and neostigmine).
Administration of antivenom (highlighted box): give the first dose (10 ml) of antivenom IV at a slow rate of 1-2 ml per minute. Subsequent doses may be injected into a saline drip, no more than 20 ml per 500 ml bag, to run in 30 mins. Repeat until symptoms resolve. Monitor breathing and other vital signs continuously. Do not run the drip into the bitten limb, which should be kept elevated and well protected.
Have adrenaline (1:1,000) at the bedside in case of anaphylaxis. If the patient has known allergies (asthma etc.), draw up the adrenaline (0.3-0.5 ml for adults and 0.1-0.3 ml for children) and have an antihistamine available. Antihistamine is NOT recommended as routine treatment for snakebite. DO NOT infiltrate the bite area with antivenom.

| Step | PPS/PW syndrome: mixed cytotoxic & neurotoxic venom | PPS syndrome: cytotoxic venom | Neurotoxic venom (mambas, non-spitting cobras) | B. syndrome: haemotoxic venom |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Snakes | Rinkhals, berg adder, desert mountain adder, garter snakes, shield-nose snake | Puff adders, Gaboon vipers, spitting cobras (Mozambique, black-necked, black, zebra), stiletto snakes, night adders, horned adders | Black and green mamba, non-spitting cobras (snouted, Cape forest) | Boomslang, vine snake |
| Supportive treatment | IV fluids; analgesia; protect airway | IV fluids; elevate limb; analgesia | IV fluids; protect airway by mask or ventilation | IV fluids; blood or blood component therapy. Heparin and anti-fibrinolytics are of no value and may be dangerous |
| Analgesia (all) | Paracetamol. NOT aspirin or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) |
| Severe envenomation anticipated if | Drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, mild pyrexia, dyspnoea, general weakness | Severe pain; swelling > 5 cm/hour; swelling to elbow or knee by 6 hours; swelling of whole limb in 12 hours; bleeding abnormalities | Metallic taste; profuse sweating; paraesthesia; excessive salivation; shortness of breath; difficult swallowing; ptosis; fasciculation | Fang punctures do not stop bleeding; severe headaches; dizziness; fainting; convulsions. NB: 20 min clot test |
| Antivenom administration (all) | Insert IV line (not in the bitten limb). Pretreatment: predose of adrenaline 0.25 mg (quarter ampoule) subcutaneously on either thigh, abdominal wall or forearm. A doctor administers the antivenom. No test dose required. | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) |
| Antivenom needed to treat (life over limb) | Rinkhals | Puff adder, spitting cobras, Gaboon adder | All species | Boomslang |
| Antivenom type and how to give | Polyvalent: add antivenom vials to 200 ml saline, infuse over 30 minutes. Example: if 8 vials are used, remove 80 ml (10 ml per vial) from the saline bag and add the 8 vials of antivenom | (same as left) | Polyvalent. Atropine + neostigmine: cobras only | Monovalent: IV push 1 ampoule/min OR diluted 50/50 in isotonic fluid infused over 15-30 minutes |
| Starting dose of antivenom IV | Rinkhals: 50 ml | Puff adder: 50-100 ml. Mozambique spitting cobra: 100 ml+. Gaboon adder: 200 ml | Black mamba, snouted cobra: 80-200 ml | Boomslang, vine snake: 20 ml |
| Additional antivenom | Monitor progression of swelling hourly. If swelling continues, give 2 additional ampoules of antivenom until swelling stops | (same as left) | Monitor neurological symptoms closely. If no improvement after 30 minutes, give an additional 4 vials. Repeat as necessary | If the blood remains incoagulable 6 hours after the first antivenom dose, repeat the dose until blood coagulability is restored |
| Monitoring (all) | Monitor for signs of reactions and anaphylaxis: urticaria, itchiness, bronchospasm, and BP every 3 minutes for hypotension, with continuous O2 saturation monitoring | (same as left) | (same as left) | (same as left) |

Administration of antivenom (highlighted box): give the first dose (10 ml) of antivenom IV at a slow rate of 1-2 ml per minute. Subsequent doses may be injected into a saline drip, no more than 20 ml per 500 ml bag, to run in 30 mins. Repeat until symptoms resolve. Monitor breathing and other vital signs continuously. Do not run the drip into the bitten limb, which should be kept elevated and well protected.
Have adrenaline (1:1,000) at the bedside in case of anaphylaxis. If the patient has known allergies (asthma etc.), draw up the adrenaline (0.3-0.5 ml for adults and 0.1-0.3 ml for children) and have an antihistamine available. Antihistamine is NOT recommended as routine treatment for snakebite. DO NOT infiltrate the bite area with antivenom.

text:
### Glasgow Coma Scale for all age groups (4 years to adult, child under 4, infant): eye, verbal and motor scores; TBI severity by GCS

**Eye Opening**

| Score | 4y to Adult | Child < 4y | Infant |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | Spontaneous | Spontaneous | Spontaneous |
| 3 | To speech | To speech | To speech |
| 2 | To pain | To pain | To pain |
| 1 | No response | No response | No response |

**Verbal Response**

| Score | 4y to Adult | Child < 4y | Infant |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | Oriented, social, speaks, interacts | Oriented, social, speaks, interacts | Coos, babbles |
| 4 | Disoriented conversation | Confused speech, disoriented, consolable, aware | Irritable cry |
| 3 | Speaking but nonsensical | Inappropriate words, inconsolable, unaware | Cries to pain |
| 2 | Moans or unintelligible sounds | Incomprehensible, agitated, restless, unaware | Moans to pain |
| 1 | No response | No response | No response |

**Motor Response**

| Score | 4y to Adult | Child < 4y | Infant |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6 | Follows commands | Normal spontaneous movements | Normal spontaneous movements |
| 5 | Localizes pain | Localizes pain | Withdraws to touch |
| 4 | Moves or withdraws to pain | Withdraws to pain | Withdraws to pain |
| 3 | Decorticate flexion | Decorticate flexion | Decorticate flexion |
| 2 | Decerebrate extension | Decerebrate extension | Decerebrate extension |
| 1 | No response | No response | No response |

Total score range: 3-15. GCS 3-8: severe TBI; GCS 9-12: moderate TBI; GCS 13-15: mild TBI.

text:
### Primary brain injury types and secondary brain injury: systemic and intracranial insults and their main causes

CT scan is the investigation of choice for head injury and cervical spine injury.

**Primary brain injury**

| Events | Main causes |
| --- | --- |
| Primary brain injury | Disruption of brain vessels; diffuse axonal injury; hemorrhagic contusion; hematoma |

**Secondary brain injury: systemic secondary insults**

| Events | Main causes |
| --- | --- |
| Hypoxaemia | Hypoventilation; aspiration pneumonia; thoracic injury; anemia |
| Hypotension | Hypovolemia; sepsis; cardiac failure; spinal cord injury |
| Hypercarbia | Respiratory depression |
| Hypocarbia | Hyperventilation, spontaneous or induced |
| Hyperthermia | Hypermetabolism; stress response; infection |
| Hyperglycemia | Hypothermia; stress response; IV dextrose infusion |
| Hypoglycemia | Inadequate nutrition |
| Hyponatremia | Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion; cerebral salt wasting |

**Secondary brain injury: intracranial secondary insults**

| Events | Main causes |
| --- | --- |
| Raised intracranial pressure and/or brain shift | Mass lesion; hydrocephalus; vasodilation; oedema; impaired cerebral venous drainage (position, ET tube ties, coughing etc.) |
| Vasospasm, stroke/infarction | Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage |
| Seizure | Cortical brain injury |
| Infection | Skull bone fracture; compound depressed skull fracture |

Reference: Royal Sussex County Hospital ICU TBI Clinical Guideline, July 2022.

### Primary brain injury types and secondary brain injury: systemic and intracranial insults and their main causes

CT scan is the investigation of choice for head injury and cervical spine injury.

**Primary brain injury**

| Events | Main causes |
| --- | --- |
| Primary brain injury | Disruption of brain vessels; diffuse axonal injury; hemorrhagic contusion; hematoma |

**Secondary brain injury: systemic secondary insults**

| Events | Main causes |
| --- | --- |
| Hypoxaemia | Hypoventilation; aspiration pneumonia; thoracic injury; anemia |
| Hypotension | Hypovolemia; sepsis; cardiac failure; spinal cord injury |
| Hypercarbia | Respiratory depression |
| Hypocarbia | Hyperventilation, spontaneous or induced |
| Hyperthermia | Hypermetabolism; stress response; infection |
| Hyperglycemia | Hypothermia; stress response; IV dextrose infusion |
| Hypoglycemia | Inadequate nutrition |
| Hyponatremia | Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion; cerebral salt wasting |

**Secondary brain injury: intracranial secondary insults**

| Events | Main causes |
| --- | --- |
| Raised intracranial pressure and/or brain shift | Mass lesion; hydrocephalus; vasodilation; oedema; impaired cerebral venous drainage (position, ET tube ties, coughing etc.) |
| Vasospasm, stroke/infarction | Traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage |
| Seizure | Cortical brain injury |
| Infection | Skull bone fracture; compound depressed skull fracture |

Reference: Royal Sussex County Hospital ICU TBI Clinical Guideline, July 2022.

text:
### Indications for brain CT after head injury: New Orleans Criteria (GCS 15) and Canadian CT Head Rule (GCS 13-15), with sensitivity and specificity

| New Orleans Criteria (GCS 15) | Canadian CT Head Rule (GCS 13-15) |
| --- | --- |
| Headache | GCS <15 at 2h |
| Vomiting | Suspected open or depressed skull fracture |
| Age > 60 | Age ≥ 65y |
| Intoxication | >1 episode of vomiting |
| Persistent antegrade amnesia | Retrograde amnesia > 30 min |
| Evidence of trauma above the clavicles | Dangerous mechanism (fall >3 ft or struck as pedestrian or fall >4 stairs) |
| Seizure | Any sign of basal skull fracture |

**Identification of patients who have an intracranial lesion on CT**

| New Orleans Criteria (GCS 15) | Canadian CT Head Rule (GCS 13-15) |
| --- | --- |
| 100% sensitive, 5% specific | 83% sensitive, 38% specific |

**Identification of patients who will need neurosurgical intervention**

| New Orleans Criteria (GCS 15) | Canadian CT Head Rule (GCS 13-15) |
| --- | --- |
| 100% sensitive, 5% specific | 100% sensitive, 37% specific |

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Traumatic Brain Injury > Patient Assessment > Flowchart for Mild Traumatic Brain Injury
text:
### Mild traumatic brain injury (GCS 13-15): assessment, CT, and discharge vs admit/transfer criteria (flowchart)

Patient with GCS 13-15.
1. History: name, age, sex, race, occupation; mechanism of injury; time of injury; loss of consciousness immediately post injury; subsequent level of alertness; amnesia (retrograde, antegrade); headache (mild, moderate, severe); vomiting.
2. General and neurologic examination; exclude systemic injuries; cervical spine and other X-rays as indicated; blood alcohol level; urine toxicology screen.
3. CT scan of the head if indicated.
4. Admit or transfer if any of: abnormal CT scan (haemorrhage or fracture); all penetrating head injuries; abnormal GCS score or deteriorating; history of prolonged loss of consciousness; focal neurologic deficit; significant alcohol/drug intoxication; CSF leakage; significant associated injuries; moderate to severe headache; no reliable companion at home.
5. Discharge if none of these criteria are met: discuss the need to return if any problem develops, or issue a warning sheet.
Source: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Manual, 10th Edition, 2018. American College of Surgeons.
