text:
### Moderate traumatic brain injury (GCS 9-12): assessment, CT, admit or transfer, and course (flowchart)

Patient with GCS 9-12.
1. Initial examination: same as mild brain injury, plus baseline blood work.
2. CT scan of the head.
3. Admit or transfer to a facility capable of definitive neurosurgical care.
4. Course:
   - Patient improves (90%): discharge when appropriate; follow up in clinic.
   - Patient deteriorates (10%): if the patient stops following simple commands, repeat CT and manage per the severe brain injury protocol.
Source: ATLS Student Manual, 10th Edition, 2018.

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Traumatic Brain Injury > Patient Assessment > Flowchart for Severe Traumatic Brain Injury
text:
### Severe traumatic brain injury (GCS 3-8): assessment, management, therapeutic agents, CT (flowchart)

Patient with GCS 3-8.
1. Assessment and management: ABCDEs; primary survey and resuscitation; secondary survey and AMPLE history.
2. Neurologic examination: GCS; pupillary light response; focal neurologic exam.
3. Therapeutic agents (usually after neurosurgeon consultation): mannitol; osmotic diuretics. Avoid hyperventilation in the first 24 hours unless there are signs of herniation.
4. CT scan of the head.
5. Admit or transfer to a facility capable of definitive neurosurgical care.
Source: ATLS Student Manual, 10th Edition, 2018.

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Traumatic Brain Injury > Pharmacological Management of Traumatic Brain Injury
text:
### Drugs in traumatic brain injury: tranexamic acid, mannitol, hypertonic saline, propofol, enoxaparin, phenytoin, paracetamol, morphine: dose, contraindications, side effects

**Antifibrinolytics: tranexamic acid reduces the risk of death in mild to moderate TBI when given within 3 hours**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tranexamic acid | 1 g Q8H IVD | Active intravascular thrombosis. Disseminated intravascular coagulation | Headache, sinus and nasal symptoms, abdominal pain, migraine, anemia, fatigue, retinal/ocular occlusion, allergic reactions |

**Hyperosmolar agents (osmotic diuretics): for intracranial hypertension and cerebral edema**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mannitol | 1 g/kg STAT | Anuria, dehydration, heart failure, intracranial bleeding, pulmonary edema | May exacerbate CHF, headache, electrolyte imbalance, acidosis, nausea, vomiting, hypo/hypertension, tachycardia |
| 3% Hypertonic Saline | Increased ICP: 1-3 ml/kg. Cerebral edema: 0.1-1 ml/kg/hr | Serum sodium > 160 mEq; serum osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg H2O | Hypotension, localized phlebitis, acid-base imbalance, hypernatremia, hypervolemia, hyperchloremia, pulmonary edema, fever |

**Anesthetics and sedatives (sedative-hypnotic): adjuvant for elevated ICP refractory to maximum hyperosmolar therapy and surgical decompression**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Propofol | 1 - 3 mg/kg STAT | If general anesthesia contraindicated; sensitivity to egg/egg products, soybeans | Hypotension, pain at injection site, apnea, anaphylaxis, may increase triglycerides with extended dosing, propofol infusion syndrome |

**Anticoagulants: prevention of venous thromboembolism, generally safe if started within 24–48 h of injury**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enoxaparin | 40 mg OD SC (adult); 0.5 mg/kg OD SC (child) | Active bleeding | Hemorrhage, bruising, thrombocytopenia, increased AST/ALT |

**Anticonvulsant: seizure treatment and prophylaxis**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phenytoin | Loading: 15-20 mg/kg. Maintenance: 300 mg IVD OD | Heart block, sinus bradycardia | Nystagmus/ataxia, hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias, SJS, peripheral neuropathy, phlebitis, gum hyperplasia with long term use |

**Analgesic / antipyretic**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Paracetamol | 1 g every 4-6 hr, max 4 g in 24 hours | Severe or active liver disease | Headache, nausea/vomiting, insomnia, constipation, pruritus |

**Narcotic analgesic (analgesia of choice in TBI)**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Morphine | 3 – 5 mg every 4 to 6 hourly | Severe asthma, respiratory depression, GI obstruction/ileus | Respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, nausea/vomiting, urinary retention, pruritus |

**Note:** Coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia: patients on warfarin can be managed with vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma (FFP), checking PT/INR 30 min after transfusion or every 4 to 6 h to keep INR < 1.4; in patients on antiplatelet agents or with thrombocytopenia, platelet transfusion is indicated. Barbiturates and propofol depress cerebral metabolism, decrease oxygen consumption, lower ICP and prevent seizures. Give prophylactic phenytoin if GCS ≤10, the head CT is abnormal, or the patient has had an acute seizure after the injury. Antipyretics control fever in acute TBI; normothermia improves ICP control and brain oxygenation. Pain management is important to avoid increased ICP.

**Hyperosmolar agents (osmotic diuretics): for intracranial hypertension and cerebral edema**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mannitol | 1 g/kg STAT | Anuria, dehydration, heart failure, intracranial bleeding, pulmonary edema | May exacerbate CHF, headache, electrolyte imbalance, acidosis, nausea, vomiting, hypo/hypertension, tachycardia |
| 3% Hypertonic Saline | Increased ICP: 1-3 ml/kg. Cerebral edema: 0.1-1 ml/kg/hr | Serum sodium > 160 mEq; serum osmolality > 320 mOsm/kg H2O | Hypotension, localized phlebitis, acid-base imbalance, hypernatremia, hypervolemia, hyperchloremia, pulmonary edema, fever |

**Anesthetics and sedatives (sedative-hypnotic): adjuvant for elevated ICP refractory to maximum hyperosmolar therapy and surgical decompression**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Propofol | 1 - 3 mg/kg STAT | If general anesthesia contraindicated; sensitivity to egg/egg products, soybeans | Hypotension, pain at injection site, apnea, anaphylaxis, may increase triglycerides with extended dosing, propofol infusion syndrome |

**Anticoagulants: prevention of venous thromboembolism, generally safe if started within 24–48 h of injury**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enoxaparin | 40 mg OD SC (adult); 0.5 mg/kg OD SC (child) | Active bleeding | Hemorrhage, bruising, thrombocytopenia, increased AST/ALT |

**Anticonvulsant: seizure treatment and prophylaxis**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Phenytoin | Loading: 15-20 mg/kg. Maintenance: 300 mg IVD OD | Heart block, sinus bradycardia | Nystagmus/ataxia, hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias, SJS, peripheral neuropathy, phlebitis, gum hyperplasia with long term use |

**Analgesic / antipyretic**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Paracetamol | 1 g every 4-6 hr, max 4 g in 24 hours | Severe or active liver disease | Headache, nausea/vomiting, insomnia, constipation, pruritus |

**Narcotic analgesic (analgesia of choice in TBI)**

| Drug | Dose and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Morphine | 3 – 5 mg every 4 to 6 hourly | Severe asthma, respiratory depression, GI obstruction/ileus | Respiratory depression, sedation, constipation, nausea/vomiting, urinary retention, pruritus |

**Note:** Coagulopathy/thrombocytopenia: patients on warfarin can be managed with vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma (FFP), checking PT/INR 30 min after transfusion or every 4 to 6 h to keep INR < 1.4; in patients on antiplatelet agents or with thrombocytopenia, platelet transfusion is indicated. Barbiturates and propofol depress cerebral metabolism, decrease oxygen consumption, lower ICP and prevent seizures. Give prophylactic phenytoin if GCS ≤10, the head CT is abnormal, or the patient has had an acute seizure after the injury. Antipyretics control fever in acute TBI; normothermia improves ICP control and brain oxygenation. Pain management is important to avoid increased ICP.

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Traumatic Brain Injury > In-Hospital Management of Traumatic Brain Injury
text:
### In-hospital management of traumatic brain injury: ICP control and ongoing care; severe TBI (GCS <8) airway, ventilation, sedation, AED, antibiotics, stress ulcer prophylaxis

The management of TBI patients needs a multidisciplinary approach to improve outcome.

**ICP control measures: ongoing care**

| Measure | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Elevate head of bed | 30-40 degrees (adult and child) |
| Hyperosmolar agents | Hypertonic saline or mannitol |
| Control blood pressure | Hypertensive crisis: treat with IV labetalol or nicardipine. Avoid hypotension (IV fluids and vasopressors) |
| Control blood sugar | 6-8 mmol/L |
| Thromboembolism prophylaxis | Enoxaparin (LMWH), compression stockings |
| Others | Enteral nutrition with target 25 - 30 kcal/kg/day by day 7. Keep Hb > 7 g/dL |

**Severe TBI (GCS < 8)**

| Measure | Details |
| --- | --- |
| Airway management | GCS < 8: intubation and admit to ICU |
| Ventilation | PaCO2 32-37 mmHg |
| Sedation for 48-72 hours | Midazolam OR propofol plus morphine |
| Prophylactic AED | Phenytoin |
| Start on empiric antibiotic | Risk of nosocomial infection and meningitis |
| Stress ulcer prophylaxis | Proton pump inhibitors, H2 receptor blockers or sucralfate |

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Traumatic Brain Injury > (g) Traumatic Brain Injury in Paediatric Population > Clinical Manifestations
text:
> **Head injury in children: presenting symptoms and signs associated with intracranial injury**
>
> Children with head trauma may present with: impaired level of consciousness (disorientation, confusion); blurred vision; headache; seizures; vomiting; amnesia. Younger children may present with lethargy or irritability.
> 
> Signs particularly associated with intracranial injury: prolonged loss of consciousness or impaired level of consciousness; disorientation or confusion; amnesia; worsening headache; repeated or persistent vomiting.

text:
### Traumatic brain injury: indications for surgical evacuation of epidural haematoma, subdural haematoma and parenchymal lesions Neuro-worsening is defined as a decrease in motor GCS > 2, new loss of pupil reactivity, interval development of pupil asymmetry > 2 mm, or a new focal motor deficit. Immediate management: medical control of ICP, normothermia and normocapnia; hyperventilate for 30 minutes if PCO2 is high (>40 mmHg); brain CT as soon as possible; consult the neurosurgical team. | Mass Lesion | Indication for Surgical Evacuation | | --- | --- | | Epidural Hematoma (EDH) | - EDH >30 cm3 regardless of GCS
- GCS <9, clot thickness >15 mm, midline shift >5 mm or focal neurologic deficits | | Subdural Hematoma (SDH) | - SDH >1 cm
- SDH associated with midline shift >5 mm
- GCS <8 with rapid decline or ICP <20 mmHg | | Parenchymal Lesions | - Progressive neurologic decline
- Mass effect
- Refractory ICH
- GCS scores of 6-8 with frontal or temporal contusions >20 cm3
- Midline shift of 5 mm and/or compression of cisterns, or lesion volume >50 cm3 |

text:
### Indications for CT in children with head injury: Canadian Assessment of Tomography for Childhood Head Injury (CATCH) medium and high risk factors; management

Initial management priorities: stabilise vital signs with a structured ABCD approach. Consider abusive head trauma in infants and children.

| Risk | Factor | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Medium Risk | Large boggy hematoma of the scalp |  |
| Medium Risk | Any sign of basal skull fracture | Hemotympanum, raccoon eyes, CSF otorrhea, Battle's sign |
| Medium Risk | Dangerous mechanism of injury | Motor vehicle collision; fall from a height ≥ 91 cm or down five stairs; falling from a bicycle without a helmet |
| High Risk | GCS score < 15 at 2h after injury; suspected open or depressed skull fracture; history of worsening headache; irritability on examination | (same as left) |

**Note:** Management should include: continuous monitoring of vital signs and, if possible, end-tidal CO2; mechanical ventilation to maintain normal oxygenation and ventilation; maintenance of a normal core temperature; sedation and analgesia, particularly during procedures and transport; fluids as required to maintain normovolemia and avoid hypotension.

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Poisoning > Management Protocol of a Poison > Decontamination by exposure type
text:
### Poisoning management by exposure type: ingested poisons (activated charcoal doses), gastric decontamination, skin, eye and inhaled poisoning Investigations: toxidromes assist diagnosis, but history may be inaccurate, so usually obtain complete blood count, liver function tests, serum lactate, arterial blood gas, ECG, urine pregnancy test in all women of childbearing age, basic serum electrolytes, BUN and creatinine. Sympathomimetics: RBG, ECG, electrolytes and renal function, LFT, creatine kinase, clotting screen (PT/PTT/INR), FBC, ABG, serum osmolality and osmolality gap; abdominal X-ray may help. Cholinergic: glucose, BUN, electrolytes, prothrombin time, LFT. | Exposure Type | Key Features / Signs | Immediate Management | Supportive / Additional Treatment | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Ingested Poisons | Nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, seizures, AKI, metabolic acidosis | - Assess airway, breathing, circulation (ABCs)
- Observe 4–24 hours
- Identify the toxin | - Activated charcoal (within 1 hr): <1 yr: 1 g/kg; 1–12 yrs: 25–50 g; >12 yrs: 25–100 g
- Do NOT induce vomiting with kerosene, petrol, corrosives
- If charcoal not available, induce vomiting only if conscious | | Gastric Decontamination | Soon after ingestion (<1–2 hours) | - Activated charcoal preferred
- Gastric lavage in selected patients | - Contraindications to lavage: unprotected airway; corrosive/petroleum ingestion; GI bleeding or obstruction
- Fluids for shock: 30 ml/kg IV NaCl or lactate | | Skin Contamination | Redness, burns, itching, chemical injury | - Remove clothing/personal items
- Flush skin with running water: 5 min for mild irritants, 15–20 min moderate/severe, 30 min corrosives, 60 min strong alkalis | - Use mild, non-abrasive soap if oily
- Protect staff (gloves, apron)
- Store removed clothes in a sealed plastic bag | | Eye Contamination | Tearing, redness, pain, blurred vision | - Irrigate with clean water: 15–20 min (general), 30 min (acid/alkali)
- Use tetracaine 1–2 drops to ease irrigation | - Evert eyelids, check all surfaces
- Use fluorescein stain if possible
- Refer to ophthalmologist if corneal/conjunctival injury or further evaluation needed | | Inhaled Poisoning | Cough, wheezing, cyanosis, respiratory distress, altered consciousness | - Move to fresh air; ventilate the area
- Give oxygen: mild 2–6 L/min (nasal cannula); moderate 6–10 L/min (mask); severe 10–15 L/min (non-rebreather); apnoea 100% O2 via BVM | - For bronchospasm: salbutamol PO 4 mg 6–8 hrly; adrenaline SC/IM 25–50 mg or IV 5–25 mg (as printed); ipratropium inhalation: 12+ yrs 250–500 mcg, 6–12 yrs 250 mcg, 0–5 yrs 125–250 mcg
- CPR if cardiac arrest occurs |

Ingested PoisonsNausea, vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, seizures, AKI, metabolic acidosis- Assess airway, breathing, circulation (ABCs)<br/>- Observe 4–24 hours<br/>- Identify the toxin- Activated charcoal (within 1 hr): <1 yr: 1 g/kg; 1–12 yrs: 25–50 g; >12 yrs: 25–100 g<br/>- Do NOT induce vomiting with kerosene, petrol, corrosives<br/>- If charcoal not available, induce vomiting only if conscious
Gastric DecontaminationSoon after ingestion (<1–2 hours)- Activated charcoal preferred<br/>- Gastric lavage in selected patients- Contraindications to lavage: unprotected airway; corrosive/petroleum ingestion; GI bleeding or obstruction<br/>- Fluids for shock: 30 ml/kg IV NaCl or lactate
Skin ContaminationRedness, burns, itching, chemical injury- Remove clothing/personal items<br/>- Flush skin with running water: 5 min for mild irritants, 15–20 min moderate/severe, 30 min corrosives, 60 min strong alkalis- Use mild, non-abrasive soap if oily<br/>- Protect staff (gloves, apron)<br/>- Store removed clothes in a sealed plastic bag
Eye ContaminationTearing, redness, pain, blurred vision- Irrigate with clean water: 15–20 min (general), 30 min (acid/alkali)<br/>- Use tetracaine 1–2 drops to ease irrigation- Evert eyelids, check all surfaces<br/>- Use fluorescein stain if possible<br/>- Refer to ophthalmologist if corneal/conjunctival injury or further evaluation needed
Inhaled PoisoningCough, wheezing, cyanosis, respiratory distress, altered consciousness- Move to fresh air; ventilate the area<br/>- Give oxygen: mild 2–6 L/min (nasal cannula); moderate 6–10 L/min (mask); severe 10–15 L/min (non-rebreather); apnoea 100% O2 via BVM- For bronchospasm: salbutamol PO 4 mg 6–8 hrly; adrenaline SC/IM 25–50 mg or IV 5–25 mg (as printed); ipratropium inhalation: 12+ yrs 250–500 mcg, 6–12 yrs 250 mcg, 0–5 yrs 125–250 mcg<br/>- CPR if cardiac arrest occurs

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Poisoning > Supportive Care
text:
### Poisoning supportive care: toxic features (COPD signs, pulmonary oedema, PE, ARDS, MI, metabolic acidosis) with diagnosis, immediate stabilisation and definitive management

| Toxic Feature | Methods to reach Diagnosis | Immediate Stabilization | Definitive Management |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Signs of COPD | History and physical exam; CXR | O2 | Bronchodilators, steroids |
| Pulmonary edema | History and physical exam; CXR; pro-BNP | O2 | Bronchodilators, steroids; nitrates, diuretics |
| Pulmonary embolism | History and physical exam; d-dimer; chest CT | O2 | Anticoagulation; thrombolysis (massive PE only) |
| Acute respiratory distress syndrome | History and physical exam; CXR | O2 | Ventilatory support |
| Myocardial infarction | History and physical exam; ECG | O2, nitrates, aspirin, anticoagulation | Revascularization (thrombolysis or PCI) |
| Metabolic acidosis | History and physical exam; metabolic panel; blood gas | O2 | Directed at underlying cause |

**Note:** The investigations depend on the poison ingested. If the toxin cannot be identified, the toxidrome (signs and symptoms) can be used.

heading_path: Chapter 6: Injuries and Trauma > Poisoning > List of common pesticides and chemical poisons with their antidotes
text:
### Antidotes and doses for common poisons: pesticides (organophosphates, carbamates, organochlorines, rodenticides), industrial chemicals (arsenic, methanol, ethylene glycol, cyanide, methaemoglobinaemia), drugs (paracetamol, iron, benzodiazepines, opioids, isoniazid, digoxin), envenomations and bites

| Group | Poison / Agent | Antidote & Dose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agricultural Pesticides | Organophosphates (malathion, acephate, dichlorvos, dimethoate, fenitrothion, monocrotophos, phorate, quinalphos) | Atropine sulfate 2 mg IM (mid-lateral outer thigh). Pralidoxime 1–2 g IV infusion (10–20 mg/mL) over 15–30 min; repeat in 1 hr if needed, then q12hr; or 30 mg/kg IV over 20 min followed by 4–8 mg/kg/hr maintenance infusion |
| Agricultural Pesticides | Carbamates (propoxur, aldicarb, carbaryl, carbofuran, methomyl) | Pralidoxime 1–2 g IV infusion (10–20 mg/mL) over 15–30 min; repeat in 1 hr if needed, then q12hr; or 30 mg/kg IV over 20 min followed by 4–8 mg/kg/hr maintenance infusion |
| Agricultural Pesticides | Organochlorines (endosulfan, gamma benzene hexachloride, heptachlor, chlordane) | Cholestyramine 4 g PO q12–24hr; increase over 1-month intervals. Maintenance: 8–16 g/day PO divided q12hr (max 24 g/day) |
| Agricultural Pesticides | Rodenticides (bromadiolone) | Vitamin K. Adults: 2.5–10 mg PO/SC; may increase to 25–50 mg; repeat in 12–48 hr. Newborn: 0.5–1 mg IM within 1 hr of birth |
| Industrial Chemicals | Arsenic | D-Penicillamine 30–40 mg/kg/day PO for 1–6 months (2 hr before or 3 hr after meals) OR dimercaprol 3 mg/kg IM deep q4hr for 48 hr, then q12hr for 10 days |
| Industrial Chemicals | Methyl alcohol | Ethanol: loading 600 mg/kg IV (7.6 mL/kg of 10% solution) or 600–700 mg/kg PO/NG (95% solution diluted to ≤20%). Maintenance 0.15 mL/kg/hr PO (IV: 1.4 mL/kg/hr of 10% ethanol) |
| Industrial Chemicals | Ethylene glycol | Folic acid/folinic acid: 60 mg IM over 12–24 hr stat, then 15 mg PO q8hr for 48–72 hr. Ethanol: same dosing as methyl alcohol. Pyridoxine HCl: 10–25 mg PO q8hr, observe at 6 hr. Thiamine: 100 mg IV; then 50–100 mg/day IM or IV; then 5–30 mg TID for 1 month |
| Industrial Chemicals | Cyanide | Hydroxocobalamin 70 mg/kg (usually 5 g) IV infusion over 15 min; an additional 5 g IV may be given based on severity and clinical response |
| Industrial Chemicals | Methemoglobinemia (nitrites, nitrates, dapsone, copper, aniline, chlorates, naphthalene) | Methylene blue 1 mg/kg IV over 5–30 min. If MetHb remains >30% or symptoms persist, repeat up to 1 mg/kg 1 hr after first dose |
| Drugs | Acetaminophen (paracetamol) | N-acetylcysteine 140 mg/kg loading dose, then 70 mg/kg q4hr for 3 days or until acetaminophen is undetectable in blood |
| Drugs | Iron | Deferoxamine 1 g IM initially, then 500 mg q8hr for 48 hr |
| Drugs | Benzodiazepines | Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV over 15 sec, then 0.1 mg at 60-sec intervals until consciousness restored. Maintain 0.3–0.6 mg based on patient and benzodiazepine used |
| Drugs | Opioids | Naloxone 0.4–2 mg PO depending on opioid amount; repeat in 2–3 min if needed |
| Drugs | Isoniazid | Pyridoxine 10–25 mg PO q8hr for 48 hr |
| Drugs | Digoxin | Digoxin-specific antibodies (DigiFab): each 40 mg vial binds 0.5 mg digoxin. Dose equimolar to ingested digoxin (76–80 mg FAB = 1 mg digoxin) |
| Envenomations & Bites | Snake bite | Anti-snake venom (ASV) polyvalent: mild 5 vials (50 mL); moderate 5–10 vials (50–100 mL); severe 10–20 vials (100–200 mL) |
| Envenomations & Bites | Dog bite (rabies exposure) | Anti-rabies human immunoglobulin 20 IU/kg |
| Envenomations & Bites | Botulism | Botulinum antitoxin: IV infusion via volumetric pump; start at 0.5 mL/min for the first 30 min to minimize allergic reactions |

source_flags: Naloxone is printed 'PO'; naloxone is given IV/IM/IN (oral naloxone is not effective for overdose). Clinician to confirm.

Isoniazid antidote 'pyridoxine 10–25 mg PO q8hr' is a prophylaxis dose; isoniazid poisoning is usually treated with IV pyridoxine gram-for-gram (about 5 g). Similar low pyridoxine dosing is given for ethylene glycol.

Snakebite antivenom volumes here differ from the venom-specific starting doses on p.182.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Acute Kidney Injury Causes
text:
### Causes of acute kidney injury by kidney region: pre-renal, intrinsic renal (tubules, interstitium, glomeruli, vessels), post-renal Acute kidney injury: a syndrome characterized by an acute decline in renal function, with many potential causes (KDIGO 2012). It can occur with pre-existing chronic kidney disease (acute on chronic). AKI is classified into three categories by cause and location of injury. | Kidney Region | Cause of Acute Kidney Injury | | --- | --- | | Pre-Renal | - Dehydration - kucatseka (enema), diarrhoea, vomiting, sweating
- Shock - cardiogenic, septic, haemorrhagic
- Drugs - BP therapy, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) | | Intrinsic Renal | - Tubules - acute tubular necrosis (from ischaemia from untreated pre-renal causes, sepsis, toxins like myoglobin in rhabdomyolysis, light chains in myeloma, radio-iodine contrast, drugs such as aminoglycosides, rifampicin, amphotericin B, tenofovir, traditional remedies, some Chinese medicines) OR tubulitis
- Interstitium - acute interstitial nephritis (from drugs, e.g. rifampicin, bactrim) and from sepsis, autoimmune
- Glomeruli - glomerulonephritis, e.g. post infection/autoimmune - can be drug induced
- Vessels - vasculitis, malignant hypertension, scleroderma, renal artery stenosis, pre-eclampsia | | Post Renal | - Urinary tract obstruction - cancer of the cervix, rectum, or prostate (also benign prostatic enlargement), renal stones, iatrogenic ureteric laceration, retroperitoneal fibrosis, intratubular crystals (e.g. acyclovir) | Pre-renal AKI is not always associated with hypovolemia; fluid administration should be based on clinical signs of hypovolemia. Kucatseka = enema.

text:
### Conditions causing acute kidney injury with examples: reduced glomerular function (pre-renal), renal parenchymal injury (intrinsic), urinary tract obstruction (post-renal)

| Category | Conditions | Examples / Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Conditions that reduce glomerular function (pre-renal) | Hypotension / Hypovolemia | Dehydration, hemorrhage, shock |
| 1. Conditions that reduce glomerular function (pre-renal) | Reduced Renal Artery Perfusion | Renal artery stenosis, aortic dissection |
| 1. Conditions that reduce glomerular function (pre-renal) | Excessive Diuresis | Seen in diabetic emergencies, hypercalcemia, or overuse of diuretics |
| 1. Conditions that reduce glomerular function (pre-renal) | Renal Venous Congestion | Common in right heart failure – may need diuretics |
| 1. Conditions that reduce glomerular function (pre-renal) | Abdominal Compartment Syndrome | After bowel surgery, or in presence of tense ascites |
| 2. Renal Parenchymal Injury (Intrinsic) | Sepsis | Sepsis-associated acute tubular necrosis (ATN) |
| 2. Renal Parenchymal Injury (Intrinsic) | Drugs | NSAIDs, timbita, aminoglycosides, radiocontrast agents |
| 2. Renal Parenchymal Injury (Intrinsic) | Endogenous toxins | Myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis), hemoglobin (hemolysis), uric acid |
| 2. Renal Parenchymal Injury (Intrinsic) | Exogenous toxins | Ethylene glycol, heavy metals |
| 2. Renal Parenchymal Injury (Intrinsic) | Autoimmune | Lupus nephritis, ANCA vasculitis |
| 2. Renal Parenchymal Injury (Intrinsic) | Neoplastic | Multiple myeloma (cast nephropathy) |
| 3. Urinary Tract Obstruction (post-renal) | Nephrolithiasis | Kidney stones |
| 3. Urinary Tract Obstruction (post-renal) | Blood clots | May occur after trauma or surgery |
| 3. Urinary Tract Obstruction (post-renal) | Sloughed papillae | Seen in analgesic nephropathy, diabetes |
| 3. Urinary Tract Obstruction (post-renal) | Intrinsic obstruction | Urethral/ureteric strictures |
| 3. Urinary Tract Obstruction (post-renal) | Extrinsic compression | Pelvic tumors, retroperitoneal fibrosis, iatrogenic (e.g., ureter injury during TAH) |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Diagnosis of Acute Kidney Injury > Algorithm for Diagnosis and Management of Acute Kidney Injury
text:
### Algorithm for diagnosis and management of acute kidney injury: history, examination, investigations, staging, referral at stage 3, volume status, pre-renal/intrinsic/post-renal causes and investigations

1. History of present illness: fluid intake and losses, oedema, severe systemic illness, shortness of breath, poor urine output or no urine output for more than 6 hours.
2. Physical signs: tachycardia, JVP, oedema, encephalopathy, dry mucous membranes, weak pulses, decreased level of consciousness.
3. Investigations: renal function, electrolytes, urine sediment, abdominal U/S, ECG if K is high.
4. Classify the AKI stage (KDIGO/AKIN): stage 1: creatinine x1.5 baseline, urine output <0.5 ml/kg/hour for 6 hours; stage 2: creatinine x2 baseline, urine output <0.5 ml/kg/hour for 12 hours; stage 3: creatinine >3x, creatinine >356 mmol/l (as printed), urine output <0.5 ml/kg/hour for 24 hours.
5. Confirm AKI.
   - Stage 3: refer to a (paediatric) nephrologist in a centre that can perform RRT. All referrals in stage 3 who are stable need to be discussed with a physician and the receiving facility before referral.
   - Stages 1 and 2: assess volume status, identify the causes, identify complications of AKI:
     - Hypovolemia → pre-renal. Investigations: CBC, LFTs, CXR, ECG, UE, echocardiogram. Differential diagnosis: dehydration (inadequate fluid intake; GI losses - vomiting, diarrhoea; third spacing - sepsis, burns, pericarditis, nephrotic syndrome; salt wasting - renal/adrenal disease); blood loss; reduced cardiac output (congestive heart failure, cardiac tamponade, cardiogenic shock); sepsis; hepatorenal syndrome.
     - Euvolemia → intrinsic renal. Investigations: serum CBC, LDH, albumin, hepatitis serology, UE; urine eosinophils; renal US + Doppler. Differential diagnosis: renal artery stenosis, venous thrombosis; vasculitis; HUS; glomerulonephritides; RPGN; TIN; acute tubular necrosis (nephrotoxic drugs, rhabdomyolysis, radiocontrast nephropathy, uric acid nephropathy, etc.).
     - Third column (obstruction; labelled 'Hypovolemia / Pre-renal' as printed). Investigations: metabolic stone profile; abdominal US/CT. Differential diagnosis: posterior urethral valves; nephro/urolithiasis; blood clot; fungal ball; tumours; retroperitoneal process; fibrosis; haematoma. Needs urologist and nephrologist consult; relieve the obstruction.
6. Drug administration & monitoring: treat underlying causes, avoid nephrotoxic drugs, IV antibiotics; monitor complications; monitor weight and urine output daily; if possible check UE, creatinine and plasma bicarbonate, Ca, PO4, FBC daily until stable.

text:
### AKI staging (KDIGO): serum creatinine and urine output criteria for stages 1-3

| Stage | Serum creatinine | Urine output (common to both) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage 1 | Increase of ≥0.3 mg/dl (≥26.5 umol/l) or increase to ≥150% to 200% (1.5- to 2-fold) from baseline | Less than 0.5 ml/kg/h for more than 6 hours |
| Stage 2 | Increase to more than 200% to 300% (>2- to 3-fold) from baseline | Less than 0.5 ml/kg/h for more than 12 hours |
| Stage 3 | Increase to more than 300% (>3-fold) from baseline, or ≥4.0 mg/dl (≥354 umol/l) with an acute increase of at least 0.5 mg/dl (44 umol/l), or on RRT | Less than 0.3 ml/kg/h for 24 hours or anuria for 12 hours |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Algorithm for Diagnosis and Management of Acute Kidney Injury > Fluid, hypertension, electrolyte and nutrition management; urgent dialysis
text:
### AKI management (algorithm, continued): fluid management, hypertension, electrolytes and acidosis (hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, acidosis), nutrition, and indications for urgent dialysis

Fluid management:
- Volume status: hypovolemia: fluid bolus NaCl 0.9% 20 ml/kg and rehydration.
- Euvolemic: insensible losses (400 ml/m2 or 30 ml/kg/day) + urine and GI losses.
- Hypervolemia: insensible losses; furosemide 2-4 mg/kg.
- If nephrotic syndrome: consider 25% albumin 0.5 to 1 g/kg/dose over 30 to 60 (min), followed by a diuretic: Lasix 1-2 mg/kg.
Hypertension:
- Furosemide if fluid overload: IV, start 1 to 2 mg/kg/dose, 2nd dose 6 hours later (max 6 mg/kg).
- Calcium channel blockers: amlodipine oral 0.05 to 0.3 mg/kg/dose OD (max 0.6 mg/kg/dose or 10 mg).
- IV labetalol 0.2 to 1 mg/kg/dose if severe hypertension.
- N.B. Avoid ACEI & ARBs in AKI.
Electrolytes and acidosis:
- Hyperkalemia: 10% calcium gluconate 0.5-1 ml/kg over 10 min + glucose ('25-5 mls' of D10W, as printed) with insulin 0.1 IU/kg; +/- salbutamol nebulised 2.5 mg (<25 kg) and 5 mg (>25 kg); +/- sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol (ml)/kg over 10-30 min; / calcium resonium (kayexalate) 1 g/kg 4-hourly with oral lactulose 2.5 ml (<1 year), 5 ml (1-5 years), 10 ml (>5 years).
- Hyponatremia: if Na <118 mmol/l, calculate the sodium deficit: Na deficit = (125 - measured Na) x weight x 0.6; give over 2 hours as hypertonic saline 3%, target 125 mmol/l.
- Hypocalcemia: 10% calcium gluconate 0.1 mg/kg (0.5 ml/kg), as printed.
- Acidosis: 8.4% NaHCO3 deficit = (18 - measured HCO3) x 0.5 x weight, or NaHCO3 1-2 mmol/kg/dose TDS.
Nutrition: adequate nutrition is mandatory; from day 2 introduce protein gradually. Requirements: 95-115 kcal/kg and protein 1.5-2 g/kg ('1.5-21 g/kg' printed). Treat underlying causes.

Urgent dialysis if: hyperkalemia > 6.5 mmol/L ('605mmol/L' printed) not responding to medical treatment; severe fluid overload with pulmonary edema resistant to furosemide; urea > 40 mmol/L (30 mmol/L in neonates); severe hyponatremia (Na <120 mEq/L) or hypernatremia (Na >160 mEq/L) or severe acidosis pH <7.2 that cannot be corrected with HCO3 due to fluid overload, or refractory; multi-system failure; anticipation of prolonged oliguria. → Refer to tertiary renal replacement therapy. All referrals requiring urgent RRT must be discussed with the physician and the receiving facility before referral.

Urgent dialysis if: hyperkalemia > 6.5 mmol/L ('605mmol/L' printed) not responding to medical treatment; severe fluid overload with pulmonary edema resistant to furosemide; urea > 40 mmol/L (30 mmol/L in neonates); severe hyponatremia (Na <120 mEq/L) or hypernatremia (Na >160 mEq/L) or severe acidosis pH <7.2 that cannot be corrected with HCO3 due to fluid overload, or refractory; multi-system failure; anticipation of prolonged oliguria. → Refer to tertiary renal replacement therapy. All referrals requiring urgent RRT must be discussed with the physician and the receiving facility before referral.
html:
Fluid management:
- Volume status: hypovolemia: fluid bolus NaCl 0.9% 20 ml/kg and rehydration.
- Euvolemic: insensible losses (400 ml/m2 or 30 ml/kg/day) + urine and GI losses.
- Hypervolemia: insensible losses; furosemide 2-4 mg/kg.
- If nephrotic syndrome: consider 25% albumin 0.5 to 1 g/kg/dose over 30 to 60 (min), followed by a diuretic: Lasix 1-2 mg/kg.
Hypertension:
- Furosemide if fluid overload: IV, start 1 to 2 mg/kg/dose, 2nd dose 6 hours later (max 6 mg/kg).
- Calcium channel blockers: amlodipine oral 0.05 to 0.3 mg/kg/dose OD (max 0.6 mg/kg/dose or 10 mg).
- IV labetalol 0.2 to 1 mg/kg/dose if severe hypertension.
- N.B. Avoid ACEI & ARBs in AKI.
Electrolytes and acidosis:
- Hyperkalemia: 10% calcium gluconate 0.5-1 ml/kg over 10 min + glucose ('25-5 mls' of D10W, as printed) with insulin 0.1 IU/kg; +/- salbutamol nebulised 2.5 mg (<25 kg) and 5 mg (>25 kg); +/- sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol (ml)/kg over 10-30 min; / calcium resonium (kayexalate) 1 g/kg 4-hourly with oral lactulose 2.5 ml (<1 year), 5 ml (1-5 years), 10 ml (>5 years).
- Hyponatremia: if Na <118 mmol/l, calculate the sodium deficit: Na deficit = (125 - measured Na) x weight x 0.6; give over 2 hours as hypertonic saline 3%, target 125 mmol/l.
- Hypocalcemia: 10% calcium gluconate 0.1 mg/kg (0.5 ml/kg), as printed.
- Acidosis: 8.4% NaHCO3 deficit = (18 - measured HCO3) x 0.5 x weight, or NaHCO3 1-2 mmol/kg/dose TDS.
Nutrition: adequate nutrition is mandatory; from day 2 introduce protein gradually. Requirements: 95-115 kcal/kg and protein 1.5-2 g/kg ('1.5-21 g/kg' printed). Treat underlying causes.

Urgent dialysis if: hyperkalemia > 6.5 mmol/L ('605mmol/L' printed) not responding to medical treatment; severe fluid overload with pulmonary edema resistant to furosemide; urea > 40 mmol/L (30 mmol/L in neonates); severe hyponatremia (Na <120 mEq/L) or hypernatremia (Na >160 mEq/L) or severe acidosis pH <7.2 that cannot be corrected with HCO3 due to fluid overload, or refractory; multi-system failure; anticipation of prolonged oliguria. → Refer to tertiary renal replacement therapy. All referrals requiring urgent RRT must be discussed with the physician and the receiving facility before referral.

text:
### Definitions of AKI, AKD (acute kidney diseases and disorders), CKD and NKD (no kidney disease): functional and structural criteria

| Acronym | Functional Criteria | Structural Criteria |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AKI | Increase in SCr by > 50% within 7 d, OR increase in SCr by > 0.3 mg/dl (>26.5 umol/l) within 48 h, OR oliguria | No criteria |
| CKD | GFR < 60 ml/min per 1.73 m² for < 3 mo (as printed) |  |
| AKD | AKI, OR decrease in GFR by > 35% or increase in SCr by > 50% for < 3 mo | Kidney damage > 3 mo (as printed) |
| NKD | GFR > 60 ml/min per 1.73 m²; stable SCr without AKI/AKD/CKD | No damage |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Schematic for AKI/AKD Follow up According to Level of Health Facility
text:
### AKI/AKD follow-up by severity: who follows up and when, from short stage 1 AKI (non-nephrology care) to stage 3D or prior CKD 4 (nephrology within 1 week) (ADQI schematic)

Follow-up after AKI/AKD, from least to most severe (left to right in the schematic; non-nephrology care providers at the mild end, nephrology at the severe end):
1. Stage 1 AKI of short duration (1 day); SCr normal or returns to baseline; hospital-limited event in a healthy patient → consider KAMPS bundle within 1 year.
2. Stage 1 AKI lasting 1-2 days; limited comorbidities; no prior CKD; SCr not returning to baseline → consider KAMPS in 6 months.
3. Prolonged stage 1 AKI (3-6 days) or stage 2 AKI of shorter duration (1-3 days); increasing comorbidities (advancing age); SCr persistently elevated (<25% above pre-existing baseline) → labs in the next 3-6 weeks with long-term KAMPS/nephrology appointment (within the next several months).
4. Prolonged stage 2 AKI with urine analysis showing injury (duration >7 days); multiple comorbidities (cancer, prior AKIs, mild CKD at baseline); SCr persistently elevated >25% above prior baseline in some recovery → labs within days of discharge and follow-up with nephrology; appointment/KAMPS within weeks.
5. Prolonged stage 3 AKI and persistent other forms of AKI or kidney disease; history of prior AKI, significant CV disease, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and advanced CKD → labs within days of discharge and follow-up with nephrology.
6. AKI stage 3D (dialysis), recovered and non-recovered; prior CKD 4; recurrent AKI/AKD → KAMPS or WATCH-ME labs within days of discharge and follow-up with nephrology within 1 week.

Example: a patient with CKD G4, regardless of AKI severity, should be followed by a nephrologist within 1 week. Abbreviations: 3D, dialysis; SCr, serum creatinine; UA, urine analysis; WATCH-ME, weight assessment, access, teaching, clearance, hypotension, medications; KAMPS (kidney function, awareness, medications, pressure, sick-day protocol). Reproduced from Acute Dialysis Quality Initiative (ADQI) XXII.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Requirements for AKI screening by level of health facility
text:
### AKI screening requirements by level of health facility: primary care clinic, health centre/regional hospital, tertiary care | Primary Care Clinic | Health Center/Regional Hospital | Tertiary Care | | --- | --- | --- | | - Vital signs
- Weight (kg)
- Height (m or cm)
- Urine dipstick
- Good history & physical exam
- Medication & OTC review | - Includes all primary care assessments
- Urine analysis
- Urine microscopy, culture & sensitivity
- Blood tests: FBC, BUN, electrolytes, CO2/bicarbonate, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, glucose, LFTs, uric acid, HIV, hepatitis B & C, RPR
- Estimate GFR (Cockcroft-Gault if no lab eGFR)
- Blood cultures
- Abdominal ultrasound scan
- Cardiac monitoring | - Includes all health centre/regional hospital assessments
- Autoimmune serology (ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM)
- Myeloma screen (serum protein electrophoresis, urine Bence Jones proteins, serum free light chains)
- Urine stone analysis
- CT scan, intravenous pyelogram (IVP), urodynamic studies
- Urologist for de-obstruction
- Kidney biopsy (histopathology within 1 week) |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Patient Assessment
text:
### AKI patient assessment: vital signs targets, history, life-threatening effects, cardiac monitoring, ultrasound, urine analysis, chest X-ray | Assessment Domain | Details | | --- | --- | | Vital Signs | - Pulse
- Blood pressure: aim MAP > 65 mmHg and < 110 mmHg (MAP = DBP + 1/3 PP; PP = SBP - DBP)
- Urine output: aim > 0.5 mL/kg/hour | | Patient History | - Presenting complaint
- Past medical, surgical, OBGYN, urology history
- Systems enquiry: nervous, musculoskeletal, endocrine, respiratory, cardiovascular, GI, ENT, dermatological
- Drug/toxin history (including OTC and herbal remedies)
- Urine output history
- Occupational history (e.g., laborer in hot weather) | | Life-Threatening AKI Effects | - Pulmonary edema: SpO2, clinical signs, arterial blood gas (ABG)
- Hyperkalemia: ABG, electrolytes
- Metabolic acidosis: ABG | | Cardiac Monitoring | - ECG for hyperkalemia signs, LV hypertrophy, heart block, myocardial ischemia | | Imaging: Abdominal Ultrasound | - Exclude urinary tract obstruction (urgent de-obstruction needed)
- Assess kidney size (normal: 9–12 cm), appearance, and echogenicity | | Urine Analysis | - Dipstick: specific gravity, protein, blood, leukocytes
- Microscopy: granular casts → ATN / GN; red cell casts / dysmorphic RBCs → RPGN; leukocytes → pyelonephritis / AIN | | Chest X-ray | - Assess for fluid overload (pulmonary edema), cardiomegaly, pericardial effusion, or cardiomyopathy
- Exclude pulmonary-renal syndrome (look for infiltrates) |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Non-Pharmacological Management of Acute Kidney Injury
text:
### Non-pharmacological management of AKI by level of care: primary care clinic vs health centre and hospitals | Primary Care Clinic | Health Center, Regional Hospital, Referral Hospital | | --- | --- | | - Stop intake of all salt and potassium containing foods and fluids
- For dehydration (watch out for tachycardia, hypotension, capillary refill > 2 seconds, low jugular venous pressure, dry armpits): encourage fluid intake, to 10 mL/kg/day plus visible fluid losses, to avoid fluid overload
- Remove nephrotoxic medications
- Avoid fluid overload in heart failure and advanced kidney failure
- Avoid nephrotoxins – avoid use of herbal remedy mixes | - As previous PLUS:
- Give oxygen, and nurse in semi-Fowler's position if patient has respiratory distress
- Adequate nutritional support: enough energy and adequate protein. Consider enteral/parenteral nutrition
- Monitor fluid input and output
- MDT client care depending on underlying cause of AKI |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Pharmacological Management of Acute Kidney Injury > Fluid Challenge/Inotropes
text:
### AKI fluid challenge and inotropes: adults (500 ml boluses up to 2 L, adrenaline infusion) vs children (oral rehydration by dehydration severity, 20 ml/kg bolus) Adjunct therapies are directed by the underlying cause: crystalloids for rehydration (preferably balanced solutions such as Ringer Lactate); relieve obstruction urgently; treat sepsis; immunosuppression as directed; treat electrolytes (hypercalcaemia); treat right heart failure (diuretics); relieve intra-abdominal pressure. Furosemide stress test: IV furosemide 1 mg/kg (furosemide-naïve) or 1.5 mg/kg (already on it); >200 ml urine over the next 2 hours suggests intact tubular function and likely recovery; <200 ml predicts ongoing dysfunction that may need dialysis. | Adults | Children | | --- | --- | | Fluid bolus of 500 ml isotonic fluid (preferably Ringer Lactate) over 15 minutes and reassess (BP, pulse, JVP, urine output), up to a total of 2 litres, to achieve mean arterial pressure >65 mmHg.
Start inotropes if adequate fluid challenge but still hypotensive, to avoid fluid overload and ensure tissue perfusion, e.g. adrenaline 4 mg (4 amps) in 200 ml of N/S IV at 10 ml/hr.
REMEMBER to look for hypoglycaemia/sepsis/other associated complications and start treatment as indicated. Request Intensive Care Unit review urgently. | Rehydrate per protocol for age and body weight.
Mild dehydration: oral rehydration solution 5 ml (1 teaspoon) every 5 minutes to replace losses, OR 10 ml/kg body weight for each loose stool.
Moderate dehydration: 5 ml oral rehydration solution every 5 minutes to a total of 50-100 ml/kg body weight over 2-4 hours.
Severe dehydration and failed oral rehydration: start cautious rehydration with a bolus of 20 ml/kg isotonic fluid such as Ringer Lactate IV, followed by maintenance IV fluids per paediatric protocols.
URGENT REFERRAL FOR ICU CARE. DO NOT OVERHYDRATE, AS IT IS LINKED TO INCREASED MORTALITY. |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Pharmacological Management of Acute Kidney Injury > Hyperkalaemia in AKI
text:
### Hyperkalaemia (K ≥6 mmol/l) in AKI: adults vs children: calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose, bicarbonate, salbutamol, potassium binder, furosemide, dialysis If hyperkalemia (≥6 mmol/l): cardiac monitor (risk of bradycardia, asystole, and ventricular arrhythmias). Fluid overload in kidney failure: IV furosemide at high doses (at least 120 mg, maximum 500 mg in 24 hours in adults); oxygen; isordil 5 mg sublingually; IV nitrate; morphine 2.5 mg IV titrated, maximum 10 mg, monitoring BP; urgent dialysis (referral to a centre with haemodialysis). | Adults | Children | | --- | --- | | - Stabilize myocardium with bolus IV calcium gluconate 10% at 10 ml over 2 minutes (maximum 20 ml). DO NOT GIVE AT THE SAME TIME/SAME DRIP AS SODIUM BICARBONATE.
- Shift potassium with ONLY 5 units (five units) short acting insulin (Actrapid) in 50 ml of dextrose 50% over 30 minutes (higher insulin amounts can accumulate in kidney failure and cause dangerous hypoglycaemia).
- Shift with salbutamol nebulizer at 10-20 mg every 1-2 hours (MONITOR FOR TACHYCARDIA AND ARRHYTHMIAS).
- Potassium binder such as sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) 15 g mixed in 100 ml water once daily (CAUTION – DO NOT GIVE IF BOWEL PATHOLOGY).
- If overloaded, give furosemide IV 40-80 mg to aid urinary potassium loss.
- Urgent referral for dialysis, or acute peritoneal dialysis locally per protocol. | - Stabilize myocardium with bolus IV calcium gluconate 0.5 ml/kg over 2-5 minutes.
- Shift potassium with dextrose 10% at 5 ml/kg IV bolus; if severe hyperkalemia, dextrose 10% 5 ml/kg IV bolus + Actrapid (short acting insulin) 0.1 units/kg (ESSENTIAL TO CHECK GLUCOSE EVERY 15-30 MINUTES AND CORRECT IF LOWER THAN 4 MMOL/L).
- Shift potassium with sodium bicarbonate (8.4%) 1-2 mmol/kg IV over 5 minutes.
- Shift potassium with salbutamol nebulizer – 2.5 mg if <25 kg and 5 mg if >25 kg, given 1-2 hourly (MONITOR FOR TACHYCARDIA AND ARRHYTHMIAS).
- DO NOT GIVE KAYEXALATE TO CHILDREN, AS IT CAN CAUSE NECROTISING ENTEROCOLITIS.
- If fluid overloaded, give furosemide IV 1-2 mg/kg; can repeat after 6 hours (individual dose not to exceed 6 mg/kg).
- Urgent referral for dialysis, or acute peritoneal dialysis locally per protocol while awaiting transfer or specialist review. |

text:
### Clinical contexts for fluid administration in patients with or at risk of AKI: reasons, benefits, challenges and risks by age, setting, comorbidity and acute condition | Clinical context | Reasons for fluid administration and potential benefits | Challenges and risks of fluid administration | | --- | --- | --- | | Age and demographics: children, adults | - Diseases with volume losses
- Indications likely to be context-dependent | - Narrow window between hypovolemia and fluid overload
- Clear adverse effects of fluid overload
- Adverse effects of 'one size fits all' approach to fluid management
- Uncertain definition of clinically significant fluid overload
- In patients with heart disease, poor cardiac reserve to tolerate hypovolemia and hypervolemia
- In patients with diastolic dysfunction, risk of potentiating venous hypertension and renal congestion in fluid overload | | Settings: resource-limited; pre-hospital, ward, ICU | - Specific conditions including diarrheal illness
- Impetus toward early resuscitation
- Dynamic phases of illness associated with hypovolemia | - Differing spectrum of disease
- Potentially delayed presentation to secondary care
- Limited range of therapeutic options
- Lack of advanced hemodynamic monitoring
- Inappropriate administration of maintenance fluid
- Risk of 'fluid-creep' leading to insidious fluid overload | | Comorbid diseases: CKD; CHF or severe valvular disease | - Inability to conserve salt and water
- Poor cardiac reserve to tolerate hypovolemia | - Risk of hypovolemia
- Inability to handle fluid excess
- Predisposition to AKI
- Potentiation of adverse effects of fluid overload
- Potentially pre-existing interstitial edema
- Higher CVP associated with worsening kidney function
- Precipitation of fluid accumulation | | Acute conditions: dehydration, hypovolemia, hemorrhage, sepsis, cardiogenic shock, major surgery, nephrotoxic exposure, abdominal compartment syndrome, ARDS, rhabdomyolysis/crush injury | - Acute free water deficit
- Salt and water deficit
- Acutely impaired oxygen delivery
- Intravascular hypovolemia
- Inability to tolerate hypovolemia
- Venodilation due to inotropic drugs
- Anesthesia-induced venodilation and vasodilation
- Perioperative fluid losses
- Dilution of filtered toxins
- Maintenance of visceral and renal perfusion
- Reduced cardiac preload due to high intrathoracic pressure
- Dilution of myoglobin
- Intravascular hypovolemia due to fluid losses to injured muscle | - Challenges of managing relative water and sodium deficits
- Need for consensus on optimal endpoints of resuscitation
- Dilution of hemoglobin may offset effects of fluid resuscitation on oxygen delivery
- Endothelial dysfunction, capillary leak, fluid losses to interstitium and vasodilation
- Lack of evidence for goal-directed hemodynamic therapy
- Risk of pulmonary edema
- Association between high CVP and adverse kidney outcome
- Inappropriate administration of maintenance fluid and 'fluid creep' leading to insidious fluid overload
- Risk of fluid overload
- Risk of venous hypertension
- Risk of worsening alveolar edema
- Development/worsening of compartment syndrome | | Timing: biomarker-positive states; AKI stage | - Prevention of progression to overt AKI
- Reversal of early AKI | - Presence of early renal injury does not signify need for volume replacement
- Inappropriate attempts to 'reverse' established AKI resulting in fluid overload | | Oliguria/anuria | - Oliguria as an indication of acute compensated hypovolemia | - Multiple etiologies of oliguria beyond hypovolemia
- Vicious cycle of fluid overload resulting in worsening kidney function | AKI, acute kidney injury; ARDS, acute respiratory distress syndrome; CHF, congestive heart failure; CVP, central venous pressure; ICU, intensive care unit. Source: Kidney International (2020) 98, 294-309.

text:
### Complications of acute kidney injury: short term (fluid overload, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, uraemia, hypocalcaemia, drug toxicity) and long term (CKD, mortality, CV risk) | Short Term | Long Term | | --- | --- | | 1. Fluid overload related – pulmonary edema, hypertension
2. Electrolyte related – hyperkalemia with risks of bradycardia and asystole or ventricular fibrillation
3. Metabolic acidosis – Kussmaul respiration
4. Uraemic – uraemic pericarditis (risk of tamponade, especially following haemorrhagic conversion from heparin use during haemodialysis); uraemic encephalopathy (tremor, confusion, coma, seizures)
5. Electrolyte related – may have hypocalcaemia (seizures, tetany – though commoner in CKD)
6. Systemic toxicity from accumulation of renally cleared pharmacologic agents – e.g. gadolinium, ethambutol | 1. Progression to CKD
2. Worsening of underlying CKD
3. Mortality risk
4. Cardiovascular risk |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Acute Kidney Injury in Adults and Children > Pregnancy-Related AKI > Causes of PR-AKI
text:
### Causes of pregnancy-related acute kidney injury by trimester and postpartum (timeline), with disease-specific treatment and management of PR-AKI

Timeline of causes (bars across first, second, third trimester and postpartum):
- First trimester: hyperemesis gravidarum; septic abortion.
- Glomerulonephritis: from the first trimester through the third trimester.
- Urinary tract infection/pyelonephritis: late first trimester through the second and early third trimester.
- Preeclampsia/eclampsia/HELLP syndrome: from the second trimester into early postpartum.
- Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: second and third trimester.
- Placental abruption/haemorrhage: late second and third trimester.
- Obstruction: second and third trimester.
- Acute fatty liver: third trimester and postpartum.
- Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome: third trimester and postpartum.

Disease-specific treatment of AKI in pregnancy:
| Cause | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Hyperemesis gravidarum/prerenal causes | Hydration |
| Septic abortion/urinary tract infection | Antibiotics |
| Preeclampsia/HELLP/acute fatty liver of pregnancy | Delivery |
| Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura | Plasma exchange, rituximab |
| Atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome | Eculizumab |
| Obstructive uropathy | Analgesics, stent, nephrostomy |
| Placental abruption and haemorrhage | Control bleeding, delivery |
| Glomerulonephritis | Steroids, immunosuppression |

HELLP: hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets.
Management of PR-AKI: 1. risk reduction – close monitoring and hydration for hyperemesis gravidarum; 2. monitor for urosepsis and treat early; 3. reduce pre-eclampsia risk in patients with underlying CKD – aspirin, calcium, BP control.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Causes of CKD
text:
### Causes of chronic kidney disease by category: vascular, glomerular, tubulointerstitial, structural, others (CKDu, COVAN, chronic infections)

Chronic kidney disease is structural or functional kidney damage present for >3 months, with or without a decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

| Category | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Vascular | Hypertension, vasculitis etc. Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis, Takayasu's arteritis, fibromuscular dysplasia etc. |
| Glomerular Diseases | Diabetes, autoimmune diseases (e.g. lupus nephritis), chronic systemic infections (e.g. HIV, HBV, syphilis), drugs, neoplasia, glomerulonephritis, glomerulopathies |
| Tubulointerstitial Diseases | UTI, drug-induced interstitial nephritis (e.g. traditional herbs (timbita), rifampicin, allopurinol, fluoroquinolones, sulphonamides, beta-lactam antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors, NSAIDs), infective, autoimmune, toxins, neoplasms e.g. myeloma |
| Structural | Hereditary - polycystic kidneys, renal masses, obstruction (stones, strictures), CAKUT in children (congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract) |
| Others | Congenital - other congenital diseases (glomerular or tubular), e.g. Alport's syndrome. CKDu – CKD of unknown etiology amongst laborers in hot climates with no other traditional CKD risk factors (? due to heat and dehydration). COVAN – COVID-19 nephropathy with proteinuria. Chronic infections – HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, malaria etc. (can affect all areas of renal parenchyma). Chronic obstruction/posterior urethral valves (developmental)/vesicoureteric reflux (developmental), nephrolithiasis (kidney stones) |

A previous episode of acute kidney injury or acute kidney disease can lead to CKD; therefore all patients with a history of AKI require follow-up of renal function.
Many causes are potentially preventable or modifiable if detected early.

text:
### Measures of kidney function: direct measures (creatinine clearance, measured GFR), estimating equations for adults and children (Cockcroft-Gault, MDRD, CKD-EPI, FAS, Schwartz), and limitations | Direct measures of kidney function | Indirect measures of kidney function: estimating equation | | --- | --- | | - Creatinine clearance
- 24h urine creatinine | - eGFR | | - Measured GFR\*: inulin clearance (gold standard); radioisotopic plasma clearance (1): 125I-iothalamate, 99mTc-DTPA, 51Cr-EDTA; non-radioisotopic plasma clearance: iohexol (2) | Adults:
- Cockcroft-Gault (3): (140 - age) x weight [kg] (x 0.85 if female) / (serum creatinine [mg/dl] x 72)
- Modification of diet in renal disease (MDRD) equations (4) (not valid for eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)
- CKD-EPI creatinine equation (preferred); valid with eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2
- CKD-EPI cystatin C equations (5) (valid for eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)
- Full Age Spectrum (FAS) equation (7); valid even in eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2
Children:
- Schwartz equation and its modifications (6)
- Full-age spectrum (FAS) formulae (7) | **Limitation (applies to every row):** - No estimate of kidney function has been specifically validated for glomerular disease and/or nephrotic syndrome
- Ethnicity is often a confounding influence
- In creatinine-based formulas, hypoalbuminemia may lead to overestimation of true GFR due to increased tubular creatinine secretion (8)
- Glucocorticoids may increase serum cystatin C, potentially underestimating eGFR (9)
- Low muscle mass overestimates eGFR using creatinine-based formulae (10)
- AKI confounds all estimates, which are valid only in steady state Assessment of kidney function in glomerular disease. *In ml/min per 1.73 m2. The correct coefficient for race in GFR estimating equations is controversial (see the KDIGO CKD guideline). References: 1 Perrone et al.; 2 Gaspari et al.; 3 Cockcroft and Gault; 4 and 5 Stevens et al.; 6 Schwartz et al.; 7 Pottel et al.; 8 Branten et al.; 9 Zhai et al.; 10 Levey et al. - 24h urine creatinine | - eGFR | | - Measured GFR\*: inulin clearance (gold standard); radioisotopic plasma clearance (1): 125I-iothalamate, 99mTc-DTPA, 51Cr-EDTA; non-radioisotopic plasma clearance: iohexol (2) | Adults:
- Cockcroft-Gault (3): (140 - age) x weight [kg] (x 0.85 if female) / (serum creatinine [mg/dl] x 72)
- Modification of diet in renal disease (MDRD) equations (4) (not valid for eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)
- CKD-EPI creatinine equation (preferred); valid with eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2
- CKD-EPI cystatin C equations (5) (valid for eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2)
- Full Age Spectrum (FAS) equation (7); valid even in eGFR > 60 ml/min/1.73 m2
Children:
- Schwartz equation and its modifications (6)
- Full-age spectrum (FAS) formulae (7) | **Limitation (applies to every row):** - No estimate of kidney function has been specifically validated for glomerular disease and/or nephrotic syndrome
- Ethnicity is often a confounding influence
- In creatinine-based formulas, hypoalbuminemia may lead to overestimation of true GFR due to increased tubular creatinine secretion (8)
- Glucocorticoids may increase serum cystatin C, potentially underestimating eGFR (9)
- Low muscle mass overestimates eGFR using creatinine-based formulae (10)
- AKI confounds all estimates, which are valid only in steady state Assessment of kidney function in glomerular disease. *In ml/min per 1.73 m2. The correct coefficient for race in GFR estimating equations is controversial (see the KDIGO CKD guideline). References: 1 Perrone et al.; 2 Gaspari et al.; 3 Cockcroft and Gault; 4 and 5 Stevens et al.; 6 Schwartz et al.; 7 Pottel et al.; 8 Branten et al.; 9 Zhai et al.; 10 Levey et al. CKD-EPI, Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration; 51Cr-EDTA, chromium-51 labelled ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid; 99mTc-DTPA, technetium-diethylenetriamine pentaacetic acid.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Screening and Diagnosis of Chronic Kidney Disease > Screening Algorithm for Kidney Disease
text:
### Screening algorithm for chronic kidney disease: who to screen, tests, CKD criteria, and lifestyle, medical treatment and other considerations

1. Area population:
   - No markers of risk: do not screen; rescreen based on future patient assessment.
   - Risk factors (high blood pressure; diabetes; cardiovascular disease; family history of CKD): screen.
2. Tests: blood glucose; spot urine; blood pressure; family history. Measure kidney function (serum creatinine or cystatin C; calculate eGFR) and kidney injury (albuminuria/proteinuria).
3. Do the results indicate CKD (eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 or albuminuria/proteinuria, ACR >30 mg/mmol as printed)?
   - No: rescreen based on future patient assessment.
   - Yes:
     - Lifestyle modification: smoking cessation; well-balanced diet; regular exercise; limit sodium intake to <2 g/day.
     - Medical treatment: blood pressure, diabetes and lipid control: ACEi/ARB therapy; SGLT2 inhibition; metformin; statins.
     - Considerations: drug dosing; contrast media use; hyperkalemia; CKD/CVD factors: anaemia, bone disease, heart failure, other (hepatitis C, metabolic acidosis, etc.).
     - Retesting; follow-up office visits; referral to a nephrologist when appropriate.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Algorithm to screen, risk stratify and treat CKD
text:
### Algorithm to screen, risk-stratify and treat CKD (KDIGO-based): conditions of CKD risk, testing, classification, patient safety by eGFR, slowing progression and complications, CVD risk reduction, and when to refer to nephrology

1. Conditions of CKD risk: hypertension; diabetes; cardiovascular disease; AKI/hospitalisation history; family history of kidney disease; obesity; older age*; other high-risk comorbidities, environmental exposures, or genetic factors.
2. Consider screening for CKD: urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR) to detect albuminuria; serum creatinine and cystatin C to estimate GFR.
3. Is any of the following present for 3 months or more: eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m²; ACR >30 mg/g (3 mg/mmol); markers of kidney disease?
   - No: periodically repeat evaluation.
   - Yes: classify/risk-stratify the CKD stage; identify and treat the specific cause of CKD.
     - eGFR category (ml/min/1.73 m²): G1 ≥90; G2 60-89; G3b 30-44; G4 15-29; G5 <15 (G3a is not listed).
     - Albuminuria category: A1 (normal or mild) <30 mg/g or <3 mg/mmol; A2 (moderate) 30-300 mg/g or 3-30 mg/mmol; A3 (severe) >300 mg/g or >30 mg/mmol.

Patient safety (all patients with eGFR <60): dose medications based on eGFR; reduce the risk of AKI from volume depletion; adopt 'sick day rules' as needed; avoid dual ACEi and ARB blockade; prevent contrast-associated AKI (lowest possible radiocontrast dose; adequate hydration before, during and after the procedure, consider isotonic saline; withhold ACEi or ARBs, diuretics and other nephrotoxic agents before and after the procedure).
- eGFR 45-59: avoid prolonged NSAIDs.
- eGFR 30-44: avoid prolonged NSAIDs; use metformin with close monitoring at 50% dose.
- eGFR <30: avoid any NSAIDs; avoid bisphosphonates; avoid metformin; avoid PICC lines (access preservation); if on warfarin, monitor PT-INR closely given increased risk of bleeding.

Slowing CKD progression and reducing complications:
- Treat high blood pressure: ACEi or ARB if ACR >30 mg/g or 3 mg/mmol; diuretic often required; dietary sodium <2000 mg/day.
- Type 2 diabetes: target HbA1c <6.5% to <8.0%; metformin for those with CKD and type 2 diabetes; if the glycaemic target is not achieved with metformin and SGLT2 inhibition, add a GLP1-RA.
- CKD complications testing: anaemia – evaluate if CKD G3-G5 and Hb <13 g/dl (men) or <12 g/dl (women); treat iron deficiency first; consider erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) if Hb 9-10 g/dl (avoid Hb >11.5 g/dl). Acidosis – correct to the normal range with bicarbonate supplementation if bicarbonate <22 mmol/l in CKD G3-G5. CKD-mineral bone disease – in CKD G3-G5 check calcium, phosphate, 25-OH vitamin D and intact PTH; supplement vitamin D deficiency.
- Influenza vaccination; pneumococcal and hepatitis B vaccination in CKD G4-G5; screen for hepatitis C.

Reduction of CVD complications: CKD = CVD risk; systolic blood pressure target <120 mm Hg* (consider <130/80 mm Hg in kidney transplant recipients); start lipid-lowering therapy (CKD and age ≥50 years: statin recommended; CKD and age 18-49: statin if known CAD, diabetes mellitus, prior stroke, or high ASCVD risk); aspirin for secondary prevention unless bleeding risk outweighs benefits.

When to refer to nephrology: AKI or abrupt sustained fall in GFR; eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m²; consistent significant albuminuria (ACR >300 mg/g or 30 mg/mmol); progression of CKD; urinary red cell casts or RBC >20 per high-power field, sustained and not readily explained; CKD and hypertension refractory to 4 or more antihypertensive agents; persistent abnormalities of serum potassium; recurrent or extensive nephrolithiasis; hereditary kidney disease.

Notes (from the caption): based on KDIGO and adapted from Vassalotti et al. Care for older adults or those with limited life expectancy should be individualised. If eGFR (creatinine) is 45-59 ml/min per 1.73 m2, or in low muscle mass, chronic illness or malnutrition, order cystatin C to estimate GFR. There are no evidence-based recommendations on screening frequency; consider risk equations (e.g. CKD Prognosis Consortium). The systolic target <120 mm Hg is a level 2 recommendation; many patients may opt for a less intensive approach.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Algorithm to screen, risk stratify and treat CKD
text:
### Algorithm to screen, risk-stratify and treat CKD (KDIGO-based): conditions of CKD risk, testing, classification, patient safety by eGFR, slowing progression and complications, CVD risk reduction, and when to refer to nephrology

1. Conditions of CKD risk: hypertension; diabetes; cardiovascular disease; AKI/hospitalisation history; family history of kidney disease; obesity; older age*; other high-risk comorbidities, environmental exposures, or genetic factors.
2. Consider screening for CKD: urinary albumin-creatinine ratio (ACR) to detect albuminuria; serum creatinine and cystatin C to estimate GFR.
3. Is any of the following present for 3 months or more: eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m²; ACR >30 mg/g (3 mg/mmol); markers of kidney disease?
   - No: periodically repeat evaluation.
   - Yes: classify/risk-stratify the CKD stage; identify and treat the specific cause of CKD.
     - eGFR category (ml/min/1.73 m²): G1 ≥90; G2 60-89; G3b 30-44; G4 15-29; G5 <15 (G3a is not listed).
     - Albuminuria category: A1 (normal or mild) <30 mg/g or <3 mg/mmol; A2 (moderate) 30-300 mg/g or 3-30 mg/mmol; A3 (severe) >300 mg/g or >30 mg/mmol.

Patient safety (all patients with eGFR <60): dose medications based on eGFR; reduce the risk of AKI from volume depletion; adopt 'sick day rules' as needed; avoid dual ACEi and ARB blockade; prevent contrast-associated AKI (lowest possible radiocontrast dose; adequate hydration before, during and after the procedure, consider isotonic saline; withhold ACEi or ARBs, diuretics and other nephrotoxic agents before and after the procedure).
- eGFR 45-59: avoid prolonged NSAIDs.
- eGFR 30-44: avoid prolonged NSAIDs; use metformin with close monitoring at 50% dose.
- eGFR <30: avoid any NSAIDs; avoid bisphosphonates; avoid metformin; avoid PICC lines (access preservation); if on warfarin, monitor PT-INR closely given increased risk of bleeding.

Slowing CKD progression and reducing complications:
- Treat high blood pressure: ACEi or ARB if ACR >30 mg/g or 3 mg/mmol; diuretic often required; dietary sodium <2000 mg/day.
- Type 2 diabetes: target HbA1c <6.5% to <8.0%; metformin for those with CKD and type 2 diabetes; if the glycaemic target is not achieved with metformin and SGLT2 inhibition, add a GLP1-RA.
- CKD complications testing: anaemia – evaluate if CKD G3-G5 and Hb <13 g/dl (men) or <12 g/dl (women); treat iron deficiency first; consider erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) if Hb 9-10 g/dl (avoid Hb >11.5 g/dl). Acidosis – correct to the normal range with bicarbonate supplementation if bicarbonate <22 mmol/l in CKD G3-G5. CKD-mineral bone disease – in CKD G3-G5 check calcium, phosphate, 25-OH vitamin D and intact PTH; supplement vitamin D deficiency.
- Influenza vaccination; pneumococcal and hepatitis B vaccination in CKD G4-G5; screen for hepatitis C.

Reduction of CVD complications: CKD = CVD risk; systolic blood pressure target <120 mm Hg* (consider <130/80 mm Hg in kidney transplant recipients); start lipid-lowering therapy (CKD and age ≥50 years: statin recommended; CKD and age 18-49: statin if known CAD, diabetes mellitus, prior stroke, or high ASCVD risk); aspirin for secondary prevention unless bleeding risk outweighs benefits.

When to refer to nephrology: AKI or abrupt sustained fall in GFR; eGFR <30 ml/min/1.73 m²; consistent significant albuminuria (ACR >300 mg/g or 30 mg/mmol); progression of CKD; urinary red cell casts or RBC >20 per high-power field, sustained and not readily explained; CKD and hypertension refractory to 4 or more antihypertensive agents; persistent abnormalities of serum potassium; recurrent or extensive nephrolithiasis; hereditary kidney disease.

Notes (from the caption): based on KDIGO and adapted from Vassalotti et al. Care for older adults or those with limited life expectancy should be individualised. If eGFR (creatinine) is 45-59 ml/min per 1.73 m2, or in low muscle mass, chronic illness or malnutrition, order cystatin C to estimate GFR. There are no evidence-based recommendations on screening frequency; consider risk equations (e.g. CKD Prognosis Consortium). The systolic target <120 mm Hg is a level 2 recommendation; many patients may opt for a less intensive approach.

### KDIGO heat map for CKD: monitor or refer to nephrology by GFR category (G1-G5) and albuminuria category (A1-A3), with risk colours

The KDIGO heat map uses the eGFR and albuminuria (albumin-to-creatinine ratio, ACR) from screening to assess the risk of CKD progression and kidney failure.

| GFR category | Description | Range (ml/min per 1.73 m2) | A1: normal to mildly increased (<30 mg/g; <3 mg/mmol) | A2: moderately increased (30-300 mg/g; 3-30 mg/mmol) | A3: severely increased (>300 mg/g; >30 mg/mmol) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| G1 | Normal or high | ≥90 | — (low risk) | Monitor (moderately increased risk) | Refer\* (high risk) |
| G2 | Mildly decreased | 60-89 | — (low risk) | Monitor (moderately increased risk) | Refer\* (high risk) |
| G3a | Mildly to moderately decreased | 45-59 | Monitor (moderately increased risk) | Monitor (high risk) | Refer (very high risk) |
| G3b | Moderately to severely decreased | 30-44 | Monitor (high risk) | Monitor (very high risk) | Refer (very high risk) |
| G4 | Severely decreased | 15-29 | Refer\* (very high risk) | Refer\* (very high risk) | Refer (very high risk) |
| G5 | Kidney failure | <15 | Refer (very high risk) | Refer (very high risk) | Refer (very high risk) |

*Referring clinicians may wish to discuss with their nephrology service depending on local arrangements regarding monitoring or referring.
Colours: low risk (if no other markers of kidney disease, no CKD); moderately increased risk; high risk; very high risk.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Pharmacological management of CKD to slow progression
text:
### Interventions to slow CKD progression and reduce cardiovascular risk by GFR and albuminuria stage (lifestyle, smoking, RAS inhibition, BP, statins, glycaemia, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 RA, metabolic acidosis)

Chart of interventions across CKD stages G1-G5 (each split A1-A3); bars show where each applies:
- Lifestyle modification: all stages.
- Smoking cessation: all stages.
- RAS inhibition (a): G1 to G4/G5 (shaded lighter in G5).
- Optimize blood pressure control: all stages.
- Statins (b): all stages (lighter in G5).
- Optimize glycemic control: all stages.
- SGLT2 inhibitors (c): G1 to G4, continued (dotted) into G5.
- GLP-1 receptor agonists (d): all stages.
- Treat metabolic acidosis: G3b to G5.
- Treat underlying cause, avoid nephrotoxins, and adjust medication dosages: all stages.

Notes: (a) Unclear if and when to discontinue renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibition in advanced CKD. (b) Statins should be initiated for those beginning dialysis therapy (as printed); patients already receiving statins at dialysis initiation can continue them. (c) Applies to CKD patients with type 2 diabetes only. An SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended as first-line treatment with metformin and may also benefit persons with CKD and no diabetes. SGLT2 inhibitors should be initiated if eGFR ≥30 ml/min and can be continued through G4-G5 until dialysis initiation, when they should be stopped; there is no evidence for starting SGLT2 inhibitors if eGFR <30 ml/min per 1.73 m2. (d) Applies to CKD patients with type 2 diabetes only. A GLP-1 receptor agonist can be considered when an SGLT2 inhibitor and/or metformin is not tolerated or the glycaemic target is not reached. Dulaglutide can be used if eGFR >15 ml/min per 1.73 m2; exenatide if creatinine clearance >30 ml/min; there are limited data for liraglutide, lixisenatide or semaglutide in severe CKD. Consult dosing recommendations in CKD G4 and G5.

Also: treat anaemia (investigate the cause to exclude non-CKD causes), aiming for Hb 10-12 g/dl.

(c) Applies to CKD patients with type 2 diabetes only. An SGLT2 inhibitor is recommended as first-line treatment with metformin and may also benefit persons with CKD and no diabetes. SGLT2 inhibitors should be initiated if eGFR ≥30 ml/min and can be continued through G4-G5 until dialysis initiation, when they should be stopped; there is no evidence for starting SGLT2 inhibitors if eGFR <30 ml/min per 1.73 m2. (d) Applies to CKD patients with type 2 diabetes only. A GLP-1 receptor agonist can be considered when an SGLT2 inhibitor and/or metformin is not tolerated or the glycaemic target is not reached. Dulaglutide can be used if eGFR >15 ml/min per 1.73 m2; exenatide if creatinine clearance >30 ml/min; there are limited data for liraglutide, lixisenatide or semaglutide in severe CKD. Consult dosing recommendations in CKD G4 and G5.

Also: treat anaemia (investigate the cause to exclude non-CKD causes), aiming for Hb 10-12 g/dl.

### Principles of CKD management by stage (all stages, stage 1-3/4, stage 4-5): goals, screening, risk factors, CV care, immunisation, medication review, AKI prevention, RRT preparation, complications

| Category | All Stages (CKD 1–5) | Stage 1–3/4 | Stage 4–5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Goals | Early detection, slow progression, prevent AKI, manage CV risk, adjust meds, immunize | Delay progression, prevent acute on chronic events, manage comorbidities | Prepare for RRT, manage complications |
| Screening | Screen high-risk populations (e.g., DM, HTN, elderly) | Regular renal function tests, proteinuria assessment | As in stage 1–3, plus closer nephrology follow-up |
| Risk Factor Control | Control BP, glucose, avoid nephrotoxins, lifestyle interventions | Use ACEi/ARB if proteinuria. Lifestyle: diet, exercise, smoking cessation | Continue risk factor management, stricter control |
| Cardiovascular Care | Treat dyslipidaemia, hypertension, diabetes | Initiate statins if indicated | Intensify CV risk monitoring and treatment |
| Immunisation | Annual influenza, 5-year pneumococcal, hepatitis B if seronegative | Same as all stages | Same as all stages |
| Medication Management | Review all meds for renal dosing | Monitor for dose accumulation | Dose adjustment critical due to declining GFR |
| Preventing AKI | Educate on avoiding dehydration, NSAIDs, and nephrotoxic agents | Monitor during infections or surgeries | Same, with increased vulnerability |
| Preparation for RRT | — | — | Educate on RRT options (HD, PD, transplant), plan access |
| Complication Management | Monitor anaemia, mineral-bone disorder (CKD-MBD) | Not usually required unless abnormalities begin to show | ESA for anaemia, phosphate binders, vitamin D supplementation |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > CKD and Diabetes > Glucose-lowering agents in CKD
text:
### Glucose-lowering agents in CKD and type 2 diabetes compared: effect on CKD progression, ASCVD, heart failure, glucose-lowering efficacy, hypoglycaemia risk, weight and cost

Glucose-lowering agents usable in CKD: metformin up to eGFR ≥30 ml/min/1.73 m2 (lactic acidosis reported with lower eGFR; reduces CV risk; check B12 after 4 years). SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) are recommended in diabetic and non-diabetic kidney disease to slow CKD progression; can be used in CKD4. GLP1-RAs are cardioprotective and reduce albuminuria and GFR decline in diabetic kidney disease; some can be used in CKD4. Non-renally cleared sulphonylureas such as gliclazide may be used cautiously (hypoglycaemia still possible). DPP4 inhibitors can be used in CKD1-5; thiazolidinediones (some agents) in CKD1-5; alpha glucosidase inhibitors up to CKD3b. Glucose may 'normalize' in advanced diabetic nephropathy.

| Agent | Progression of CKD | ASCVD | Heart Failure | Glucose-lowering efficacy | Hypoglycemia risk | Weight effects | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Metformin | Neutral | Potential benefit | Potential benefit | High | Low | Neutral | Low |
| SGLT2 inhibitors | Benefits (a) | Benefits (c) | Benefits | Intermediate | Low | Loss | High |
| GLP-1 receptor agonists | Benefits (b) | Benefits (c) | Potential benefits | High | Low | Loss | High |
| DPP-4 inhibitors | Neutral | Neutral | Potential risk (c) (saxagliptin) | Intermediate | Low | Neutral | High (analogs) |
| Insulin | Neutral | Neutral | Neutral | Highest | High | Gain | Low (human) |
| Sulfonylureas | Neutral | Neutral | Neutral | High | High | Gain | Low |
| Thiazolidinediones | Neutral | Potential benefit (pioglitazone) | Increased risk | High | Low | Gain | Low |
| α-Glucosidase inhibitors | Neutral | Neutral | Neutral |  | Low | Neutral | Low |

Colour key in the PDF: neutral; potential benefit or intermediate glucose-lowering efficacy; benefits (organ protection, high efficacy, low hypoglycemia risk, weight loss, or low cost); potential risk or high cost to patient; increased risk of adverse effects.
(a) Benefit supported by primary and secondary outcome data. (b) Benefit supported by secondary outcome data. (c) Benefit or risk is agent specific.
ASCVD, atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; CKD, chronic kidney disease; DPP-4, dipeptidyl peptidase 4; GLP-1, glucagon-like peptide 1; SGLT2, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2; T2D, type 2 diabetes.

text:
### CKD in pregnancy: maternal effects and effects on the foetus; pre-eclampsia risk reduction (aspirin, calcium) CKD in pregnancy requires co-management by an obstetrician and a nephrologist. | Maternal effects of CKD | Effects of CKD on foetus | | --- | --- | | - Worsening of kidney function (higher risk if worse baseline kidney function, GFR <40 ml/min/1.73 m² and proteinuria >1 g/d; less if mild with little or no proteinuria and normal BP)
- Proteinuria (which can worsen kidney disease)
- Hypertension with risk of pre-eclampsia | - Intra-uterine growth retardation (IUGR) = low nephron mass = future risk of kidney disease & hypertension in baby
- Pre-term deliveries
- Teratogenicity (RAAS inhibitors) | **Note:** Pre-eclampsia risk reduction in CKD: aspirin 81-150 mg OD (increases vascular relaxant prostacyclin and reduces thrombogenic/vasoconstrictive thromboxane A2; trials suggest some benefit); calcium 1.5-2 g daily may help those with low calcium levels.
