heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Chronic Kidney Disease > Management in Special Populations > (k) CKD in Paediatric Population
text:
### CKD in children: definition, key points, and major causes under and over 5 years of age

Definition of CKD in children: (1) kidney damage for ≥3 months, shown by structural or functional abnormalities of the kidney, with or without decreased GFR, with one or more of: abnormalities in the composition of the blood or urine; abnormalities in imaging tests; abnormalities on kidney biopsy; or (2) GFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² for ≥3 months, with or without other signs of kidney damage. Recognise children in the early stages of CKD; regular monitoring allows control of factors that aggravate progression. The main treatable causes of CKD in children in developing countries are urinary tract abnormalities, acute kidney injury and nephrotic syndrome. Identify the cause to plan management and prognosis. Major causes are congenital abnormalities of the kidney and urinary tract, reflux nephropathy, inherited disorders, glomerular diseases, renal stones, secondary to AKI, and haemolytic uraemic syndrome/thrombotic microangiopathy.

| In < 5 years of age | In > 5 years of age |
| --- | --- |
| Congenital malformations: hypoplastic/dysplastic kidneys; reflux nephropathy; obstructive uropathy; posterior urethral valves | Glomerular disease: focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; hemolytic uremic syndrome; chronic glomerulonephritis; Alport's syndrome |
| Metabolic/genetic disorders: oxalosis; polycystic kidney disease; congenital nephrotic syndrome; Wilms' tumor | Tubulointerstitial disease: chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis; cystinosis; nephronophthisis; nephrotoxic drugs |

text:
### CKD and contrast media: effect on the kidneys and management for gadolinium (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis), iodinated contrast, and acute phosphate nephropathy

|  | Gadolinium | Radioiodine contrast media | Acute phosphate nephropathy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exposure | Gadolinium-based contrast agents (MRI scans) | Iodinated contrast | Exposure to high phosphorus levels in the presence of renal insufficiency. Usually reported following bowel preparation (e.g. for colonoscopy) with sodium phosphate containing solutions |
| Effect on Kidneys | Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis: a fibrosing disorder of the skin and viscera/systemic organs, secondary to gadolinium-based contrast agents in patients with acute and chronic renal insufficiency. First reported in patients with ESRD and AKI in 2006 (gadolinium is excreted unchanged by the kidneys) | Direct toxic effect on renal tubules, disrupting mitochondrial function, with generation of free radicals, causing apoptosis. Vasoconstriction, reducing blood flow through the medulla, with resultant ischaemia | Acute presentation with severely elevated serum phosphorus levels and AKI. Gradual worsening of renal function over weeks and months. Renal biopsy shows tubulointerstitial calcium and phosphorus deposition and damage |
| Management | Avoid in CKD stage G5, but some risk in G4. If needed, counsel the patient and arrange dialysis immediately after the procedure and for up to 2 days after (based on gadolinium pharmacokinetics) to remove the gadolinium | Hold exacerbating drugs on the day of use, e.g. metformin, diuretics. Pre- and post-hydrate with normal saline 1 ml/kg/hour or 100 ml/hour for 3-12 hours before and after contrast (lower rates if risk of pulmonary oedema). Use low-volume contrast that is not hyper-osmolar |  |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Classification of Acute Glomerulonephritis
text:
### Classification of glomerulonephritis: non-proliferative (minimal change, membranous, FSGS) vs proliferative (IgA, membranoproliferative, RPGN, post-infectious, vasculitic, Goodpasture's), features and treatment

Glomerulonephritis is classified as non-proliferative (these tend to cause nephrotic syndrome) or proliferative.
A. Non-proliferative:
- Minimal change glomerulonephritis: abnormal podocytes seen on electron microscopy. Treat with supportive care + prednisolone; most respond well.
- Membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN): thickened glomerular basement membrane; usually idiopathic. 1/3 have chronic MGN, 1/3 go into remission, 1/3 progress to renal failure.
- Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: segments of glomeruli develop sclerosis; presents with nephrotic syndrome; genetic causes identified; steroids often ineffective; 50% progress to renal failure.
B. Proliferative:
- IgA nephropathy: most common type of GN in adults; macroscopic haematuria appearing 24-48 hrs after URTI/GI infection; IgA deposits seen in the mesangial matrix.
- Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis: primary (immune mediated) or secondary (SLE, hepatitis); usually progresses to end-stage renal failure.
- Post-infectious glomerulonephritis: occurs weeks after URTI, usually Strep pyogenes; supportive treatment; resolves over 2-4 weeks.
- Rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis:
  - Vasculitic disorders: Wegener's granulomatosis (vasculitis of lungs, kidney and other organs; c-ANCA positive; treat with steroids + cyclophosphamide); microscopic polyangiitis (small vessel vasculitis; p-ANCA positive; treat with long-term steroids +/- cytotoxic agents).
  - Goodpasture's syndrome: autoimmune, anti-GBM antibody; glomerulus and lung affected; haematuria and haemoptysis; treat with steroids +/- steroid-sparing agents.

- Membranous nephropathy (most common in adults)
- Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis | - IgA nephropathy

text:
### Acute glomerulonephritis / nephrotic syndrome: investigations and differential diagnosis (primary, secondary, genetic, systemic, inflammatory and other causes) | Investigations | Differential Diagnosis | | --- | --- | | - Urine dipsticks
- Urinalysis with microscopy
- 24-hour urine protein
- Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine
- Full blood count
- Complement studies (C3, C4)
- Serum lipids
- Serum electrolytes
- Confirm the presence of nephrotic syndrome (albumin, cholesterol, urine dipstick & spot urine protein/creatinine ratio)
- Exclude an underlying systemic or exogenous cause of nephrotic syndrome that may require treatment (diabetes, HIV, VDRL, hepatitis B, lupus serology, ANA and anti-ds DNA antibody etc., underlying malignancy e.g. myeloma causing amyloidosis)
- Determine renal function (creatinine, GFR – note may be falsely low because of low muscle mass)
- Exclude complications of nephrotic syndrome (sepsis from urinary losses of immunoglobulins – e.g. ascitic tap; Doppler studies to exclude venous thrombosis)
- Determine the need for a kidney biopsy (e.g. in children: deteriorating kidney function, refractory proteinuria) | 1. Primary nephrotic syndromes: minimal change disease (MCD); focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS); membranous nephropathy; membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)
2. Secondary causes: systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE); diabetes mellitus (diabetic nephropathy); amyloidosis; infections such as HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and syphilis; drug-induced nephropathy
3. Genetic and congenital disorders: Alport syndrome; congenital nephrotic syndrome
4. Systemic diseases: multiple myeloma; systemic vasculitis; sarcoidosis
5. Inflammatory and infectious causes: IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease); post-infectious glomerulonephritis
6. Others: haematologic disorders – thrombotic microangiopathies like haemolytic-uraemic syndrome (HUS) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP); malignancies – some cancers cause paraneoplastic glomerulopathies |

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Pharmacological Management of Glomerulonephritis > Nephrotic Syndrome: definition of key terms
text:
### Nephrotic syndrome definitions: remission, relapse, frequent relapse, steroid dependence; and general management of glomerulonephritis

Management of acute glomerulonephritis: 1. low salt diet; 2. adequate but not excess protein; 3. ideally immunise before immunosuppressive therapy (pneumococcal vaccine repeated every 5 years, hepatitis B); 4. screen for infections before immunosuppressive therapy; 5. low sugar diet for those on glucocorticoids and calcineurin inhibitors.

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Remission | Urine albumin nil or trace (or proteinuria <4 mg/m2/h) for three consecutive days |
| Relapse | Urine albumin 3+ or 4+ (or proteinuria >40 mg/m2/h) for three consecutive days, having been in remission previously |
| Frequent relapse | Two or more relapses during 6 months, or more than three relapses during any 12-month period |
| Glucocorticoid steroid dependence (SDNS) | Persistent proteinuria (>2 g/g creatinine) despite high-dose prednisone 60 mg/m² (2 mg/kg) daily for 4 weeks, in the absence of infection or nonadherence to medication |

GN, glomerulonephritis; SDNS, steroid dependent nephrotic syndrome; SSNS, steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome.

### Definitions of nephrotic syndrome, nephrotic-range proteinuria and non-nephrotic-range proteinuria (adults and children) Nephrotic syndrome may present with the following ranges of proteinuria. | Nephrotic Syndrome | Nephrotic-Range Proteinuria | Non-Nephrotic-Range Proteinuria | | --- | --- | --- | | Proteinuria (adults)\*: >3.5 g per 24h; PCR >3000 mg/g (>300 mg/mmol)
Proteinuria (children)\*: >40 mg/m²/h; >300 mg/dl; 3+ on urine dipstick; PCR >2000 mg/g (>200 mg/mmol)
Hypoalbuminemia†
Edema‡
Hyperlipidemia‡ | Proteinuria (adults): >3.5 g per 24h; PCR >3000 mg/g (>300 mg/mmol)
Proteinuria (children)\*: >40 mg/m²/h; >300 mg/dl; 3+ on urine dipstick; PCR >2000 mg/g (>200 mg/mmol)
Serum albumin usually normal
Edema is usually absent or minor
Serum lipids usually normal or only mildly elevated | Variable levels of proteinuria: 0.3-3.4 g per 24h; PCR <300 mg/g (<30 mg/mmol)
Serum albumin normal
No clinical symptoms | *Essential. †Laboratory-specific values: serum albumin should be measured by bromocresol purple (BCP; colorimetric), capillary electrophoresis (CE), or immunonephelometric (iMN) methods. Bromocresol green (BCG) methods can give erroneously high results; BCG values are about 5.5 g/l higher than BCP, CE or iMN values, so the degree of hypoalbuminemia that defines NS depends on the method. ‡Variable.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Pharmacological Management of Glomerulonephritis > Nephrotic syndrome treatment
text:
### Nephrotic syndrome (children) treatment flowchart: initial prednisone, consolidation, and relapsing nephrotic syndrome (infrequent, frequent/steroid-dependent, steroid-resistant)

Initial episode:
1. Age 3-12 months or >12 years, gross haematuria, or low complement?
   - Yes: consider kidney biopsy.
   - No: intensive daily prednisone therapy 60 mg/m² (2 mg/kg).
2. Remission within 4 [weeks]?
   - No: consider kidney biopsy.
   - Yes: consolidation therapy (alternate-day prednisone) for 8 weeks: 40 mg/m² (~1.5 mg/kg) every 48 h for 4 weeks, then 20 mg/m² (~0.75 mg/kg) every 48 h for 4 weeks, then stop.

Relapsing idiopathic nephrotic syndrome:
- Infrequent relapses: prednisone 60 mg/m² daily until remission, then 40 mg/m² on alternate days for 4 weeks.
- Frequent relapses or glucocorticoid dependence:
  - Option 1: assess the alternate-day prednisone threshold. Threshold <15 mg/m² (<0.5 mg/kg) → remission → alternate-day prednisone (0.1 to <0.5 mg/kg/dose). If glucocorticoid toxicity or no remission → option 2.
  - Option 2: start a second-line agent if previous long-term glucocorticoid use with signs of toxicity.
- Glucocorticoid resistance: kidney biopsy; therapy based on histological diagnosis.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Kidney Biopsy
text:
> **When to do a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria (decision tree)**
>
> Decision tree for considering a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria:
> - The kidney biopsy is the gold standard for diagnostic evaluation of glomerular diseases. Biopsy should be performed if the result is expected to modify treatment and/or if additional prognostic information is needed.
> - Patients classically treated without a kidney biopsy diagnosis (children): steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome ≤12 years old; post-streptococcal GN.
> - Examples of conditions for which treatment may be considered without diagnostic confirmation by kidney biopsy: PLA2Rab+ (membranous nephropathy); PR3+ ANCA vasculitis; anti-glomerular basement membrane disease; Alport disease; Fabry disease; familial focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis in families with well-characterised mutations; biopsy contraindicated as judged by history, physical exam and laboratory testing; systemic lupus erythematosus.
> 
> ANCA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; MPO, myeloperoxidase; PLA2Rab+, M-type phospholipase A2 receptor antibody positive; PR3, proteinase 3. Referral to a nephrologist may include immunosuppressive treatment such as prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, angiotensin blockade.
html:
When to do a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria (decision tree)

Decision tree for considering a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria:

- The kidney biopsy is the gold standard for diagnostic evaluation of glomerular diseases. Biopsy should be performed if the result is expected to modify treatment and/or if additional prognostic information is needed.

- Patients classically treated without a kidney biopsy diagnosis (children): steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome ≤12 years old; post-streptococcal GN.

- Examples of conditions for which treatment may be considered without diagnostic confirmation by kidney biopsy: PLA2Rab+ (membranous nephropathy); PR3+ ANCA vasculitis; anti-glomerular basement membrane disease; Alport disease; Fabry disease; familial focal and segmental glomerulosclerosis in families with well-characterised mutations; biopsy contraindicated as judged by history, physical exam and laboratory testing; systemic lupus erythematosus.

ANCA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; MPO, myeloperoxidase; PLA2Rab+, M-type phospholipase A2 receptor antibody positive; PR3, proteinase 3. Referral to a nephrologist may include immunosuppressive treatment such as prednisolone, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, angiotensin blockade.

Decision tree for considering a kidney biopsy in patients with proteinuria and/or glomerular haematuria:

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Pharmacological Management of Glomerulonephritis > Treatment algorithm for NS in a newly nephrotic child
text:
### Treatment algorithm for nephrotic syndrome in a newly nephrotic child: by age and syndromic features; steroid response; frequent relapser, infrequent relapser, steroid-dependent, non-responder

New nephrotic syndrome in a child:
- ≥12 years of age, syndromic features or family history (as printed; see flag): biopsy and/or genetic testing + referral to a specialty centre.
- ≤12 years of age, no syndromic features or family history: glucocorticoids* (oral prednisone or prednisolone).
  - No response after 4 or 6 weeks: genetic testing; kidney biopsy; calcineurin inhibitor; renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade.
  - Complete responder: glucocorticoids* for 8 or 12 weeks, then by course:
    - Frequent relapser: cyclophosphamide; levamisole; mycophenolate mofetil; rituximab; calcineurin inhibitor.
    - Infrequent relapser: glucocorticoids*.
    - Steroid-dependent: mycophenolate mofetil; rituximab; calcineurin inhibitor; cyclophosphamide.

Refer to a clinical trial where appropriate. NS, nephrotic syndrome. The management of glomerular disease depends on the type/cause and is individualised by a specialist according to the kidney biopsy histology.

heading_path: Chapter 7: Nephrology > Glomerular Disease > Histology based treatment of Glomerular Disease
text:
### Histology-based treatment of glomerular disease: minimal change disease (children and adults), membranous nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, pauci-immune necrotising GN: regimens, doses and special considerations

Letters before drugs (A, C, S, D) are the medicine level codes used in the guideline.

| Histological Pattern | Treatment Regime | Special Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Steroid sensitive. Initial: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2/d or 2 mg/kg/d [max 60 mg/d] for 6 weeks (complete 6 weeks of initial treatment if remission is attained at 4 weeks). Continue: A: prednisolone 40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg (alternate days) for 6 weeks if remission was attained by 4 weeks of initial treatment; after 6 weeks of alternate-day therapy taper and stop within 6 weeks (taper by 5-10 mg a week) | In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Relapsing steroid sensitive: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2 or 2 mg/kg [max 60 mg/d] until in complete remission for 3 days, THEN A: prednisolone single dose on alternate days (40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg per dose; maximum 40 mg on alternate days) for at least 4 weeks. text:
### Histology-based treatment of glomerular disease: minimal change disease (children and adults), membranous nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, pauci-immune necrotising GN: regimens, doses and special considerations

Letters before drugs (A, C, S, D) are the medicine level codes used in the guideline.

| Histological Pattern | Treatment Regime | Special Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Steroid sensitive. Initial: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2/d or 2 mg/kg/d [max 60 mg/d] for 6 weeks (complete 6 weeks of initial treatment if remission is attained at 4 weeks). Continue: A: prednisolone 40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg (alternate days) for 6 weeks if remission was attained by 4 weeks of initial treatment; after 6 weeks of alternate-day therapy taper and stop within 6 weeks (taper by 5-10 mg a week) | In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Relapsing steroid sensitive: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2 or 2 mg/kg [max 60 mg/d] until in complete remission for 3 days, THEN A: prednisolone single dose on alternate days (40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg per dose; maximum 40 mg on alternate days) for at least 4 weeks. S: levamisole (PO) 2.5 mg/kg on alternate days for 12 months | In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Frequent relapse/steroid dependent: S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/d for 10-12 weeks [max 168 mg/kg cumulative dose] OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: everolimus 0.5-2 mg 12-hourly OR S: sirolimus 1-3 mg 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses; S: rituximab 375-1000 mg/m2 | Monitor calcineurin inhibitor toxicity/levels |
| Minimal Change Disease: children | Steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome: S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone high dose |  |
| Minimal Change Disease: adults | D: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg 24-hourly (maximum 80 mg) OR alternate-day single dose of 2 mg/kg (maximum 120 mg) – 4 weeks if remission; continue to 16 weeks if complete remission is not achieved | Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Check HbA1c monthly. Screen for osteoporosis |
| Minimal Change Disease: adults | Frequent relapse/steroid dependent/resistant (idiopathic only): D: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg [max 80 mg] daily or alternate-day 2 mg/kg [max 120 mg] for 4-16 weeks. OR, if intolerant of steroids or steroid resistant: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (then titrate) | Exclude secondary causes. Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Monitor levels |
| Membranous nephropathy (idiopathic only) | Children: alternating monthly treatment with methylprednisolone + prednisolone (months 1, 3 & 5) and oral cyclophosphamide (months 2, 4 & 6): D: methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg for 3 days, then prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg for 27 days; S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg for 30 days. Alternative regimens: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg in two divided doses with prednisolone 0.15 mg/kg/day for 6 months; S: tacrolimus 0.2 mg/kg in two divided doses without prednisolone | Exclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated |
| Membranous nephropathy (idiopathic only) | Adults: S: cyclophosphamide; A: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day; D: methylprednisolone IV monthly. Alternative regimens: S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 6 months OR S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses. If albumin <25 g/l + thrombosis risk: C: warfarin 5 mg PO [refer to DVT anticoagulation] | Exclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated |
| Membranoproliferative GN | S: cyclophosphamide OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone |  |
| IgA Nephropathy | Initial supportive care for 3-6 months: C: enalapril (PO) 10-20 mg 24-hourly OR C: lisinopril (PO) 2.5-10 mg 24-hourly. For persistent proteinuria >1 g/d for 6 months (adults and children): A: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/day for 6 months (as printed) | Other registered ACEI or ARBs may be used as in the Hypertension section |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | All patients: S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 6 mg/kg/day maintenance. Class II with proteinuria >3 g/day: treat as minimal change disease above |  |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | Class III and class IV, initial 6 months: D: methylprednisolone (IV slow) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days monthly AND S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 500-1000 mg/m2 monthly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly, titrating to 1.5 g 12-hourly if tolerated, OR S: mycophenolate sodium. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1.5-2.5 mg/kg/d OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) for 6 months OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose) | Oral prednisolone less effective; 60 mg/day may be given. A shorter, more frequent regimen (Euro-Lupus) may be used: cyclophosphamide 500 mg every two weeks x 6 doses |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | Class V + persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria: as class III and IV |  |
| Pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing glomerulonephritis | Initial: S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks x 3 doses, then every three weeks for 3-6 months, OR S: cyclophosphamide oral 1.5-2 mg/kg daily for 3-6 months; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg slowly over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then prednisolone 1 mg/kg, tapered to 30 mg in one week and then to 5 mg by 4-6 months. Severe disease: S: rituximab 1 g followed 14 days later by another 1 g, OR S: rituximab 375 mg/m2 per week for 4 weeks; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then A: prednisolone 1 mg/kg tapered as above. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1-2 mg/kg/d for 18 months OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium | S: haemodialysis. S: plasmapheresis in special indications |

### Histology-based treatment of glomerular disease: minimal change disease (children and adults), membranous nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN, IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis, pauci-immune necrotising GN: regimens, doses and special considerations

Letters before drugs (A, C, S, D) are the medicine level codes used in the guideline.

S: levamisole (PO) 2.5 mg/kg on alternate days for 12 months | In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function |

| Minimal Change Disease: children | Steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome: S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone high dose |  |

OR, if intolerant of steroids or steroid resistant: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (then titrate) | Exclude secondary causes. Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Monitor levels |

Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated |

Alternative regimens: S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 6 months OR S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses. If albumin <25 g/l + thrombosis risk: C: warfarin 5 mg PO [refer to DVT anticoagulation] | Exclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated |
| Membranoproliferative GN | S: cyclophosphamide OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone |  |
| IgA Nephropathy | Initial supportive care for 3-6 months: C: enalapril (PO) 10-20 mg 24-hourly OR C: lisinopril (PO) 2.5-10 mg 24-hourly. For persistent proteinuria >1 g/d for 6 months (adults and children): A: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/day for 6 months (as printed) | Other registered ACEI or ARBs may be used as in the Hypertension section |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | All patients: S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 6 mg/kg/day maintenance. Class II with proteinuria >3 g/day: treat as minimal change disease above |  |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | Class III and class IV, initial 6 months: D: methylprednisolone (IV slow) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days monthly AND S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 500-1000 mg/m2 monthly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly, titrating to 1.5 g 12-hourly if tolerated, OR S: mycophenolate sodium. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1.5-2.5 mg/kg/d OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) for 6 months OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose) | Oral prednisolone less effective; 60 mg/day may be given. A shorter, more frequent regimen (Euro-Lupus) may be used: cyclophosphamide 500 mg every two weeks x 6 doses |
| Lupus nephritis (adult) | Class V + persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria: as class III and IV |  |
| Pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing glomerulonephritis | Initial: S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks x 3 doses, then every three weeks for 3-6 months, OR S: cyclophosphamide oral 1.5-2 mg/kg daily for 3-6 months; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg slowly over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then prednisolone 1 mg/kg, tapered to 30 mg in one week and then to 5 mg by 4-6 months. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1-2 mg/kg/d for 18 months OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium | S: haemodialysis. S: plasmapheresis in special indications |

Continue: A: prednisolone 40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg (alternate days) for 6 weeks if remission was attained by 4 weeks of initial treatment; after 6 weeks of alternate-day therapy taper and stop within 6 weeks (taper by 5-10 mg a week)In children biopsy is indicated for: 1. steroid resistant NS; 2. late failure to respond following initial response; 3. decreasing kidney function
Relapsing steroid sensitive: A: prednisolone 60 mg/m2 or 2 mg/kg [max 60 mg/d] until in complete remission for 3 days, THEN A: prednisolone single dose on alternate days (40 mg/m2 or 1.5 mg/kg per dose; maximum 40 mg on alternate days) for at least 4 weeks. S: levamisole (PO) 2.5 mg/kg on alternate days for 12 months
Frequent relapse/steroid dependent: S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg/d for 10-12 weeks [max 168 mg/kg cumulative dose] OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose) OR S: everolimus 0.5-2 mg 12-hourly OR S: sirolimus 1-3 mg 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses; S: rituximab 375-1000 mg/m2Monitor calcineurin inhibitor toxicity/levels
Steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome: S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone high dose
Minimal Change Disease: adultsD: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg 24-hourly (maximum 80 mg) OR alternate-day single dose of 2 mg/kg (maximum 120 mg) – 4 weeks if remission; continue to 16 weeks if complete remission is not achievedSlow taper after remission over 6 months. Check HbA1c monthly. Screen for osteoporosis
Frequent relapse/steroid dependent/resistant (idiopathic only): D: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/kg [max 80 mg] daily or alternate-day 2 mg/kg [max 120 mg] for 4-16 weeks. OR, if intolerant of steroids or steroid resistant: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses (then titrate)Exclude secondary causes. Slow taper after remission over 6 months. Monitor levels
Membranous nephropathy (idiopathic only)Children: alternating monthly treatment with methylprednisolone + prednisolone (months 1, 3 & 5) and oral cyclophosphamide (months 2, 4 & 6): D: methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg for 3 days, then prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg for 27 days; S: cyclophosphamide 2 mg/kg for 30 days. Alternative regimens: S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg in two divided doses with prednisolone 0.15 mg/kg/day for 6 months; S: tacrolimus 0.2 mg/kg in two divided doses without prednisoloneExclude secondary causes. Monitor for 6 months before starting unless life-threatening symptoms OR rising creatinine. Do not use if serum creatinine >309 micromol/l [CKD patient]. Kidney biopsy might be repeated
Adults: S: cyclophosphamide; A: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day; D: methylprednisolone IV monthly. Alternative regimens: S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 6 months OR S: cyclosporine 3.5-5 mg/kg/d in 2 divided doses. If albumin <25 g/l + thrombosis risk: C: warfarin 5 mg PO [refer to DVT anticoagulation]
Membranoproliferative GNS: cyclophosphamide OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1200 mg/m2/d in two divided doses OR S: mycophenolate sodium AND A: prednisolone
IgA NephropathyInitial supportive care for 3-6 months: C: enalapril (PO) 10-20 mg 24-hourly OR C: lisinopril (PO) 2.5-10 mg 24-hourly. For persistent proteinuria >1 g/d for 6 months (adults and children): A: prednisolone (PO) 1 mg/day for 6 months (as printed)Other registered ACEI or ARBs may be used as in the Hypertension section
Lupus nephritis (adult)All patients: S: hydroxychloroquine (PO) 6 mg/kg/day maintenance. Class II with proteinuria >3 g/day: treat as minimal change disease above
Class III and class IV, initial 6 months: D: methylprednisolone (IV slow) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days monthly AND S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 500-1000 mg/m2 monthly OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly, titrating to 1.5 g 12-hourly if tolerated, OR S: mycophenolate sodium. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1.5-2.5 mg/kg/d OR S: mycophenolate mofetil (PO) 0.5-1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodium OR S: cyclosporine 4-5 mg/kg/d (starting dose) for 6 months OR S: tacrolimus 0.1 mg/kg/d (starting dose)Oral prednisolone less effective; 60 mg/day may be given. A shorter, more frequent regimen (Euro-Lupus) may be used: cyclophosphamide 500 mg every two weeks x 6 doses
Class V + persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria: as class III and IV
Pauci-immune focal and segmental necrotizing glomerulonephritisInitial: S: cyclophosphamide (IV) 15 mg/kg every 2 weeks x 3 doses, then every three weeks for 3-6 months, OR S: cyclophosphamide oral 1.5-2 mg/kg daily for 3-6 months; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg slowly over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then prednisolone 1 mg/kg, tapered to 30 mg in one week and then to 5 mg by 4-6 months. Severe disease: S: rituximab 1 g followed 14 days later by another 1 g, OR S: rituximab 375 mg/m2 per week for 4 weeks; AND D: methylprednisolone (IV) 250-1000 mg over 30 min for 3 days as induction, then A: prednisolone 1 mg/kg tapered as above. Maintenance: S: azathioprine (PO) 1-2 mg/kg/d for 18 months OR S: mycophenolate mofetil 1 g 12-hourly OR S: mycophenolate sodiumS: haemodialysis. S: plasmapheresis in special indications

text:
### Coordinated care of pregnant patients with glomerular disease: prepregnancy, antenatal, delivery and postnatal actions Glomerular disease in pregnancy and women of child-bearing age (15-49 years): safer immunosuppression and adjuncts are azathioprine, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine), glucocorticoids, and hydroxychloroquine. Preferred contraception: products that do not contain estrogen. | Stage | Actions | | --- | --- | | Prepregnancy | - Discuss timing of contraception; contraception advice if needed; fertility assessment if needed
- Assess disease activity, with repeat biopsy confirmation if necessary; optimize blood pressure control
- Change to non-teratogenic medications and provide reassurance about continuation of safe medications
- Explain the risk of pregnancy complications and the need for heightened surveillance | | Antenatal | - Target BP <140/90 mmHg
- Oral glucose tolerance test (especially important in women taking glucocorticoids or calcineurin inhibitors)
- Start low dose aspirin; consider vitamin D and calcium supplements
- Frequent fetal monitoring if concerns about fetal well-being: up to twice weekly BPPs, up to placental Dopplers, 2-weekly growth scans
- Baseline and serial kidney function, proteinuria (albumin-creatinine or protein-creatinine ratios or 24h collections) and markers of disease activity
- Monitoring of calcineurin inhibitor levels if required
- Consider venous thromboembolism prophylaxis if risk factors, e.g. nephrotic syndrome, previous venous thromboembolic events, high body mass index | | Delivery | - Delivery if fetal or maternal decompensation
- NOT at a pre-specified gestation
- Glucocorticoids for fetal lung maturation at least 24 h and up to 7 d before anticipated delivery if <34 weeks gestation | | Postnatal | - Encourage breastfeeding
- Careful surveillance for active glomerulonephritis
- Calcineurin inhibitor level if dose changed in pregnancy
- Continue venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for at least 6 weeks if necessary
- Emotional support | Adapted from Blom K, Odutayo A, Bramham K, et al. Pregnancy and glomerular disease: a systematic review of the literature with management guidelines. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2017;12:1862-1872. BP, blood pressure; BPP, biophysical profile; q2, every 2.

### Contraception in women with glomerular disease: unintended pregnancy rates (perfect and typical use), contraindications and other considerations by method

| Contraceptive Method | Unintended pregnancy rate within 1st year of use (%) Perfect use | Unintended pregnancy rate within 1st year of use (%) Typical use | Contraindications in glomerular disease | Other considerations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Estrogen-containing methods (pill, patch, ring) | 0.3 | 9 | Lupus; venous thromboembolism; vascular disease | Breast cancer risk; cervical cancer risk with immunosuppression; venous thromboembolism risk in nephrotic syndrome |
| Progesterone-only pill | 0.3 | 9 | None | Longest re-dosing interval with desogestrel (may improve typical use); possible breast cancer risk, especially >40 yr |
| Progesterone intrauterine device (Mirena) | 0.2 | 0.2 | None | Possible breast cancer risk, especially >40 yr; effective with immunosuppression, no evidence of increased infection |
| Progesterone implant (Nexplanon) | 0.05 | 0.05 | None | Possible breast cancer risk, especially >40 yr |
| Copper intrauterine device | 0.6 | 0.8 | None | No associated hormone risk |
| Male condom | 2 | 18 | Ineffective for long-term use | Protects against human immunodeficiency virus and sexually transmitted infection |
| Female condom | 5 | 21 |  |  |
| None | 85 | 85 |  |  |

text:
### ADHD medicines for children over 6 and adults: methylphenidate (immediate and extended release) starting dose, titration, maximum, contraindications and side effects

Treatment targets: minimise the impact of ADHD symptoms on function; maximise the ability to compensate or cope; strengthen positive behaviours while reducing negative ones; promote academic functioning and cognition. Initiate medicine only when psychosocial interventions have failed.

| Group | Drug | Dosage and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Children >6 years: CNS stimulants | Methylphenidate HCl | Initial dose 5-10 mg PO OD (morning) or BD (morning and lunchtime). Increase by 5-10 mg every 1-2 months. Max 60 mg/day | Not for children <6 years old; consider psychosocial interventions and mood stabilizers first | Insomnia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, restlessness, tremor, worsening of Tourette's syndrome |
| Children >6 years: CNS stimulants | Methylphenidate HCl extended release | Initial dose 18 mg PO OD (morning) or BD (morning and lunchtime). Increase by 18 mg every 1-2 months. Max 54 mg/day | Not for children <6 years old; consider psychosocial interventions and mood stabilizers first | Insomnia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, restlessness, tremor, worsening of Tourette's syndrome |
| Adults: CNS stimulants | Methylphenidate HCl | Initial dose 10-20 mg PO OD (morning) or BD (morning and lunchtime). Increase by 10 mg every 1-2 months. Max 60 mg/day | Not for children <6 years old; consider psychosocial interventions and mood stabilizers first | Insomnia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, restlessness, tremor, worsening of Tourette's syndrome |
| Adults: CNS stimulants | Methylphenidate HCl extended release | Initial dose 18-36 mg PO OD (morning) or BD (morning and lunchtime). Increase by 18 mg every 1-2 months. Max 72 mg/day | Not for children <6 years old; consider psychosocial interventions and mood stabilizers first | Insomnia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, restlessness, tremor, worsening of Tourette's syndrome |

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Autism Spectrum Disorder > Pharmacological Management of ASD
text:
### Autism spectrum disorder medicines: antipsychotics (risperidone, aripiprazole) for psychosis, aggression or unmanageable behaviour; SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline) for depression and suicidal ideation

**For psychosis, aggression, or unmanageable behaviour**

| Indication / Class | Drug | Dosage and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Antipsychotics | Risperidone | Initial dose 0.5-1 mg OD to BD. Increase by 0.25-1 mg every 3-14 days. Max 6 mg/day | Hypertension, diabetes, obesity | Comatose status, circulatory collapse, extrapyramidal symptoms, drowsiness, orthostatic hypotension |
| Antipsychotics | Aripiprazole | Initial dose 2 mg OD to BD. Increase by 2 mg every 3-14 days. Max 15 mg/day | Allergy to aripiprazole | Headache, dizziness, anxiety, insomnia, nausea, vomiting, weight gain |

**Manage depression and suicidal ideation**

| Indication / Class | Drug | Dosage and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Antidepressant (SSRI) | Fluoxetine | Initial dose 10-20 mg OD PO. Max 60-80 mg/day | Concomitant monoamine oxidase inhibitors | Headache, insomnia, nervousness, dizziness |
| Antidepressant (SSRI) | Sertraline | Initial dose 25-50 mg OD PO. Max 200 mg/day | Concomitant monoamine oxidase inhibitors | Nausea, diarrhoea, dyspepsia, dizziness |

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Classification
text:
### Classification of seizures: generalised (tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, epileptic spasms) and focal (aware, impaired awareness): consciousness, duration, features, typical age

Epilepsy is a chronic noncommunicable brain disorder characterised by recurrent unprovoked seizures (two or more unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart). This module covers convulsive epilepsy. With proper treatment, most people can be seizure-free.

| Category | Type | Consciousness | Duration | Key Clinical Features | Typical Age/Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Generalized | Tonic–clonic | Lost | 2–5 min | Fall, stiffening → jerking, frothing, tongue bite, incontinence, postictal sleep/confusion | Most common |
| Generalized | Absence | Briefly lost | 5–30 sec | Blank stare, stops activity, eye rolling, no fall, no confusion after | School-aged children, frequent, provoked by hyperventilation |
| Generalized | Myoclonic | Usually preserved | Seconds | Sudden shock-like jerks of limbs/body | Often in epileptic syndromes |
| Generalized | Epileptic spasms (infantile spasms) | Variable | Seconds (clusters) | Head/trunk flexion, arm abduction, knee bending | Infants <1 yr, developmental delay |
| Focal | Focal aware (simple partial) | Preserved | Seconds | Local twitching, sensory changes, déjà vu, hallucinations | Patient aware of event |
| Focal | Focal impaired awareness (complex partial) | Impaired | 1–3 min | Aura, staring, automatisms (lip smacking, picking clothes), confusion, amnesia | Slow recovery, may appear aggressive |

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Epilepsy Algorithm of Assessment and Management
text:
> **Epilepsy assessment and management algorithm: 8 assessment steps, emergency management of seizures >5 min, when to refer, first aid at home**
>
> Assessment:
> 1. Person presents with episodes of convulsions (fits, shaking, stiffening), witnessed or reported.
> 2. Confirm 2+ unprovoked seizures (not febrile, not substance-related, not syncope). Onset, duration, frequency?
> 3. Rule out other causes: hypoglycaemia, head injury, meningitis, stroke, eclampsia, substance withdrawal.
> 4. Assess: postictal confusion? Tongue-biting? Urinary incontinence? Aura? Birth trauma history?
> 5. Check current medications; assess for pregnancy in women of childbearing age.
> 6. Assess functional impairment: school, work, driving, daily activities, social life.
> 7. Screen for mental health comorbidities (depression, anxiety).
> 8. Diagnosis: epilepsy confirmed → proceed to management.
> 
> EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT (seizure > 5 min): call for emergency help immediately; diazepam 10-20 mg IV/PR or lorazepam 4 mg IV for status epilepticus; airway – place in recovery position, ensure breathing; DO NOT restrain; DO NOT put anything in the mouth; monitor blood glucose; give thiamine if alcohol-related.
> 
> When to refer: first seizure (confirm diagnosis); seizures not controlled after 2 drug trials; pregnancy + epilepsy (specialist input needed); status epilepticus; suspected structural cause (tumour, stroke).
> 
> First aid at home (advise carers): lay the person on their side, head turned to the side; ensure the airway is clear, loosen tight clothing; time the seizure and stay until fully conscious; no food/water until fully alert; seek help if the seizure lasts >5 min, there is no recovery, or injury; epilepsy is NOT contagious.
html:
Epilepsy assessment and management algorithm: 8 assessment steps, emergency management of seizures >5 min, when to refer, first aid at home

Assessment:

1. Person presents with episodes of convulsions (fits, shaking, stiffening), witnessed or reported.

2. Confirm 2+ unprovoked seizures (not febrile, not substance-related, not syncope). Onset, duration, frequency?

3. Rule out other causes: hypoglycaemia, head injury, meningitis, stroke, eclampsia, substance withdrawal.

4. Assess: postictal confusion? Tongue-biting? Urinary incontinence? Aura? Birth trauma history?

5. Check current medications; assess for pregnancy in women of childbearing age.

6. Assess functional impairment: school, work, driving, daily activities, social life.

7. Screen for mental health comorbidities (depression, anxiety).

8. Diagnosis: epilepsy confirmed → proceed to management.

EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT (seizure > 5 min): call for emergency help immediately; diazepam 10-20 mg IV/PR or lorazepam 4 mg IV for status epilepticus; airway – place in recovery position, ensure breathing; DO NOT restrain; DO NOT put anything in the mouth; monitor blood glucose; give thiamine if alcohol-related.

When to refer: first seizure (confirm diagnosis); seizures not controlled after 2 drug trials; pregnancy + epilepsy (specialist input needed); status epilepticus; suspected structural cause (tumour, stroke).

First aid at home (advise carers): lay the person on their side, head turned to the side; ensure the airway is clear, loosen tight clothing; time the seizure and stay until fully conscious; no food/water until fully alert; seek help if the seizure lasts >5 min, there is no recovery, or injury; epilepsy is NOT contagious.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Epilepsy Management — Pharmacological Treatment
text:
### Antiepileptic medicines: sodium valproate, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, lamotrigine: adult and child doses, contraindications, side effects; principles of AED treatment

Antiepileptic medications: start one medication at the lowest dose and increase slowly until seizures are controlled. 1. Start low and go slow with a single AED as monotherapy, chosen by seizure type and epilepsy syndrome; titrate to the maximal dose. 2. If the first AED is ineffective at the maximum tolerated dose, introduce an alternative AED slowly without tapering the first. 3. If there is a good response to the second AED, consider withdrawing the original gradually. 4. If the first add-on AED is ineffective or has undesirable side effects, withdraw it slowly and replace it with another add-on AED. 5. If seizures are not controlled on two AEDs, some patients may benefit from a third. 6. Prefer an add-on AED with a different mode of action. 7. Review the diagnosis if seizures continue despite this approach and 2-3 years have elapsed.

| Class | Drug | Dosage and Frequency | Contraindications | Side Effects |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Anticonvulsant | Sodium valproate | Adults: 200 mg TDS PO; maintenance 400-1800 mg/day divided into 3 doses. Children: 10-15 mg/kg/day PO divided into 2 doses; maintenance <20 kg: 20-40 mg/kg/day; >20 kg: 20-30 mg/kg/day | Hepatic impairment; von Willebrand disease | Tremor, dizziness, weight gain, alopecia, diuresis, thrombocytopenia, impaired hepatic function |
| Anticonvulsant | Carbamazepine | Adults: 200 mg BD PO; maintenance 800-1200 mg/day divided into 2 doses. Children: 10-20 mg/kg/day PO divided into 2 doses; maintenance 20-30 mg/kg/day | Absence and myoclonic seizures; bone marrow suppression; hypersensitivity to tricyclic antidepressants | Blurred/double vision, nystagmus, ataxia, drowsiness, hyponatremia, rash, cytopenia, liver dysfunction, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis |
| Anticonvulsant | Phenytoin | Adults: 100 mg TDS PO; maintenance 300-900 mg/day divided into 3 doses. Children: 5-8 mg/kg/day divided into 2 doses | Absence and myoclonic seizures; febrile convulsions | Gingival hypertrophy, rash, confusion, fever, slurred speech, double vision, ataxia, bone marrow depression, hepatitis |
| Barbiturate | Phenobarbital | Adults: 30 mg NOCTE PO; maintenance 30-120 mg/day divided into 2 doses. Children: 3-5 mg/kg/day divided into 2 doses | Airway obstruction; dyspnea; marked hepatic impairment | Nausea, rash, sedation, lethargy, dependence, alteration of sleep cycle, hyperactivity, ataxia, liver dysfunction |
| Anticonvulsant | Lamotrigine | Adults: 25 mg every other day [with valproate], 25 mg OD [without valproate]; maintenance 100-200 mg/day [with valproate], 100-400 mg/day [without valproate]. Children: 0.15 mg/kg/day [with valproate], 0.3 mg/kg/day [without valproate]; maintenance 1-3 mg/kg/day [with valproate], 4.5-7.5 mg/kg/day [without valproate] | Hypersensitivity to the drug or its ingredients. Be cautious and titrate slowly if used with sodium valproate | Drowsiness, dizziness, diplopia, rash, cytopenia, liver injury, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis |

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Psychoeducation, cautions and follow-up
text:
> **Epilepsy psychoeducation and psychosocial interventions, cautions and special populations (drug interactions, pregnancy, children, PLHIV), and follow-up**
>
> Psychoeducation & psychosocial interventions:
> - Epilepsy is caused by abnormal electrical brain activity, NOT spirits or witchcraft.
> - Chronic condition: medication controls seizures in most if taken daily.
> - People with epilepsy can marry, work, have children and lead normal lives.
> - Avoid open fires, swimming alone, heights, heavy machinery, alcohol excess.
> - Observe local driving laws; may qualify for disability benefits.
> - All AEMs: taper slowly; an abrupt stop causes breakthrough seizures.
> - Review every 3-6 months; check adherence and side effects.
> 
> Cautions & special populations:
> - Check drug-drug interactions: AEMs reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives and antiretrovirals.
> - Rare: severe bone marrow depression, Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
> - Pregnancy: consult a specialist; supplement folate; valproate contraindicated.
> - Children: weight-based dosing; monitor growth and development.
> - PLHIV: check interactions with antiretrovirals before prescribing.
> - (Printed in the same cell:) minimum 2 years seizure-free before [stopping AEMs].
> 
> Follow-up (every 1-3 months initially, then 3-6 monthly): review seizure frequency (decreased or stopped?); check medication adherence and side effects; assess functional status (school, work, daily activities); screen for depression/anxiety comorbidity; if no seizures for 2+ years, discuss gradual tapering with a specialist; if seizures continue despite an adequate dose, increase the dose, check adherence, or refer to a specialist.
html:
Epilepsy psychoeducation and psychosocial interventions, cautions and special populations (drug interactions, pregnancy, children, PLHIV), and follow-up

Psychoeducation & psychosocial interventions:

- Epilepsy is caused by abnormal electrical brain activity, NOT spirits or witchcraft.

- Chronic condition: medication controls seizures in most if taken daily.

- People with epilepsy can marry, work, have children and lead normal lives.

- Avoid open fires, swimming alone, heights, heavy machinery, alcohol excess.

- Observe local driving laws; may qualify for disability benefits.

- All AEMs: taper slowly; an abrupt stop causes breakthrough seizures.

- Review every 3-6 months; check adherence and side effects.

Cautions & special populations:

- Check drug-drug interactions: AEMs reduce the efficacy of hormonal contraceptives and antiretrovirals.

- Rare: severe bone marrow depression, Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

- Pregnancy: consult a specialist; supplement folate; valproate contraindicated.

- Children: weight-based dosing; monitor growth and development.

- PLHIV: check interactions with antiretrovirals before prescribing.

- (Printed in the same cell:) minimum 2 years seizure-free before [stopping AEMs].

Follow-up (every 1-3 months initially, then 3-6 monthly): review seizure frequency (decreased or stopped?); check medication adherence and side effects; assess functional status (school, work, daily activities); screen for depression/anxiety comorbidity; if no seizures for 2+ years, discuss gradual tapering with a specialist; if seizures continue despite an adequate dose, increase the dose, check adherence, or refer to a specialist.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Systematic approach to long-term pharmacological treatment
text:
### Systematic approach to long-term pharmacological treatment of epilepsy: when to start AEDs, monotherapy, second AED, referral, re-evaluation, surgery and other options

When to start AEDs: immediate AED therapy is usually not necessary after a single seizure; it is generally started after two or more unprovoked seizures.

1. Initial AED monotherapy. Select the AED based on seizure type/syndrome, age, sex, childbearing potential, comorbidities, concomitant medications, adverse effects, interaction profile.
2. If failure: second AED, as monotherapy or add-on.
3. If failure: referral to a tertiary care centre (a).
4. Diagnostic re-evaluation (epilepsy yes/no, seizure types, syndrome, adherence, dosing), then: resective surgery; additional drug trials; neurostimulatory and dietary approaches (b).
Options at tertiary level: epilepsy surgery; ketogenic diet; vagus nerve stimulation; deep brain stimulation.

heading_path: Chapter 8: Neurology > Epilepsy > Status Epilepticus > Treatment Algorithm for Status Epilepticus
text:
### Management algorithm for status epilepticus in adults (ICU): stabilisation 0-5 min, first-line benzodiazepines 5-15 min, second-line valproate or phenytoin 15-30 min, third-line anaesthetic infusions after 30 min

Epilepsy emergencies: (i) acute repetitive seizures; (ii) status epilepticus.

0-5 minutes (stabilisation):
1. Stabilise the patient: assess airway, breathing, circulation.
2. Time the seizure onset; monitor vital signs (ECG, BP, HR, temperature).
3. Finger-stick blood glucose. If glucose <60 mg/dl, give 50 ml of 50% dextrose IV.
4. Laboratory investigations: electrolytes, CBC, liver and renal function tests.
Does the seizure continue? No → routine medical care. Yes →

5-15 minutes (first-line therapy): IV diazepam ('0.5 - 0.2 mg/kg/dose' as printed), max 10 mg, OR IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max not printed).
Does the seizure continue? No → routine medical care. Yes →

15-30 minutes, on ward (second-line therapy): valproate (VPA) 30 mg/kg loading dose and 4-8 mg/kg every 8 hr maintenance, OR phenytoin 20 mg/kg loading dose and '1.5 mg' every 8 hr maintenance (as printed).
Does the seizure continue? No → routine medical care. Yes →

After 30 minutes, on ward (third-line therapy):
1. Ketamine 1-2 mg/kg bolus and 1-2 mg/kg/hr continuous infusion for a minimum of 24 hr.
2. Propofol 1-3 mg/kg bolus and 5-10 mg/kg/hr continuous infusion for 24 hr.
3. Thiopental 3-5 mg/kg bolus and '3-3 mg/kg/hr' continuous infusion for 24 hr (as printed).

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Cervical Cancer > Cervical Cancer Screening & Treatment Algorithm
text:
### Cervical cancer screening and treatment algorithm: HIV-negative women vs women living with HIV (HPV DNA testing, VIA/VILI triage, screen-and-treat, stop age)

A. General population (HIV-negative women):
1. Age 25-50 years: HPV DNA testing; screen every 5 years.
2. HPV negative: rescreen in 5 years. HPV positive: triage testing.
3. VIA every 2 years (rescreen in 2 years):
   - Negative: rescreen in 2 years.
   - Positive: refer for LEEP/colposcopy.
4. Stop screening after age 50 + two negative tests.

B. Women living with HIV:
1. HIV positive, age 25+ OR at diagnosis: HPV DNA testing; screen every 3 years.
2. HPV negative: rescreen in 3 years. HPV positive: triage testing.
3. VIA every year or VILI every year (return in 1 year):
   - Negative: return in 1 year.
   - Positive: refer for LEEP/oncology.
4. Stop screening after age 50 + two negative tests.

Single-visit screen-and-treat: SCREEN → TRIAGE → TREAT (same day) → FOLLOW-UP; same-day care when feasible.
VIA: visual inspection with acetic acid. VILI: visual inspection with Lugol's iodine.

### Cervical cancer screening and management summary: HIV-negative women vs women living with HIV (start/stop age, test, intervals, triage, treatment, service model)

Cervical cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death among women in Eswatini (incidence 84.5 per 100,000 women, the highest in the world). Women living with HIV have a six-fold increased risk.

| Component | General Population (HIV-Negative Women) | Women Living with HIV |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start Age | 25 years | 25 years or at HIV diagnosis (whichever first) |
| Stop Age | After 50 years with 2 consecutive negative screens | After 50 years with 2 consecutive negative screens |

| HPV Screening Interval (if negative) | Every 5 years | Every 3 years |
| If HPV Positive | Triage (VIA / colposcopy / cytology) | Triage (VIA / colposcopy / cytology) |
| Alternative Method (if HPV unavailable) | VIA | VIA ± VILI |
| VIA/VILI Interval | Every 2 years | Annually (every year) |
| Screening Approach | Screen-and-treat | Screen-and-treat integrated into HIV care |
| If VIA/VILI Negative | Rescreen at interval | Rescreen at interval |
| If VIA/VILI Positive & eligible | Same-day cryotherapy/thermal ablation | Same-day cryotherapy/thermal ablation |
| If not eligible for ablation | Refer for LEEP/colposcopy | Refer for LEEP/colposcopy/oncology |
| Service Delivery Model | Primary care, MCH/OPD clinics | Routine HIV clinic visits (provider-initiated) |

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Cervical Cancer > Management by VIA result
text:
### Management by VIA screening result: negative, positive eligible for ablation, positive ineligible (LEEP), suspicious for cancer: eligibility, action and follow-up

| VIA Screening Result | Treatment Eligibility / Findings | Clinical Action & Procedure | Follow-Up Timeline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| VIA Negative | No lesions or suspicious areas identified | Discharge: return to routine screening (annual for HIV+; 2 years for HIV-) | 12 - 24 months (based on HIV status) |
| VIA Positive (eligible for ablation) | Lesion ≤75% of ectocervix; TZ fully visible (type 1); no endocervical extension; no suspicion of cancer | Ablative treatment (same visit): thermal ablation or cryotherapy | 12 months (repeat VIA) |
| VIA Positive (ineligible for ablation) | Large lesion (≥75% coverage); high-grade lesion suspected; tissue diagnosis needed | Refer for LEEP | 6 months (VIA or HPV) |
| Suspicious for Cancer | Visible mass/cauliflower growth; bleeds easily on contact; extension to vaginal walls | Urgent referral to secondary/tertiary level for colposcopy and biopsy | Immediate (per specialist) |

text:
### Cervical cancer screening in special populations: women living with HIV (on ART/PrEP), pregnant women, HIV-negative women

Because HIV significantly increases the risk of cervical cancer, screening must be integrated into routine care.

| Population | Screening Rule | Key Clinical Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HIV-positive women | Annual VIA screening | Integrate into ART initiation and routine follow-up. |
| On ART / PrEP | Annual VIA screening | Adherence reduces but does not eliminate risk. |
| Pregnant women | Screen per HIV status | VIA is safe. Defer treatment until post-delivery unless cancer is suspected. |
| HIV-negative | Every 2 years | Use community health workers and registries for recall. |

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Adult Lymphomas > Investigations
text:
### Adult lymphoma investigations: biopsy, pathology, laboratory tests and radiology Lymphoma: no routine screening is available; patients are suspected from symptoms (enlarged lymph nodes, chills, weight loss, fatigue, swollen abdomen, early satiety, chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath or cough, severe or frequent infections, easy bruising or bleeding). High-risk groups: EBV infection, HTLV-1, Kaposi sarcoma, immunosuppression (HIV or non-HIV related), H. pylori infection, autoimmune disorders (Sjogren's syndrome, Hashimoto's thyroiditis), exposure to pesticides, radiation and chemotherapy. | Diagnostic Category | Investigation | | --- | --- | | Biopsy | - A whole node excision biopsy by a medical officer
- Bone marrow aspirate trephine (BMAT) | | Pathology | - A full pathology report with IHC and cell of origin defined
- Blood smear
- Immunohistochemistry (often CD45, CD20, CD3 etc.) | | Laboratory Tests | - A full biochemistry report, including KFT, LFT, uric acid, LDH, CMP, blood glucose
- FBC and differential count
- Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
- CD4 count and viral load for eligible patients
- Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), hepatitis C virus and HIV tests | | Radiology | - Echocardiogram report
- Contrasted CT scan – must include neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis
- PET/CT scan for Deauville scoring, if available | **Note:** REFER TO A HIGHER LEVEL FACILITY FOR FURTHER INVESTIGATION AND MANAGEMENT.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Risk Stratification for Breast Cancer
text:
### Breast cancer risk stratification by family history and genetics: above average, moderately increased, high risk | Risk Level | Criteria | | --- | --- | | Above Average Risk | - No family history
- One first-degree relative or 1–2 second-degree relatives diagnosed at age 50 or older | | Moderately Increased Risk | - A first-degree relative diagnosed before age 50
- Two or more first-degree relatives on the same side of the family diagnosed at any age | | High Risk | - Known to carry a breast cancer susceptibility gene mutation (e.g. BRCA1 or BRCA2)
- Strong family history with at least two first-degree relatives affected, plus other features | **Note:** General population screening should begin at age 35 with clinical and self-exam. High-risk clients start 8-10 years earlier than the index case (e.g. those with BRCA mutations may start at age 25). High risk: radiation to the chest in childhood or adulthood; familial breast and ovarian cancer; male breast cancer in the family; presenting with a breast lump; breast cancer in a first-degree relative under 50.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Recommended diagnostics for breast cancer
text:
### Breast cancer diagnostics: biopsy techniques, pathology, laboratory tests and radiology for staging Screening modalities: breast self-examination (breast awareness); clinical breast examination by a trained health worker; breast ultrasound; mammography; FNA; tissue biopsy (incision, excision or tru-cut); MRI in selected cases. | Diagnostic Category | Investigation | | --- | --- | | Biopsy | - Biopsy techniques: excision; lumpectomy; tru-cut biopsy
- Ultrasound guided biopsies are preferred | | Pathology | - A full pathology report including immunohistochemistry (IHC) | | Laboratory Tests | - A full biochemistry report, including KFT and LFT
- FBC and differential count | | Radiology | - Echocardiogram report
- Contrasted CT scan to include chest, abdomen and pelvis to rule out metastasis
- Chest X-ray prior to surgery to rule out effusions
- Bone scan in locally advanced breast cancers on the radiologist's recommendation if CT does not show metastasis; diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with MRI to image the spine. Note: DWI is recommended in place of a bone scan if a bone scan is not available
- Bilateral mammogram required for every patient for staging: the mammogram should include bilateral and axillary ultrasound; lymph nodes: routine supraclavicular ultrasound |

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > How to Advise Client on Breast Self-Examination
text:
> **Breast self-examination: how to advise clients (looking, touching, lying down, lymph nodes)**
>
> 1. By looking: stand before a mirror and look at both breasts and nipples – once with both arms beside your body; once with both hands on your hips; once with both arms raised and arms behind your head.
> 2. By touching: raise your left arm. Use the pads of 3 or 4 fingers of the right hand to examine your left breast; repeat on the right side. Examine once in lines up and down the breast from outside and inside; once in circles around the breast, making smaller circles towards the nipple; once in wedges starting from outside towards the nipple and back again.
> 3. While lying down: lie on your back, left arm over your head and a pillow under your left shoulder. Examine your left breast with your right hand as described before; repeat for the right side. This position flattens the breast and makes it easier to examine.
> 4. Lymph nodes: place your left hand on your waist. With your right hand try to find enlarged lymph nodes in the left underarm area and around your collar bone; repeat on your right side. An enlarged lymph node feels like a corn kernel or a bean.
html:
Breast self-examination: how to advise clients (looking, touching, lying down, lymph nodes)

1. By looking: stand before a mirror and look at both breasts and nipples – once with both arms beside your body; once with both hands on your hips; once with both arms raised and arms behind your head.

2. By touching: raise your left arm. Use the pads of 3 or 4 fingers of the right hand to examine your left breast; repeat on the right side. Examine once in lines up and down the breast from outside and inside; once in circles around the breast, making smaller circles towards the nipple; once in wedges starting from outside towards the nipple and back again.

3. While lying down: lie on your back, left arm over your head and a pillow under your left shoulder. Examine your left breast with your right hand as described before; repeat for the right side. This position flattens the breast and makes it easier to examine.

4. Lymph nodes: place your left hand on your waist. With your right hand try to find enlarged lymph nodes in the left underarm area and around your collar bone; repeat on your right side. An enlarged lymph node feels like a corn kernel or a bean.

Examine once in lines up and down the breast from outside and inside; once in circles around the breast, making smaller circles towards the nipple; once in wedges starting from outside towards the nipple and back again.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Clinical Breast Examination > What to look out for and palpation sequence
text:
> **Clinical breast examination: what to look out for (lump, pulled-in nipple, dimpling, skin changes, redness/rash, discharge) and the palpation sequence**
>
> What to look out for during CBE (illustration): lump; pulled-in nipple; dimpling; skin changes; redness/rash; dripping (nipple discharge).

> Sequence to follow when performing breast palpation: 1. upper outer quadrant; 2. upper inner quadrant; 3. lower inner quadrant; 4. lower outer quadrant; 5. nipple-areola area; 6. axillary (underarm) quadrant.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Breast Cancer > Early Referral Flow Chart for Suspected Breast Cancer
text:
### Early referral flowchart for suspected breast cancer: urgent referral to the specialised breast unit, booking, or surgical clinic, by likelihood of malignancy

Suspected lump → provider-initiated clinical breast exam (PI-CBE) and direct referral to the specialised breast unit (SBU):
- High likelihood of malignancy → URGENT REFERRAL TO SBU (call and inform the SBU): suspicious lump (fixed, hard, irregular); palpable axillary lymph node; ulceration; nodules on the skin; skin tethering; nipple retraction; nipple discharge (e.g. bloody).
- Unsure → book SBU: palpable lump in women >25 years; non-lactational breast infection/abscess.
- Unlikely to be malignant → book for surgical clinic: palpable lump in women <25 years; breast pain with normal PI-CBE; family history with normal PI-CBE; lactation-associated infection with non-resolution/recurrence.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Childhood Cancers > Warning Signs of Childhood Cancers (St. Siluan's signs)
text:
### Warning signs of childhood cancers (St. Siluan's signs): seek help, eye, lump, unexplained symptoms, aches, neurological signs, with likely cancers and actions

Childhood cancers arise between birth and 19 years. The most common are leukaemias (about 28%), brain and spinal cord tumours (about 26%), neuroblastoma (about 6%), Wilms tumour (5%), lymphomas, rhabdomyosarcoma, retinoblastoma and bone cancers (osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma). A high index of suspicion and early detection are critical.

| Letter | Category | Key Signs & Symptoms | Actions/Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S | Seek | Seek medical help early for ongoing symptoms: prolonged symptoms; symptoms persist after treatment; symptoms return after initially disappearing | Seek medical help; return to the same clinic/doctor for follow-up |
| I (E) | Eye | White spot in the eye (leukocoria) → possible retinoblastoma; loss of red eye reflex; new squint or sudden blindness → possible brain tumour; bulging eyeball → possible eye cancer or retro-orbital tumour | Urgent referral to an ophthalmologist or paediatrician |
| L | Lump | Lump in the abdomen, pelvis, head, arms, legs, testicle or glands; Wilms' tumour (age 3–4 years); consider neuroblastoma, lymphoma | Refer every lump to a doctor. If treated for TB without confirmation and not improving after 2 weeks → re-evaluate, consider biopsy |
| U | Unexplained | Unexplained fever for over two weeks; weight or appetite loss; fatigue; pallor; easy bruising and bleeding | Possible leukaemia or solid tumours; requires thorough clinical assessment |
| A | Ache | Aching bones, joints, back and easy fractures. Aches and pains in bones and back are not common in children and should raise suspicion | Possible leukaemia or sarcoma; needs critical evaluation |
| N | Neurological | Change in walk, balance or speech; regression of milestones; slurred speech; continuous headaches (>1 week) with or without vomiting; early morning vomiting; cranial nerve palsy; enlarged head (hydrocephalus) | Possible brain tumour; prompt referral and neuroimaging as needed |

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Childhood Cancers > Warning Signs of Childhood Cancer: suspicious clinical features
text:
### Warning signs of childhood cancer: signs and symptoms with the clinical features that make them suspicious (pallor, fever, infections, lymphadenopathy, bleeding, headache, masses, bone pain and others)

| Signs and Symptoms | Suspicious Clinical Features |
| --- | --- |
| Paleness, fatigue, and malaise | Especially if persistent and associated with signs of bone marrow infiltration (unexplained fever, recurrent infections, bleeding diathesis) and/or lymphadenopathy |
| Fever | Prolonged (>2 weeks) without apparent cause, associated with weight loss, night sweats, paleness, petechiae, mass, bone pain and lymphadenopathy |
| Recurrent or persistent infections | Associated with paleness, petechiae, weight loss, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly or palpable mass |
| Anorexia and weight loss | Prolonged and unjustified, especially with other warning signs (recurrent infections, fever, paleness, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly) |
| Localized lymphadenopathy | Persistent or progressive, not resolving in 4-6 weeks or unresponsive to antibiotics; size >2 cm, hard, painless, supraclavicular or epitrochlear |
| Generalized or localized (lymphadenopathy) | Associated with fever, night sweats, weight loss, malaise, paleness and hepatosplenomegaly |
| Hemorrhagic manifestations (petechiae, ecchymosis, recurrent epistaxis, bleeding gums) | Persistent or combined with other signs of bone marrow infiltration (paleness, fatigue, recurrent infections) |
| Headache | Recent onset, in the morning or waking the child at night, without a history of migraine, associated with vomiting or neurological symptoms (cranial palsy, motor or sensory signs), occipital location, worse when lying down |
| Impaired school performance and mood changes | Recent onset, progressive and not explained |
| Palpable abdominal mass | Any mass (except in the neonatal period) is suspicious for malignancy, especially with vomiting, abdominal pain, constipation, hematuria or hypertension |
| Hepatomegaly | Must always be investigated, even in asymptomatic cases |

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Childhood Cancers > Childhood Cancer Referral Pathway
text:
### Childhood cancer referral pathway: primary clinic identification, urgent referral, workup, MDT, confirmation, paediatric oncology

1. Primary clinic (e.g. GP, school nurse): identify suspected cancer using the SILUAN signs (significant, unexplained, rapid onset, ongoing symptoms, night sweats).
2. Urgent referral to a health centre/regional hospital.
3. Initial workup and assessment: physical exam, blood tests, imaging as needed.
4. Multidisciplinary team (MDT): paediatric oncologist, radiology, radiotherapy (as printed 'ratiology'), pathology, surgery.
5. Confirmation of diagnosis.
6. Referral to paediatric oncology for management (treatment planning, supportive care).

text:
### Colorectal cancer risk factors: modifiable vs non-modifiable

| Modifiable Risk Factors | Non-modifiable Risk Factors |
| --- | --- |
| Excess body fat | Family history of colorectal cancer |
| Sedentary lifestyle | Advanced polyps |
| Westernized diet including processed/pre-packed meats, fried foods, fast food etc. | Polyposis syndrome (FAP, MAP) |
| Processed meats | Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) |
| Red meats | Black race |
| Smoking | Older age |
| Alcohol | Male gender |

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Oral & Maxillofacial Cancers > Diagnostic Algorithm
text:
### Oral lesion diagnostic algorithm: clinical diagnosis, follow-up vs biopsy, adjuvant diagnostic techniques and urgent referral

Photographs show the steps of the oral examination.

1. Oral lesion → previous clinical diagnosis based on clinical data.
2. Lesion resolves with or without therapy → follow-up.
3. Lesion changes, persists or progresses → perform a biopsy → identification of the histological entity, with or without malignancy → follow-up (or repeat biopsy).

Adjuvant diagnostic techniques: 1. oral cytology; 2. salivary biomarkers; 3. light-based techniques (auto-fluorescence, spectroscopy, chemiluminescence); 4. tissue staining.

Diagnostic workup: if there is any suspicion that a lesion may be oral cavity cancer, document the lesion site and size, take a clinical photograph if possible, and make an urgent referral to an oral & maxillofacial surgeon who is part of a head and neck oncology MDT. Any oral lesion (including a patch or ulcer) that fails to resolve in 2-3 weeks should raise suspicion.

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Prostate Cancer > Screening and Diagnosis of Prostate Cancer > PSA levels
text:
### PSA-based prostate cancer screening: risk stratification for PSA under 4 ng/ml by age (EAU 2022), and recommendations for PSA 4-10 and >10 ng/ml in men 50-75

Prostate screening every two years for men above 50 with risk factors. Discuss screening at age 45 for men at high risk (African American, first-degree relative with prostate cancer at an early age) and at age 40 for very high risk (several first-degree relatives with early prostate cancer). DRE by a trained health worker, with annual PSA and rectal or pelvic ultrasound. Those with above-average risk start earlier at the clinician's discretion.

**PSA under 4 ng/ml: risk stratification (EAU 2022)**

| Category / PSA level | Definition | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low Risk | PSA <1 in those <40 years; PSA <2 in those 41-60 years | Repeat screening after 5 - 8 years |
| High Risk | PSA >1 in those <40 years; PSA >2 in those 41-60 years | Repeat screening after 2 years |

**PSA above 4 ng/ml in men 50-75 years**

| Category / PSA level | Definition | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4-10 ng/ml |  | 1. If DRE is normal, repeat after 4-6 weeks; if it increases, refer for urologist review. 2. If DRE abnormal, refer to urologist. 3. If available, determine the free to total PSA ratio and PSA density, and consult |
| > 10 ng/ml |  | Refer to urologist |

### Prostate cancer diagnosis and staging investigations: biopsy, pathology, PSA tests, radiology, other

Signs and symptoms: may be asymptomatic; LUTS (urgency/frequency, dysuria, nocturia, poor stream, straining); haematuria, poor erectile function, bone pain, bladder outlet obstruction, urinary retention, chronic renal failure, rectal bleeding.

| Diagnostic Category | Investigation |
| --- | --- |
| Biopsy | Biopsy (trans-rectal ultrasound-guided biopsy is the current standard) |
| Pathology | A full histology report |
| Laboratory Tests | Prostate specific antigen (PSA) test and its isoforms: PSA doubling time; PSA density; PSA velocity; PSA ratio, free to bound |
| Radiology | Ultrasound pelvis and abdomen; chest X-ray; if PSA >20, bone scan, or MRI DWI (high risk) if bone scan unavailable; CT scan; MRI pelvis (prostate-specific sequences) |
| Other | Endoscopy and other specialized tests as indicated and available |

heading_path: Chapter 9: Oncology > Prostate Cancer > Summary Guideline for Management by Risk Category
text:
### Prostate cancer management by risk category (very low, low, high risk): observation, active surveillance, radiotherapy, radical prostatectomy, hormone therapy

Management depends on stage, risk category, age, comorbidities and life expectancy, performance status, resources, hormone sensitivity in metastatic disease, and the patient's wishes. Options: watchful waiting; active surveillance; surgery (radical prostatectomy, TURP etc.); radiotherapy (external beam, brachytherapy); hormonal therapy (medical or surgical castration, bilateral orchiectomy); chemotherapy; supportive care (pain management, bisphosphonates such as zoledronate). Localised disease: radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy with or without hormones. Metastatic hormone-sensitive: bilateral orchiectomy (cheaper than medical therapy) or hormonal therapy as ADT or combined androgen blockade (CAB). Castration-resistant: second-line hormonal agents (enzalutamide, abiraterone) and/or chemotherapy (docetaxel).

| Risk category | Recommended Treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Very Low Risk | Life expectancy <10 yrs: observation. Life expectancy 10-20 yrs: active surveillance. Life expectancy >20 yrs: active surveillance, radiotherapy (EBRT or brachytherapy), or radical prostatectomy (RP) +/- pelvic lymph node dissection (LND) if >2% risk of LN involvement (Roach or Partin tables) |
| Low Risk | Life expectancy <10 yrs: observation. Life expectancy >10 yrs: RT alone, RP +/- pelvic LND, or active surveillance. If RP with positive margins → adjuvant RT (preferred) or expectant management |
| High Risk | Radiotherapy (3DCRT/IMRT with IGRT +/- brachytherapy boost) + long-term hormone therapy (2-3 yrs; neoadjuvant, concurrent and adjuvant). 4-6 months of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) considered for select patients with a single adverse feature with Gleason score 6-7. Consider whole pelvis radiotherapy. Consider RP with pelvic LND only for selected patients with low-volume disease and no fixation. Adjuvant RT +/- short-term ADT for positive margins or pT3 disease |

ADT: androgen deprivation therapy; CAB: combined androgen blockade; EBRT: external beam radiation therapy; IGRT: image-guided radiation therapy; IMRT: intensity-modulated radiation therapy; LN: lymph node; LND: lymph node dissection; RP: radical prostatectomy; RT: radiotherapy; 3DCRT: three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy.
