heading_path: Chapter 10: Ophthalmology > Cataract > Screening and Diagnosis of Cataract
text:
### Cataract screening, diagnosis and management workflow: assessment, ruling out other causes, impact on daily life, referral, early vs significant cataract, surgery; referral rules

1. Patient presents with visual complaints: gradual, painless vision loss; glare, haloes, blurred vision.
2. Clinical assessment: visual acuity; lens exam (cloudiness); red reflex.
3. Rule out other causes of vision loss: retinal disease; glaucoma; refractive errors.
4. Confirm the cataract diagnosis.
5. Assess the impact on daily life: daily activities; bilateral/unilateral; uncorrectable with glasses.
6. Refer to an ophthalmologist: full evaluation; biometry.
   - Mild/early cataract: monitor; improve lighting; adjust glasses.
   - Affects daily life (significant cataract): surgery (phacoemulsification + IOL); post-operative care: eye drops, follow-up, patient education.

REFER ALL SEVERE/SIGNIFICANT CATARACT CASES TO AN EYE SURGEON FOR CATARACT SURGERY. Refer clients with comorbidities such as HTN/DM, and pregnant women with cataract, to an ophthalmologist once a year from diagnosis for routine screening. Refer children immediately: a white pupil in a child may be an eye tumour, and late referral may lead to permanent loss of vision, squint, loss of the eye or loss of life.

heading_path: Chapter 10: Ophthalmology > Diabetic Retinopathy > Classification of DR
text:
### Diabetic retinopathy classification by severity (no DR, mild/moderate/severe NPDR, PDR, DME): defining features, management and follow-up interval

| DR Severity | Defining Features | Management | Follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| No DR | No microvascular abnormalities | Control blood glucose levels, serum lipid levels, and blood pressure | 1-2 yrs |
| Mild NPDR | Microaneurysms only | Control blood glucose levels, serum lipid levels, and blood pressure | 6-12 mo |
| Moderate NPDR | Microaneurysms and other signs (dot and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots), but not severe NPDR | Control blood glucose levels, serum lipid levels, and blood pressure | 3-6 mo |
| Severe NPDR | Intraretinal haemorrhages (>20 in each of 4 quadrants), definite venous beading (in at least 2 quadrants), or apparent IRMA (in at least 1 quadrant), but not PDR | Consider PRP | <3 mo |
| PDR | Neovascularization of the optic disc or elsewhere, preretinal haemorrhage, or vitreous haemorrhage | Strongly consider PRP; consider vitrectomy for persistent vitreous haemorrhage or tractional retinal detachment | <1 mo (variable) |
| DME | Retinal thickening in the macula | Consider focal laser photocoagulation, anti-VEGF therapy, or corticosteroid therapy for centre-involving DME | 1-3 mo |

No DR: no apparent retinopathy; NPDR: non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy; PDR: proliferative diabetic retinopathy; DME: diabetic macular oedema. Fundus photographs show normal fundus, moderate NPDR, severe NPDR and PDR (courtesy of Medscape Education).

heading_path: Chapter 10: Ophthalmology > Diabetic Retinopathy > Screening flowchart for diabetic retinopathy
text:
### Diabetic retinopathy screening flowchart: visual acuity and fundus findings → routine re-examination, non-urgent referral, or urgent referral

1. Diabetes history, medical history, current medication, biochemical parameters.
2. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) with current spectacles, and ophthalmoscopy or fundus photography.
   - VA better than 6/12 (20/40) and no DR → routine re-examination.
   - VA 6/12 (20/40) or worse, or mild or moderate NPDR → non-urgent referral for refraction and assessment.
   - Severe NPDR, DME, or PDR → urgent referral.
*Need to optimise medical treatment: glycaemic control, hypertension, and lipids.
DME = diabetic macular oedema; NPDR = non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy; PDR = proliferative diabetic retinopathy; VA = visual acuity.

text:
### Diabetic retinopathy screening schedule: timing of first and subsequent retinal examination by risk factor (type 1, type 2, complications, poor control, other)

| Risk Factors | 1st retinal examination | Subsequent examination |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type 1 DM | Within 5 years of diagnosis and after onset of puberty | Annually |
| Type 2 DM | At time of diagnosis | Annually |
| Evidence of other diabetic complications, e.g. CVD, renal disease (nephropathy), foot ulcers (neuropathy) | Immediately | As recommended by eye care provider |
| Poor glycaemic control | Immediately | As recommended by eye care provider |
| Other risk factors: hyperlipidemia, smoking, cataract surgery, obesity, anaemia, leukaemias etc. | At time of diagnosis / immediately | As recommended by eye care provider |

**Note:** Screening by health care workers (medical officers and nursing staff): visual acuity with a Snellen or illiterate E chart; penlight torch to examine the external eye, pupillary reaction etc. Symptoms are absent early; later fluctuating or blurred vision, spots or floaters, dark or empty areas in vision, total loss of vision.

heading_path: Chapter 10: Ophthalmology > Glaucoma > Screening and Diagnosis of Glaucoma
text:
### Acute (angle-closure) vs chronic (open-angle) glaucoma: onset, pain, redness, vision, pupil, cornea, IOP, optic nerve, age, family history, urgency; who to screen

Who must be screened (risk factors): adults ≥40 years; family history of glaucoma; high IOP; diabetes, hypertension, migraines, sickle cell anaemia; eye injuries or certain eye surgery; prolonged corticosteroid use, especially eye drops. Screening: all health workers take visual acuity with a Snellen chart and examine the external eye with a penlight torch.

| Feature | Acute Glaucoma (Angle Closure) | Chronic Glaucoma (Open Angle) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | Sudden | Gradual |
| Pain | Severe eye pain | Usually painless |
| Redness | Present, typically unilateral | Usually absent |
| Vision Changes | Sudden vision loss; haloes around lights | Gradual peripheral vision loss (tunnel vision) |
| Headache | Unilateral, temporal | Rare |
| Nausea/Vomiting | Common | Rare |
| Pupil | Mid-dilated, fixed, non-reactive | Usually normal |
| Cornea | Cloudy or hazy | Clear |
| Anterior Chamber | Shallow | Normal depth |
| Intraocular Pressure (IOP) | Markedly elevated; eye feels hard on palpation | Elevated; eye may feel tense on palpation |
| Optic Nerve | May appear swollen in acute phase | Shows cupping/damage on fundoscopy |
| Age Group | Usually >40 years | Usually >40 years, earlier in Black individuals |
| Family History | Not prominent | First-degree relatives at higher risk |
| Urgency | Ophthalmological emergency – urgent referral | Chronic, but requires monitoring and long-term management |

Primary open-angle glaucoma has no symptoms in early stages, so routine intraocular pressure checks and fundus examination should be done in everyone aged 40 and above by qualified eye care personnel.
All suspected cases of glaucoma should be referred to qualified eye care personnel for confirmation of diagnosis and a treatment plan.

heading_path: Chapter 10: Ophthalmology > Glaucoma > Pharmacological Management of Glaucoma
text:
### Glaucoma medicines: acute glaucoma (acetazolamide, glycerol, timolol) and chronic glaucoma stepwise (timolol/betaxolol, latanoprost/bimatoprost, brimonidine, pilocarpine, acetazolamide): dose, frequency, duration

**Acute glaucoma (refer to ophthalmologist immediately)**

| Step | Medicine | Dose | Frequency | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First | Acetazolamide PO | 250-500 mg | Once |  |
| Or | Glycerin as glycerol | 1 ml/kg | Once |  |
| Plus | Timolol 0.25-0.5% | Instil 1 drop | Twice daily | 2 weeks |

**Chronic glaucoma**

| Step | Medicine | Dose | Frequency | Duration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First line | Timolol 0.25 or 0.5% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Twice daily | Long term |
| Or | Betaxolol 0.25 or 0.5% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Twice daily | Long term |
| If adherent with no good response, add (or first line if beta-blockers contraindicated) | Latanoprost 0.005% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Twice daily (as printed) | Long term |
| Or | Prostamide bimatoprost 0.03% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Twice daily (as printed) | Long term |
| If intolerant of or not responding to prostaglandin analogue | Brimonidine 0.15-0.2% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Twice daily | Long term |
| Failure to respond (consult a specialist first) | Pilocarpine hydrochloride 2% or 4% eye drops | Instil 1 drop in the eyes | Four times daily | Review |
| Severe cases or while waiting for surgery | Acetazolamide PO | 250 mg | Four times daily | Review |

**Note:** Acute glaucoma: also treat pain and nausea/vomiting. Acetazolamide contains sulphur: do not use in patients allergic to sulphur. Glycerol is a concentrated sugar solution: do not give to diabetic patients. Prostaglandin analogues may be first line when beta-blockers are contraindicated, or second line on beta-blockers if the target IOP reduction is not reached. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in overt asthma (may cause an acute asthma attack soon after instillation). Pilocarpine causes long-standing pupil constriction; use only when the patient is prepared for glaucoma surgery, or as an alternative when timolol is contraindicated.

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Types and Characteristics of Pain
text:
### Types of pain (nociceptive somatic, visceral, inflammatory; neurogenic; functional): characteristics, mechanisms and example drug treatments

Pain is 'an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage' (IASP).

| Type of Pain | Subtype | Characteristics | Mechanisms | Examples of pharmacologic treatments |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nociceptive | Somatic (tissue injury) | Superficial (skin) or deep pain (muscle, fascia, tendon) | Mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli | Acetaminophen, Na+ blockers, NSAIDs, steroids, opioids |
| Nociceptive | Visceral (irritable bowel, cystitis) | Constant or cramping. Poor localization. Autonomic responses | Visceral distension | NSAIDs, antispasmodics, opioids |
| Nociceptive | Inflammatory (musculoskeletal) | Localized or diffuse pain, hyperalgesia, allodynia | Associated with localized inflammation | NSAIDs, steroids |
| Neurogenic | Neuralgia, radiculopathy, causalgia, CNS lesions | Spontaneous, paroxysmal pain, allodynia, hyperalgesia | Peripheral or CNS lesions | Anticonvulsants, opioids, antidepressants |
| Neurogenic | Functional (FM, thalamic syndromes, irritable bowel syndrome) | Diffuse deep pain, hyperalgesia, allodynia | Dysregulation of excitatory or inhibitory mechanisms in CNS | Antidepressants, anticonvulsants, opioids, cannabinoids |

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Management of Pain > WHO Analgesic Ladder
text:
### WHO analgesic ladder for adult pain: step 1 non-opioid (mild), step 2 weak opioid (moderate), step 3 strong opioid (severe), with drug categories

Pain scores on the numerical rating scale: none 0; mild 1-3; moderate 4-6; severe 7-10.
- Step 1, mild pain (0-3): non-opioid +/- adjuvant.
- Step 2, moderate pain (4-6): weak opioid +/- non-opioid +/- adjuvant.
- Step 3, severe pain: strong opioid +/- non-opioid +/- adjuvant.
Step up if pain persists or increases; step down if pain decreases.

Categories of drugs:
- Non-opioids: ibuprofen or other NSAID, paracetamol (acetaminophen), or aspirin.
- Weak opioids: codeine, tramadol, or low-dose morphine.
- Strong opioids: morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone, buprenorphine.
- Adjuvants: antidepressant, anticonvulsant, antispasmodic, muscle relaxant, bisphosphonate, or corticosteroid.
Combining an opioid and a non-opioid is effective, but do not combine drugs of the same class. Time doses by drug half-life ('dose by the clock'); do not wait for pain to recur.

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Analgesics: doses and cautions
text:
### Analgesics for palliative pain management: non-opioids (paracetamol, ibuprofen, diclofenac), weak opioids (tramadol, codeine), strong opioid (morphine): doses, cautions and contraindications

| Category | Drug and Dosage | Caution and Contraindications |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-Opioid | Paracetamol: 500 mg-1 g 6-8 hourly | Hepatotoxicity. Maximum dose 4 g per day |
| Non-Opioid | Ibuprofen: 400 mg 6-8 hourly | Give with food. Maximum dose 1.2 g. Avoid in asthma and peptic ulcer. Lower dose if liver impairment |
| Non-Opioid | Diclofenac: 50 mg 8-12 hourly | Give with food; avoid in asthma and peptic ulcer. Maximum dose 150 mg |
| Weak Opioid | Tramadol: 50-100 mg 4-6 hourly | Caution in epileptic patients. Maximum dosage 240 mg daily (as printed). Give laxatives to avoid constipation unless the patient has diarrhoea |
| Weak Opioid | Codeine: 30-60 mg 4 hourly | Caution in epileptic patients. Maximum dosage 240 mg daily (as printed). Give laxatives to avoid constipation unless the patient has diarrhoea |
| Strong Opioid | Morphine: start with 2.5-20 mg q4h (immediate release); give 8-24 hourly for slow release. 5%-20% of the daily dose is used as the starting dose for breakthrough pain | Low-dose morphine is given if the maximum weak-opioid dose does not work. No ceiling dose for morphine (increase gradually until pain is controlled). Pethidine can be used for acute pain (NOT for chronic pain) |

Less commonly used strong opioids in our settings: fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone, methadone.

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Palliative Care in the Trajectory of the Patient's Illness
text:
### Palliative care across the illness trajectory, and palliative care tasks by level (referral hospital, regional hospital, health centre/primary clinic, home)

Trajectory (diagram): from presentation/diagnosis, therapies to modify disease (curative, restorative intent) decrease over time while therapies to relieve suffering and/or improve quality of life (palliative care) increase; palliative care continues through life closure and active dying to death, followed by bereavement care.

Palliative care by level:
- Referral hospitals: holistic assessment and reassessment; appropriate pain and symptom management; holistic care with specialised management (radiotherapy, chemotherapy, surgery).
- Regional hospitals: holistic assessment and reassessment; appropriate pain and symptom management; initiate or adjust the PC regimen for mild, moderate or severe symptoms; plan continued PC after discharge to a lower level or home; refer to referral hospitals for specialised management.
- Health centre/primary care clinic: visit the patient at home in the first week after discharge if possible; holistic pain assessment; pain and symptom management using the WHO ladder; emotional support; liaise with CHWs who visit patients at home; request oral morphine solution for PC patients in the HC catchment area; request advice from the regional hospital if needed; refer complicated cases to the regional hospital.
- Home: recognise and report inadequately relieved pain or other physical, psychological or social distress, and improper use of morphine or other medicines; provide emotional support; educate the family on daily care (feeding, hygiene, mobility, medications).

text:

| Opioid | Mild to moderate CKD stages 1, 2, (3) | Advanced CKD stages (3), 4, 5 (eGFR <30 mL/min) |

| Codeine | YES, reduced dose | AVOID |
| Tramadol | YES, reduced dose | Maybe (4), reduced dose |
| Buprenorphine (3) | YES | YES, reduced dose |
| Morphine | YES, reduced dose | AVOID |
| Hydromorphone | YES, reduced dose | Use with caution, reduced dose |
| Oxycodone | YES, reduced dose | AVOID (4) |
| Fentanyl (1,2) | YES (1) | YES, reduced dose |
| Methadone (1,2) | YES (1,2) | YES, with caution (1,2) |

heading_path: Chapter 11: Palliation > Pain Management > Adjuvant Analgesics for Bone and Neuropathic Pain
text:
### Adjuvant analgesics for bone and neuropathic pain: dexamethasone, amitriptyline, gabapentin, pregabalin: indications, doses and key notes

| Class | Indications | Common Drugs & Doses | Key Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Steroids | Pain caused by pressure (e.g. stretched liver capsule, raised ICP, Pancoast tumour) | Dexamethasone: 8–16 mg once daily before noon; if effective, reduce by 2 mg/day after 3 days | Stop after 5 days if no response |
| Antidepressants | Neuropathic pain | Amitriptyline: 10–75 mg at night; start low, increase every 2–3 days until pain controlled or side effects limit use | Sedating – useful at night; caution in elderly |
| Anticonvulsants | Neuropathic pain | Gabapentin: start 300 mg at night → increase by 300 mg every 2–3 days (night → BD → TDS → 600 mg BD); max 2400 mg/day; if no benefit after 900 mg/day, unlikely to be effective | Titrate slowly to minimise dizziness & somnolence. Caution: renal impairment |
| Anticonvulsants | Neuropathic pain | Pregabalin: start 50 mg TDS or 75 mg BD; doses >300 mg/day rarely give extra benefit | Titrate slowly to minimise dizziness & somnolence. Caution: renal impairment |

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Classification > Wagner grades
text:
### Diabetic foot ulcer classification (Wagner grades 0-5): description and category

Diabetic foot: infection, ulceration or destruction of tissues of the foot associated with neuropathy and/or peripheral arterial disease in people with diabetes. About 80% of non-traumatic lower limb amputations in diabetes are preceded by a foot ulcer.

| Ulcer Grade | Description | Category |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | No ulcer but high-risk foot (e.g. deformity, callus, or ischaemia) | Non-ulcer stage |
| 1 | Superficial ulcer involving only the skin | Non-gangrenous ulcer |
| 2 | Deep ulcer, extending into tendon, bone, or joint capsule, but without bony involvement or abscess | Non-gangrenous ulcer |
| 3 | Deep ulcer with abscess, osteomyelitis, or joint sepsis (confirmed clinically or by X-ray) | Non-gangrenous ulcer |
| 4 | Localized gangrene (e.g. toe, heel, forefoot) | Gangrenous ulcer |
| 5 | Extensive gangrene involving the whole foot | Gangrenous ulcer |

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Algorithm A: foot assessment and risk
text:
### Diabetic foot algorithm A: foot assessment in all patients with diabetes, active foot problems, and risk stratification (high, moderate, low) with actions

All patients with diabetes → foot assessment: skin; neurological; vascular; musculoskeletal.
1. Active foot problem? (any of: ulceration; spreading infection; critical limb ischaemia; gangrene; suspicion of acute Charcot neuroarthropathy or an unexplained hot, red, swollen foot with or without pain)
   - Yes → Algorithm B.
   - No → 2.
2. Previous history of ulceration, amputation, or on renal replacement therapy? Yes → HIGH RISK: early referral to podiatrist/surgical department for further care.
3. Deformity/neuropathy/non-critical limb ischaemia → MODERATE RISK: refer to NCD clinic/podiatrist/surgical department for further review.
4. Callus alone → LOW RISK: total contact insole; foot care education; yearly screening.
5. Normal findings → foot care education; yearly screening.
*Risk categories as in the diabetic foot risk stratification table.

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Algorithm B: active foot problems
text:
### Diabetic foot algorithm B: management of active foot problems by ulcer type, infection and ischaemia (outpatient, oral antibiotics, multidisciplinary foot care team)

Active foot problems*:
- Without ulcer (UT grade 0): manage as outpatient by foot protection services.
- With ulcer:
  - Superficial (UT IA): manage as outpatient by foot protection services.
  - Infection:
    - Superficial ulcer not requiring surgical intervention (UT IB): oral antibiotics (outpatient, foot protection services).
    - Deep ulcer requiring surgical intervention (UT IIB/IIIB): refer to the multidisciplinary foot care team.
  - Ischaemia (pulses not palpable) (UT IC/IIC/IIIC): refer to the multidisciplinary foot care team.
  - Infection and ischaemia (UT ID/IID/IIID): refer to the multidisciplinary foot care team.
*Refer urgently for admission if the patient presents with general illness (e.g. sepsis or diabetic [emergency]).

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Screening > Tuning Fork Examination
text:
> **How to perform the 128 Hz tuning fork test for diabetic neuropathy**
>
> 1. Ask the patient to close his/her eyes.
> 2. Tap a 128 Hz tuning fork and place it on the patient's sternum to confirm vibration.
> 3. Tap the tuning fork and place it on a bony prominence of the foot (distal phalanx of the great toe).
> 4. Ask the patient to tell you when vibration is felt on the foot and when it stops.
> 5. If sensation is impaired, continue to assess more proximally (e.g. mid-dorsal foot, medial malleolus, mid-fibula, patella).
> 6. Repeat on the other leg.
> Note: any bony prominence of the foot can be tested, but the best point for the vibration test is the great toe.
html:
How to perform the 128 Hz tuning fork test for diabetic neuropathy

1. Ask the patient to close his/her eyes.

2. Tap a 128 Hz tuning fork and place it on the patient's sternum to confirm vibration.

3. Tap the tuning fork and place it on a bony prominence of the foot (distal phalanx of the great toe).

4. Ask the patient to tell you when vibration is felt on the foot and when it stops.

5. If sensation is impaired, continue to assess more proximally (e.g. mid-dorsal foot, medial malleolus, mid-fibula, patella).

6. Repeat on the other leg.

Note: any bony prominence of the foot can be tested, but the best point for the vibration test is the great toe.

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Key Steps in Diabetic Foot Ulcer (DFU) Management
text:
### Key steps in diabetic foot ulcer management: risk stratification, MDT, assessment, debridement, infection, moist healing, advanced therapies, offloading, metabolic control, monitoring, referral

1. Risk stratification (Wagner, UT, SINBAD).
2. Multidisciplinary team (endocrinology, podiatry, surgery, nursing, dietitian).
3. Comprehensive assessment (wound, vascular, neuropathy, labs).
4. Debridement (sharp, enzymatic, autolytic, etc.).
5. Infection management (antibiotics, osteomyelitis care).
6. Moist wound healing (appropriate dressings).
7. Advanced therapies (NPWT, skin substitutes, HBOT, PRP).
8. Offloading (total contact cast is the gold standard; walkers; footwear).
9. Glycaemic & metabolic control.
10. Monitoring & documentation (weekly to biweekly, photos).
11. Referral criteria (no healing, infection, ischaemia).
html:
1. Risk stratification (Wagner, UT, SINBAD).
2. Multidisciplinary team (endocrinology, podiatry, surgery, nursing, dietitian).

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Diabetic Foot > Off-Loading Techniques for DFUs
text:
### Off-loading techniques for diabetic foot ulcers: total contact cast, removable cast walkers, cushioned footwear, custom orthotics, wheelchair/bed rest: indications, advantages, disadvantages, care

Off-loading reduces chronic pressure on the ulcer (which prevents healing and can lead to tissue damage, infection and amputation), promotes healing (better blood flow, regulated inflammation, collagen formation), and lowers infection risk (less friction and moisture).

| Technique | Description | Indications | Advantages | Disadvantages | Care Considerations |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Total Contact Cast (TCC) | Cast that encompasses the foot & ankle, redistributing pressure | Moderate–severe plantar DFUs; no infection or significant ischaemia | Gold standard for off-loading; promotes wound healing; reduces recurrence & re-ulceration | Hard to monitor wound; skin maceration risk; fall/ambulation difficulty | Keep dry & intact; weekly reviews for skin breakdown or infection |
| Removable Cast Walkers (RCWs) / Braces | Custom-fitted, removable devices for off-loading | Mild–moderate DFUs, or if TCC not feasible | Allows wound inspection & hygiene; more comfortable & easier to use | Less effective than TCC; compliance issues if removed too often | Use with proper footwear; patient education on strict off-loading |
| Cushioned Footwear | Shoes with cushioned insoles, rocker soles, or extra depth | Mild DFUs; patients needing frequent ambulation | Comfortable & non-invasive; redistributes pressure, especially combined with other techniques | Not effective for moderate–severe ulcers; requires consistent use | Regular podiatry inspection & fitting |
| Custom Orthotics | Tailored insoles/orthotics to redistribute pressure | DFUs on forefoot or heel | Individualized to foot anatomy; less cumbersome than casts/walkers | Requires precise fitting; wear out & need replacement | Educate patients on maintenance; ensure proper shoe fit |
| Wheelchair / Bed Rest | Eliminates weight-bearing through immobilization | Severe DFUs, or with major vascular/neuropathic issues | Removes pressure completely; can combine with NPWT | Reduces mobility & quality of life; risk of pressure sores from immobility | Monitor skin, nutrition, and mental health closely |

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Peripheral Neuropathy > Guide to Clinical diagnosis of Peripheral Neuropathies
text:
### Peripheral neuropathy types: distal symmetric polyneuropathy, mononeuropathy, mononeuropathy multiplex, hereditary neuropathies: clinical features and common causes

Peripheral neuropathies are disorders of peripheral nerve cells and fibres affecting motor, sensory and autonomic fibres; classified as mononeuropathies, multifocal neuropathies and polyneuropathies, and as axonal, demyelinating or mixed.

| Type | Clinical Features | Common causes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distal Symmetric Polyneuropathy | Length-dependent: diffuse involvement affects distal segments first; symptoms occur below the knees before affecting the fingertips | Most common cause: diabetes. Chronic idiopathic axonal polyneuropathy, alcohol, chemotherapy induced |
| Mononeuropathy | Symptoms restricted to the distribution of a single nerve, myotome, or dermatome; asymmetric reflexes | Entrapment neuropathies, e.g. carpal tunnel, peroneal nerve entrapment; post-traumatic neuropathies; diabetes |
| Mononeuropathy multiplex | Occurrence of several concurrent mononeuropathies | Autoimmune vasculitis etiologies |
| Hereditary neuropathies | Distal calf atrophy, hammertoes, pes cavus; motor deficits ≥ sensory deficits; diffuse areflexia | Genetic diseases |

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Peripheral Neuropathy > Treatment of Neuropathic Pain in Diabetic Foot
text:
### Treatment of painful diabetic neuropathy (flowchart): first-line anticonvulsants or antidepressants, second-line SNRIs, opioid-like drugs, topicals, third-line SSRIs and opioids

Patient presenting with painful neuropathy → rule out other causes of neuropathy → establish treatment goals → optimise glycaemic control.
- First-line therapy: anticonvulsants (pregabalin, gabapentin) or antidepressants (TCAs and SNRIs: amitriptyline, duloxetine).
- Second-line therapy: SNRIs (venlafaxine or desvenlafaxine); opioid-like drugs (tramadol or tapentadol ER); topical treatments (lidocaine 5% patch or capsaicin 0.075% cream).
- Third-line therapy: SSRIs (citalopram or paroxetine or escitalopram); opioids (oxycodone controlled release).
ER = extended release; SNRI = serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; SSRI = selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor; TCA = tricyclic antidepressant. Adapted from Snyder MJ, Gibbs LM, Lindsay TJ. Treating Painful Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy: An Update. Am Fam Physician. 2016;94(3):227-34.

heading_path: Chapter 12: Podiatry > Peripheral Neuropathy > Medicines for painful diabetic neuropathy: doses
text:
### Medicines for painful diabetic neuropathy: SNRIs, opioid-like drugs, topicals, anticonvulsants, amitriptyline: doses, maximum doses and cautions

**Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors**

| Medicine | Usual dose | Maximum dose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Duloxetine | 60 mg daily or divided twice daily | 120 mg daily or divided twice daily |
| Venlafaxine | 150 mg daily | 225 mg daily |
| Desvenlafaxine | 200 mg daily | 400 mg daily |

**Notes (applies to every row in this section):** Side effects: nausea, vomiting, dry mouth, constipation, decreased appetite, insomnia, dizziness, somnolence, blurred vision, increased sweating and fatigue. Advise taking with food to reduce nausea

**Opioid-like medications**

| Medicine | Usual dose | Maximum dose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tramadol | 50 mg every 4 to 6 hours | 100 mg every 6 hours; maximum 400 mg daily | Lowers seizure threshold; avoid in epilepsy or at risk of seizures |
| Tapentadol ER | 100 mg twice daily | 250 mg twice daily | Lowers seizure threshold; avoid in epilepsy or at risk of seizures |

**Topical medications**

| Medicine | Usual dose | Maximum dose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lidocaine 5% patch | 1 patch daily | 3 patches daily |  |
| Capsaicin 0.075% cream | Four times daily | NA |  |
| Isosorbide dinitrate spray | 30 mg at bedtime applied to the bottom of the feet | NA |  |

**Anticonvulsants**

| Medicine | Usual dose | Maximum dose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pregabalin | 300 mg divided twice daily | 600 mg divided twice daily | Side effects: dizziness, sedation, GI symptoms and mild peripheral oedema. Use cautiously in heart failure and with thiazolidinediones (cases of decompensated heart failure reported); renal insufficiency (creatinine clearance ≤30 ml/min/1.73 m2) requires dose adjustment |
| Gabapentin | 1,200 mg divided three times daily | 3,600 mg divided three times daily | Side effects: dizziness, sedation, GI symptoms and mild peripheral oedema. Dose adjustment recommended in renal impairment |

**Tricyclic antidepressant**

| Medicine | Usual dose | Maximum dose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Amitriptyline | 25 mg daily at bedtime | 150 mg daily at bedtime or divided twice daily | Side effects: dry mouth, sedation, disturbed vision, arrhythmia, palpitations, postural hypotension, urinary retention and constipation. Contraindicated in cardiovascular disease (unstable angina, recent MI, heart failure, abnormal cardiac conduction) and glaucoma. Caution in elderly patients |

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Screening and Diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder
text:
> **Major depressive disorder: 8-step assessment, DSM-5/ICD-11 criteria (5 of 9 for 2+ weeks), severity classification and when to refer urgently**
>
> Assessment steps:
> 1. Screen: 'Have you felt sad/depressed most of the time for the past 2 weeks?' AND 'Have you lost interest in activities you usually enjoy?'
> 2. Assess core symptoms: 5 or more of 9 criteria present for 2+ weeks.
> 3. Assess functional impairment: work, relationships, self-care, daily activities.
> 4. RULE OUT: bipolar disorder (past mania?), psychosis, medical causes (hypothyroidism, anaemia, HIV, stroke, diabetes).
> 5. Screen for suicide/self-harm: 'Do you have thoughts of harming yourself or not wanting to live?'
> 6. Assess alcohol and substance use (may co-occur or cause symptoms).
> 7. Determine severity: mild / moderate / severe (any psychotic features?).
> 8. DIAGNOSIS confirmed if 5+ criteria are met, at least 1 being depressed mood or anhedonia.
> 
> DSM-5 / ICD-11 criteria (5 of 9, lasting 2+ weeks): depressed mood most of the day (or irritability in children/adolescents); markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia); significant weight loss/gain or appetite change; insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day; psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable by others); fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day; feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt; difficulty concentrating or making decisions; recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.
> 
> Severity: mild – few symptoms beyond the minimum, mild functional impairment; moderate – between mild and severe, moderate impairment; severe – most symptoms, marked impairment, may have psychotic features.
> 
> When to refer urgently: active suicidal ideation with plan or intent; psychotic features (hallucinations, delusions); severe self-neglect or inability to care for self; no response after 2 adequate medication trials; suspected bipolar disorder.

Assessment steps:

1. Screen: 'Have you felt sad/depressed most of the time for the past 2 weeks?' AND 'Have you lost interest in activities you usually enjoy?'

2. Assess core symptoms: 5 or more of 9 criteria present for 2+ weeks.

3. Assess functional impairment: work, relationships, self-care, daily activities.

4. RULE OUT: bipolar disorder (past mania?), psychosis, medical causes (hypothyroidism, anaemia, HIV, stroke, diabetes).

5. Screen for suicide/self-harm: 'Do you have thoughts of harming yourself or not wanting to live?'

6. Assess alcohol and substance use (may co-occur or cause symptoms).

7. Determine severity: mild / moderate / severe (any psychotic features?).

8. DIAGNOSIS confirmed if 5+ criteria are met, at least 1 being depressed mood or anhedonia.

DSM-5 / ICD-11 criteria (5 of 9, lasting 2+ weeks): depressed mood most of the day (or irritability in children/adolescents); markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia); significant weight loss/gain or appetite change; insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day; psychomotor agitation or retardation (observable by others); fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day; feelings of worthlessness or excessive/inappropriate guilt; difficulty concentrating or making decisions; recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation.

Severity: mild – few symptoms beyond the minimum, mild functional impairment; moderate – between mild and severe, moderate impairment; severe – most symptoms, marked impairment, may have psychotic features.

When to refer urgently: active suicidal ideation with plan or intent; psychotic features (hallucinations, delusions); severe self-neglect or inability to care for self; no response after 2 adequate medication trials; suspected bipolar disorder.

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Depression Management – Pharmacological Treatment
text:
### Antidepressants for moderate-severe depression: fluoxetine, amitriptyline, imipramine, sertraline, escitalopram: starting and usual doses and notes; psychoeducation and cautions

Consider antidepressants for moderate-severe depression. Discuss with the person: not addictive; takes 2-4 weeks for effect; must be taken for 9-12 months minimum after remission.

| Drug | Starting Dose | Usual Dose | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fluoxetine (SSRI) | 10-20 mg mane | 20-60 mg/day | First-line; only SSRI recommended for adolescents ≥12 yrs; avoid with MAOIs |
| Amitriptyline (TCA) | 25-50 mg nocte | 75-150 mg/day | Effective; caution in cardiac disease, elderly, overdose risk |
| Imipramine (TCA) | 25-50 mg nocte | 75-200 mg/day | Alternative TCA; monitor ECG if cardiac risk present |
| Sertraline (SSRI) | 25-50 mg/day | 50-200 mg/day | Good tolerability; preferred in elderly and cardiac disease |
| Escitalopram (SSRI) | 5-10 mg/day | 10-20 mg/day | Well tolerated; fewer drug interactions; good for elderly |

**Note:** Psychoeducation & psychosocial interventions: depression is very common and NOT a sign of weakness or laziness; negative thoughts about self, world and future are symptoms, not reality; encourage regular activity, social engagement and pleasurable activities, regular sleep/wake times and meals; Problem Management Plus (PM+, WHO behavioural activation + problem solving); group interpersonal therapy (IPT); Thinking Healthy (CBT approach for perinatal depression); medications are NOT addictive (9-12 month course); never stop antidepressants abruptly – taper gradually. Cautions & special populations: if a manic episode occurs STOP the antidepressant immediately (may be bipolar disorder); do not combine antidepressants (serotonin syndrome); SSRIs may increase suicidal ideation in adolescents/young adults – weekly monitoring for the first 4 weeks; pregnancy: avoid if possible, if severe use the lowest effective dose with specialist input; breastfeeding: fluoxetine and sertraline generally safer; elderly: start low, go slow, monitor for falls and hyponatraemia (SSRIs); epilepsy: avoid tricyclics (lower seizure threshold).

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Suicide Risk Assessment and Follow-up
text:
> **Depression: suicide risk assessment (mandatory), risk-level actions, follow-up schedule and PHQ-9 rescreening**
>
> SUICIDE RISK ASSESSMENT – mandatory in all depression cases. Ask directly: 'Are you having thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?' If YES, assess: plan? method? intent? previous attempts? access to means (medications, weapons)?
> - HIGH RISK: hospitalise / urgent referral; remove access to lethal means immediately.
> - MEDIUM RISK: safety plan; close follow-up within 2-3 days; involve a trusted person/carer.
> - ALL risk levels: do not leave alone; mobilise social support; document the safety plan.
> 
> FOLLOW-UP – depression (2 weeks initially, then monthly, then every 3 months):
> - Weeks 2-4: assess side effects and suicidal ideation (especially adolescents on SSRIs).
> - Weeks 4-6: has mood/interest improved? If no response, increase the dose or switch medication.
> - Weeks 8-12: full remission expected; reinforce adherence for the full course (9-12 months minimum).
> - After 9-12 months symptom-free: discuss gradual tapering over weeks to months.
> - 3+ recurrent episodes: consider long-term maintenance therapy.
> - Screen for re-emergence of symptoms at every follow-up after stopping treatment.
> 
> PHQ-9 can be used for screening and follow-up: clients scoring 0-9 are rescreened every 6 months; those scoring 10 and above are reassessed 2 weeks after the initial visit and then at every follow-up visit.
html:
Depression: suicide risk assessment (mandatory), risk-level actions, follow-up schedule and PHQ-9 rescreening

SUICIDE RISK ASSESSMENT – mandatory in all depression cases. Ask directly: 'Are you having thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?' If YES, assess: plan? method? intent? previous attempts? access to means (medications, weapons)?

- HIGH RISK: hospitalise / urgent referral; remove access to lethal means immediately.

- MEDIUM RISK: safety plan; close follow-up within 2-3 days; involve a trusted person/carer.

- ALL risk levels: do not leave alone; mobilise social support; document the safety plan.

FOLLOW-UP – depression (2 weeks initially, then monthly, then every 3 months):

- Weeks 2-4: assess side effects and suicidal ideation (especially adolescents on SSRIs).

- Weeks 4-6: has mood/interest improved? If no response, increase the dose or switch medication.

- Weeks 8-12: full remission expected; reinforce adherence for the full course (9-12 months minimum).

- After 9-12 months symptom-free: discuss gradual tapering over weeks to months.

- 3+ recurrent episodes: consider long-term maintenance therapy.

- Screen for re-emergence of symptoms at every follow-up after stopping treatment.

PHQ-9 can be used for screening and follow-up: clients scoring 0-9 are rescreened every 6 months; those scoring 10 and above are reassessed 2 weeks after the initial visit and then at every follow-up visit.

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Pharmacological Management of Major Depressive Disorder
text:
### Pharmacological management of major depressive disorder by line: TCA and SSRIs (1st), duloxetine (2nd), valproate and flunarizine (3rd), lorazepam for insomnia, antipsychotics (haloperidol, sulpiride, aripiprazole; risperidone, olanzapine 2nd line) for psychotic depression

General prescribing rules: 1. prescribe one antidepressant or antipsychotic at a time; 2. consider second line after the maximum dose for at least 8 weeks without significant improvement; 3. do not prescribe anti-muscarinics routinely; manage side effects.

| Line | Class | Drug | Dosage and frequency | Contraindications |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1st line | Tricyclic antidepressants | Amitriptyline | Initial dose 25 mg PO nocte for 3 days then 50 mg PO nocte. Maximum dose 200 mg/24 hrs | Urine retention, constipation, arrhythmia |
| 1st line | Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors | Fluoxetine | Initial dose 10-20 mg PO nocte. Maximum dose 60-80 mg/24 hours | Use with caution: bipolar disorder in a manic phase (may be useful for depressive phases); bleeding disorders such as haemophilia; type 1 or type 2 diabetes |
| 1st line | Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors | Sertraline | Initial dose 25-50 mg PO nocte. Maximum dose 200 mg/24 hours | Use with caution: bipolar disorder in a manic phase (may be useful for depressive phases); bleeding disorders such as haemophilia; type 1 or type 2 diabetes |
| 2nd line | Serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor | Duloxetine | Initial dose 30 mg PO nocte | Urolithiasis, AGE (as printed), cognitive dysfunction |
| 3rd line | Anticonvulsant | Sodium valproate | 200 mg twice a day | Pregnancy, hepatic impairment |
| 3rd line | Calcium-channel blocker | Flunarizine | 5 mg nocte | Depression; constipation |

**PLUS sedatives if insomnia (MDD with insomnia)**

| Line | Class | Drug | Dosage and frequency | Contraindications |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sedative for insomnia | Benzodiazepine | Lorazepam PO | 1-2 mg nocte for 7 days | Myasthenia gravis, sleep apnoea, bronchitis, and COPD |

**PLUS antipsychotics if psychotic symptoms (MDD with psychosis)**

| Line | Class | Drug | Dosage and frequency | Contraindications |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1st line | Typical antipsychotic | Haloperidol | Initial dose 1.5-3 mg PO nocte. Maximum dose 20 mg/24 hours | Previous acute stroke or coma; severe intoxication with alcohol or other CNS depressants; allergy to haloperidol or other butyrophenones; heart disease |
|  | Selective D2 dopamine receptor antagonist | Sulpiride | Initial dose 50 mg PO nocte. Maximum dose 200 mg/24 hours | Hypersensitivity to sulpiride; pre-existing breast cancer or other prolactin-dependent tumours; phaeochromocytoma; intoxication with other centrally-active drugs; concomitant levodopa; acute porphyria; comatose state or CNS depression; bone-marrow suppression |

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Major Depressive Disorder > Special cases
text:
### Major depressive disorder special cases: children under 12, pregnancy and breastfeeding, psychotic depression, bipolar depression, emerging mania, PLHIV drug interactions

| Special Case | Intervention |
| --- | --- |
| If younger than 12 years | No antidepressants; provide counselling then refer |
| Pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers | Antidepressants should be avoided as far as possible, then refer |
| Depression with psychotic symptoms | Prescribe antidepressants + antipsychotics |
| BAD (bipolar affective disorder), depressive phase | Prescribe mood stabilizer + antidepressant + antipsychotic |
| If symptoms of mania emerge during treatment of depression | Immediately stop antidepressants and refer |
| PLHIV | Nevirapine may decrease the level of fluoxetine; ritonavir increases levels of amitriptyline and fluoxetine; darunavir decreases the level of sertraline; fluvoxamine increases levels of PIs and NNRTIs; carbamazepine is contraindicated as it increases levels of PIs and NNRTIs (as printed) |

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Substance Use Disorder > Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome
text:
### Alcohol withdrawal syndrome: benzodiazepine (lorazepam) dosing, PAWSS and CIWA-Ar/SAWS assessment, outpatient vs inpatient

Alcohol withdrawal starts 4-12 hours after the last drink (anxiety, agitation, tremor, sympathetic activation; severe: seizures and delirium tremens, potentially fatal); symptoms may last up to 5 days. Mild to moderate withdrawal can be managed as an outpatient in primary care with benzodiazepines; severe withdrawal or complicating conditions need inpatient management. Use the PAWSS to predict severe withdrawal (score <4 = low risk, suitable for outpatient care).

| Class | Drug | Dosage and Frequency | Contraindications |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sedatives for insomnia: benzodiazepine | Lorazepam PO | 1-2 mg nocte for 7 days | Myasthenia gravis, sleep apnoea, bronchitis, and COPD |

**Note:** Where withdrawal symptoms are present, assess severity with a validated instrument: the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, Revised (CIWA-Ar), or the self-completed 10-item Short Alcohol Withdrawal Scale (SAWS).

text:
### Medicines for alcohol dependence: acamprosate, naltrexone (oral and XR injectable), disulfiram, gabapentin, topiramate: doses and contraindications

Alcohol dependence: three main classes of drugs are recommended: (i) organosulfonic acids, (ii) opiate antagonists, (iii) alcohol antagonists.

| Line | Class | Drug | Dosage and Frequency | Contraindications / Cautions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1st line | Organosulfonic acids | Acamprosate | Weight <60 kg: 666 mg once daily at breakfast and 333 mg twice daily at midday and night (maximum 1332 mg). Adults >60 kg: 666 mg TID. Start as soon as the patient has abstained from alcohol, within 7 days | Do not prescribe if CrCl <30 mL/min or eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2. Hypersensitivity to the active substance or excipients. Breast-feeding women |
| 1st line | Opiate antagonists (recommend XR naltrexone if adherence to oral is a concern; start naltrexone even if patients continue to use alcohol) | Naltrexone oral | Initial dose 25 mg OD; increase to 50 mg per day over about 1 week. Maintenance 50 mg once daily; if adverse events, consider 25 mg once daily. Maximum 100 mg daily | Absolute contraindication: acute hepatitis or liver failure; taking opioid analgesics; currently physically dependent on opioids, including those maintained on opioid agonists (e.g. methadone) or partial agonists (e.g. buprenorphine); acute opioid withdrawal |
| 1st line | Opiate antagonists (recommend XR naltrexone if adherence to oral is a concern; start naltrexone even if patients continue to use alcohol) | XR naltrexone, long-acting injectable | Initial: oral naltrexone 50 mg once daily for at least 3 days. Maintenance: 380 mg intragluteal injection every 28 days | Absolute contraindication: acute hepatitis or liver failure; taking opioid analgesics; currently physically dependent on opioids, including those maintained on opioid agonists (e.g. methadone) or partial agonists (e.g. buprenorphine); acute opioid withdrawal |
| 2nd line | Alcohol antagonists | Disulfiram | 500 mg once daily for 1 to 2 weeks, then 250 mg once daily. Maintenance 250 mg once a day (range 125-500 mg). Maximum 500 mg once a day | Absolute contraindication: recent or concomitant metronidazole, paraldehyde, alcohol or alcohol-containing preparations (e.g. cough syrups, tonics); coronary artery disease; recent myocardial infarction; psychoses; acute hepatitis or acute liver failure |
| 3rd line | Anticonvulsants (not FDA approved but found beneficial) | Gabapentin | Initial 300 mg once daily; increase by 300 mg every 1 to 2 days by response and tolerability. Maintenance individualised, generally in 3 divided doses, up to 2,400 mg or 3,600 mg per day | Caution: gabapentin can be misused for its psychoactive effect, alone or with opioids, benzodiazepines and alcohol |
| 3rd line | Anticonvulsants (not FDA approved but found beneficial) | Topiramate | Initial 25 mg once daily; increase by 50 mg each week to a maximum of 400 mg daily in 2 divided doses. Maintenance 200-400 mg daily in 2 doses. Moderate-to-severe renal impairment: 50% dose reduction | Halve the dose in adults with CrCl ≤70 mL/min or eGFR ≤70 mL/min/1.73 m2 |

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Anxiety Disorders > Pharmacological Management of Generalized Anxiety Disorder
text:
### Generalized anxiety disorder medicines: SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline) first line, plus lorazepam if insomnia

Generalized anxiety disorder responds better to psychotherapy and low-dose SSRIs. Prescribing rules: one antidepressant at a time; do not prescribe anti-muscarinics routinely, manage side effects.

| Line | Class | Drug | Dosage and Frequency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1st line | Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors | Fluoxetine | Initial dose 10-20 mg PO nocte. Maximum dose 60-80 mg/24 hours |
| 1st line | Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors | Sertraline | Initial dose 25 mg PO nocte. Maximum dose 200 mg/24 hours |

**Contraindications (applies to every row):** Use with caution: bipolar disorder in a manic phase (may be useful for depressive phases); bleeding disorders such as haemophilia; type 1 or type 2 diabetes

**PLUS a sedative with anxiolytic effect if insomnia is a presenting symptom (GAD with insomnia)**

| Line | Class | Drug | Dosage and Frequency | Contraindications |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sedative for insomnia | Benzodiazepine | Lorazepam PO | 1-2 mg nocte for 7 days | Myasthenia gravis, sleep apnoea, bronchitis, and COPD |

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Suicide > Warning Signs of Suicidal Behaviour
text:
> **Warning signs of suicidal behaviour**
>
> Warning signs to look out for: feeling like a burden; being isolated; increased anxiety; talking about feeling trapped or in unbearable pain; increased substance use; looking for a way to access lethal means; increased anger or rage; extreme mood swings; expressing hopelessness and having no reason to live; sleeping too little or too much; talking or posting about wanting to die or to kill oneself; making plans for suicide; giving away prized possessions; showing rage or talking about seeking revenge; suddenly coming out of being hopeless; not wanting to complete projects one has started.

heading_path: Chapter 13: Psychiatry > Suicide > Diagnostic Features of Suicidal Behaviour
text:
> **Diagnostic features of suicidal behaviour disorder (DSM-5)**
>
> a. The act: 1. has been attempted within the last 24 months; 2. does not meet criteria for non-suicidal self-injury (self-injury to produce a positive mood); 3. is not applied to suicidal ideation or preparatory acts; 4. was not initiated during a state of delirium or confusion; 5. was not undertaken solely for a political or religious objective.
> b. The behaviour or its consequences cause clinically significant distress or interference in interpersonal, academic, or other important areas of functioning.
> c. The behaviour does not occur exclusively during psychotic episodes, delirium, substance intoxication, or substance withdrawal.
html:
Diagnostic features of suicidal behaviour disorder (DSM-5)

a. The act: 1. has been attempted within the last 24 months; 2. does not meet criteria for non-suicidal self-injury (self-injury to produce a positive mood); 3. is not applied to suicidal ideation or preparatory acts; 4. was not initiated during a state of delirium or confusion; 5. was not undertaken solely for a political or religious objective.

b. The behaviour or its consequences cause clinically significant distress or interference in interpersonal, academic, or other important areas of functioning.

c. The behaviour does not occur exclusively during psychotic episodes, delirium, substance intoxication, or substance withdrawal.

c. The behaviour does not occur exclusively during psychotic episodes, delirium, substance intoxication, or substance withdrawal.
